text:
EN
EN
EUROPEAN
COMMISSION
Brussels, 21.1.2026
SWD(2026) 4 final
COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT
Accompanying the documents
Commission Delegated Regulation amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1172
with regard to the integrated administration and control system in the common
agricultural policy
Commission Implementing Regulation amending Implementing Regulation (EU)
2022/1173 laying down rules for the application of Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 of the
European Parliament and of the Council with regard to the integrated
administration and control system in the common agricultural policy
Commission Implementing Regulation amending Implementing Regulation (EU)
2022/128 as regards the annual performance clearance, the multi-annual
performance monitoring and the scrutiny of transactions
Commission Delegated Regulation amending Regulation (EU) 2022/126
supplementing Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 of the European Parliament and of the
Council with additional requirements for certain types of intervention specified by
Member States in their CAP Strategic Plans for the period 2023 to 2027 and under
Regulation as well as rules on the ratio for the good agricultural and environmental
conditions (GAEC) standard 1
{C(2026) 281 final} - {C(2026) 283 final} - {C(2026) 267 final} - {C(2026) 371 final}
1
1. INTRODUCTION
On 19 February 2025, the Commission adopted ‘A Vision for Agriculture and Food’1 setting
out a pathway for the EU actions towards achieving an attractive, competitive, resilient, future-
oriented and fair agri-food system for current and future generations of farmers and agri-food
operators. The Vision called for unnecessary bureaucratic and regulatory burden to be reduced,
a key step to support the competitiveness of the farming sector and of the entire agri-food value
chain, including a more streamlined and strategic implementation of the Common Agricultural
Policy (CAP).
On 14 May 2025, drawing on and responding to extensive feedback from stakeholders, the
Commission proposed a comprehensive simplification package of the basic legislation
underpinning the current CAP (2023-2027), that is the CAP Strategic Plan and the
Horizontal Regulations2. This package3 delivers in the following areas: (i) on-farm
simplification and streamlining of requirements to better adjust to different situations and to
various farming practices; (ii) streamlining support for smaller and medium-sized farms; (iii)
providing measures that can help boost competitiveness; and (iv) increasing Member States’
flexibility in managing CAP strategic plans (CAP Plans). With modifications, the proposal was
adopted by the co-legislators and then published on 31 December 20254.
This proposal was accompanied by a staff working document, documenting the stakeholders’
feedback and assessing impacts of the proposed changes on administrative costs borne by
farmers and national administrations5.
At the time, the Commission also published a roadmap6 to deliver additional improvements
via the CAP’s secondary legislation.
This staff working document (Section 2) provides an assessment of impacts on administrative
costs resulting from simplification of the following:
• Commission Delegated Regulation amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1172
concerning the integrated administration and control system (IACS) as regards the
scope of the quality assessments of the geo-spatial application system and of the area
monitoring system (changes to Articles 4 and 5 of this Delegated Regulation);
• Commission Implementing Regulation amending Implementing Regulation (EU)
2022/1173 concerning the integrated administration and CAP control system as
1 Commission Communication ‘A Vision for Agriculture and Food Shaping together an attractive farming and
agri-food sector for future generations’, COM (2025) 75 final
2 Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 and Regulation (EU) 2021/2116, respectively
3 COM(2025) 236 final
4 Regulation (EU) 2025/2649 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 December 2025 amending
Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 as regards the conditionality system, types of intervention in the form of direct
payment, types of intervention in certain sectors and rural development and annual performance reports and
Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 as regards suspensions of payments, annual performance clearance and controls
and penalties (OJ L, 2025/2649, 31.12.2025, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/2649/oj).
5 SWD(2025) 236 final
6 Roadmap for simplifying the CAP legal framework to reduce burden on farmers and national administrations
2
regards the obligation to record the use of plant protection products in the geo-spatial
aid application (change to Article 8(3)(f) of this Implementing Regulation);
• Commission Implementing Regulation amending Implementing Regulation (EU)
2022/128 as regards the scrutiny of transactions (change to Article 46 of this
Implementing Regulation);
• Commission delegated Regulation amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/126 as
regards approval of operational programmes of transnational (associations of) producer
organisations, market withdrawals, rules on marketing standards, and minimum control
rate for hemp cultivation (changes of Articles 2, 22, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 32a, 33 and 48
and Annexes I, V and VII).
Where data for estimates was available, the impacts were quantified, otherwise the document
provides a qualitative appreciation of burden reduction7. The available figures are summarised
in the annex to this document.
This document does not cover other adjustments of the secondary legislation that solely
translate the simplifications pursued in the underlying basic act, and which were already
assessed in the above-mentioned staff working document.
2. SIMPLIFICATION MEASURES AND THEIR IMPACT ON ADMINISTRATIVE
COSTS
2.1. Amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1172 as regards the scope of the
quality assessments of the geo-spatial application (GSA) system and of the area
monitoring system (AMS)
The main IACS components, including GSA and AMS, are subject to an annual quality
assessment to evaluate if the IACS is achieving its aims, and to improve how it works (as
regards the correct number of hectares for the CAP´s output and result indicators)8.
The amendment introduces the following changes:
• Limiting the scope of AMS and GSA quality assessment only to monitorable
eligibility conditions, which will make it possible to simplify further the Union-level
methodology (ULM) for IACS quality assessment and considerably reduce the
necessity of field visits.
Impact on national administrations
A quantification of the impact of this change relies on the provisional information provided by
all Member States as they report their IACS quality assessments’ results in QUAP portal
(Quality Assessment Platform):
• Number of eligibility conditions for area-based interventions under the current CAP
Plans:
7 Quantification is based on many assumptions and should be viewed as such. Isolating specific administrative
costs is also difficult and limited availability of data impedes the robustness of the calculations.
8 For further information and previous improvements of this framework, see SWD(2024) 360 final of 10.12.2024
3
Overall, Member States reported 6 500 eligibility conditions. This represents an
average of 233 eligibility conditions per Member State (across 28 CAP Plans), but with
differences among them depending on the design of the interventions done by each
Member State (for instance, ten Member States have more than 300 eligibility
conditions, while eleven Member States have fewer than 150). This figure provides a
comparative insight into the design of the interventions, that can also ultimately
illustrate the greater or lesser burden of requirements that have been set.
• Rate of monitorable and non-monitorable eligibility conditions in the current design of
CAP Plans:
Overall, 54% of the reported eligibility conditions can be considered monitorable,
including administrative checks (carried out for all claimed parcels, and therefore in
line with monitoring principles applied in AMS). In contrast, 46% were reported as
non-monitorable, requiring field visits or requesting specific documentation,
performed on a sample of the population of claimed parcels. There is also a significant
variability among Member States: nine countries have more than 90% of their
eligibility conditions monitorable (four of them 100%), and three have less than 10%
of monitorable eligibility conditions. This figure is crucial, since it allows a more
accurate estimation of the intensity in the implementation of AMS.
Number of claimed parcels with at least one non-monitorable eligibility condition:
Based on the figures reported by all Member States, the number of parcels in the
samples of IACS quality assessments is around 120 000. Those which have at least one
non-monitorable eligibility condition requiring a field visit, or a similar task in terms
of workload, amount to more than 77 600 (65%). This figure of 77 600 parcels
represents the maximum workload that could be saved by public administrations.
Whenever the quality assessment sample is already part of the ‘on-the-spot checks’
sample, the workload reduction is limited. However, a certain share of the monitored
population of parcels would need field visits for the quality assessment exercise in case
the result is not conclusive (i.e. cloud cover, very small parcels). An estimation between
15-20% of field visits in monitored parcels should represent a conservative share,
according to the current capabilities of the available technology. In previous years,
between 84 000 and 86 000 parcels had field visits (77 600 + [15%/20%]*42 400),
while for claim year 2026 only 18 000 to 20 000 would need to be visited. This leads
to a final estimation of savings between 64 000 and 68 000 parcels not having to be
inspected on the field.
• Saving of costs in the IACS quality assessment exercise:
Taking the previous element into consideration, the savings could vary for each
Member State from EUR 11 000 to EUR 540 000 depending on the number of non-
monitorable eligibility conditions that are concerned. An estimation of around EUR 60
per parcel inspected (or similar task), is considered, according to the field inspections
daily gross cost of EUR 250 and an average rate of 4-5 parcels visited per day due to
the scattered location of the parcels that are part of the quality assessment samples.
4
This represents a saving of EUR 3.7-4 million (i.e. an average of EUR 3.85 million)
at EU level when this simplification enters into force for claim year 2026, which
corresponds to more than 50% of the costs of performing IACS quality assessment in
the previous years.
Impact on farmers
These changes will reduce significantly the number of on-farm visits that national authorities
need to make to perform the annual IACS quality assessment. It is currently estimated that
more than 21 000 farmers are involved in the assessment of non-monitorable eligibility
conditions every year, in the IACS quality assessment exercise, at EU level. Consequently,
these farmers will have more time to dedicate to their own work, as they will spend less time
dealing with on-farm visits by national authorities. Note that, for those interventions where the
eligibility conditions are fully monitorable, no further on-the-spot checks are needed under the
proposed system.
Overall, the proposed simplifications, combined with the full implementation of the AMS,
would reduce stress factors for farmers as a well-functioning IACS system allows farmers to
participate in CAP interventions in an efficient manner, reducing the likelihood of sanctions,
and receiving financial support in an accurate and timely manner.
The main objective of the amendment is to focus the quality assessment of the area monitoring
system and the geo-spatial application only on monitorable eligibility conditions, which are
defined in Article 10(3) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1173. This will
allow the alignment of the quality assessment exercise with the scope of the area monitoring
system. The main practical impact will be the reduction of the number of farm visits and the
burden for farmers in the context of the quality assessment exercise. However, as for the
information referring to the non-monitorable eligibility conditions, it will be based on the
results of the control systems implemented by the Member States. Therefore, the proposed
amendments do not impact the original policy objectives.
2.2. Amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1173 as regards the obligation to
record the use of plant protection products in the geo-spatial aid application
(GSA)
The amendment introduces the following changes:
• Deletion of the obligation that the GSA shall contain, where relevant, information
on the use of plant protection products for parcels under interventions for sustainable
and reduced use of pesticides under eco-schemes and environmental, climate-related
and other management commitments9.
Impact on national administrations
9 Articles 31 and 70 of the Regulation (EU) 2021/2115, respectively
5
The fact that the registration of plant protection products in the GSA will no longer be
mandatory will provide Member States with greater flexibility to manage their own systems,
ultimately leading to a reduction of costs since there will be no need to develop and maintain
a dedicated Information and Technologies system to manage those registries. However, these
cost reductions for national administration are not possible to quantify since it depends on the
approach taken by each Member State.
The proposed amendment does not preclude Member States from implementing that obligation
where they consider it appropriate. It should be remembered that the requirement of record-
keeping of plant protection products is necessary as laid down in the Regulation concerning
the placing of plant protection products on the market10.
Impact on farmers
The deletion of the obligation to record the use of plant protection products in the GSA is
expected to reduce the burden for farmers regarding the time spent performing this task and
allows more time to be spent on farm management or other tasks of the farmer’s choosing.
As mentioned in the Commission staff working document SWD(2025) 236, based on the
results of the simplification study, farmers spend an average of 56 hours11 annually on preparing
and submitting CAP aid applications, of which 9.6% is spent on administrative tasks related to
conditionality and 56% of that time for other elements of aid application(s) (the remainder
being recording and reporting).
Taking into consideration the above, it can be estimated that there will be a reduction by 20%12
of the overall workload for farmers for recording and reporting tasks when preparing and
submitting CAP aid applications due to the deletion of the obligation to record the use of plant
protection products, that would correspond, on average, to 4 hours per concerned GSA. In case
of use of external advisory services, due to their technical expertise, it can be estimated a
reduction on average, of 2 hours per concerned GSA.
In case of internal costs (administrative tasks performed by the beneficiary), each hour of work
is estimated to correspond to EUR 11.2513. In case of the use of external advisory services, a
sum of EUR 32.7014 per hour can be assumed as the cost incurred by a beneficiary for the tasks
10 Article 67(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009
11 According to ‘Study on simplification and administrative burden for farmers and other beneficiaries under the
CAP’ farmers taking part in the European Commission targeted consultation on simplification of 2024 declared
to spend an average of seven working days annually on administrative tasks
12 Based on expert judgment
13 According to ‘Study on simplification and administrative burden for farmers and other beneficiaries under the
CAP’ farmers incur an estimated average annual cost of EUR 630 attributed to internal costs (e.g. working days
spent on administrative tasks) (an additional amount of EUR 600 corresponds to external advisory services,
totalling an estimated average annual cost of EUR 1 230 due to administrative burden arising from 2023-2027
CAP for farmers and other CAP beneficiaries)
14 Based on ‘Eurostat Structure of earnings survey, Labour Force Survey data for Non-Wage Labour Costs’
(update of 14.3.2025)
6
related to recording and reporting plant protection products under the preparation and
submission of a GSA.
The estimated number of beneficiaries, benefitting from the deletion of the requirement to
report information on the use of plant protection products for parcels under interventions for
sustainable and reduced use of pesticides is around 3.5 million for financial year 2024 (claim
year 2023). These include beneficiaries under eco-schemes (2.8 million) and environmental,
climate-related and other management commitments (730 000). Taking these figures into
account and the fact that 78%15 of EU farmers use paid external support for aid-related
administrative tasks, this results in estimated savings up to EUR 215 million annually for
these farmers in all Member States.
The objective of the amendment is to avoid reporting the same piece of data more than once
and, therefore, does not impact the original policy objectives.
2.3. Amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/128 as regards the scrutiny of
transactions
Scrutiny of transactions under the CAP refers to the process of checking the validity of
transactions through financial records of beneficiaries (undertakings) as regards market
measures and sectoral interventions to ascertain whether transactions financed under the CAP
have actually been carried out and have been correctly executed. Member States need to
appoint a special service in the administration that performs this task and has the right to access
commercial documents and carry out checks in third countries as well.
The amendment entails the following:
• Simplified process for scrutiny of transactions conducted by the special service
appointed for scrutiny in the Member States.
The purpose of the change is to strike the right balance between the current relevance of
scrutiny of transactions considering the substantial evolution of the management and control
system of the CAP in the last 20 years and the resources that need to be deployed by Member
States for this specific ex-post control annually in all Member States16. The simplification
entails allowing Member States to select the sample of transactions based on a risk analysis
rather than establish a sample based on a minimum coverage.
Impacts of simplification concerning scrutiny of transactions
Currently, around 1 150 controls are carried out annually. The costs of controls may vary
depending on whether it involves checking third country undertakings on the spot or not. For
national administrations, the simplification is estimated to reduce by half the controls carried
out, but the cost savings cannot be quantified. Depending on the type of the control, this can
15 According to the aforementioned ‘Study on simplification and administrative burden for farmers and other
beneficiaries under the CAP’
16 selected on the basis of Article 46 (1)(2) and (3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/128
7
bring benefits to CAP beneficiaries by reducing the time and cost entailed in attending a
control or providing additional information.
The proposed changes do not compromise the original policy objectives, as Member States
should have an efficient management and control system in place as per Article 59 of
Regulation (EU) 2021/2116. Furthermore, following Annex I of Regulation (EU) 2022/127
Member States should define the control system based on a risk analysis, which allows efficient
use of resources in performing the necessary controls addressing the most relevant risks. This
should in general cover the ex-spot controls as well, if considered necessary based on the risk
analysis.
Thus, in fact the proposed changes would align the requirements for scrutiny of transactions
with the general conditions set out for the overall management and control system of a Member
State.
2.4. Amending delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/126 as regards approval of
operational
programmes
of
transnational
(associations
of)
producer
organisations, market withdrawals, rules on marketing standards, and minimum
control rate for hemp cultivation
The draft amendments to this act fall into two categories:
• Amendments that solely translate simplification changes to the underlying basic acts
(CAP Strategic Plan Regulation 2021/2015 and Horizontal Regulation 2021/2016, the
“Omnibus III” proposal). These amendments do not entail any additional cost
reductions and are thus not included in this assessment. The effects of these changes
have already been assessed in a staff working document accompanying the Omnibus
III proposal17.
• Modifications that introduce additional simplification are listed and assessed in terms of
reducing administrative burden in section 2 below. Where data for estimates was
available, the impacts were quantified, otherwise the document provides a qualitative
appreciation of burden reduction18. The available figures are summarised in the annex.
The amendment introduces the following changes:
• Specification that approval of the operational programmes of transnational
(associations of) producer organisations, financed under the CAP sectoral
interventions, takes place in the Member States where these organisations have their
head offices.
• Removal of various prescriptive rules in relation to market withdrawals in sectoral
interventions managed by producer organisations implementing approved operational
17 SWD(2025) 236 final
18 Quantification is based on many assumptions and should be viewed as such. Isolating specific administrative
costs is also difficult and limited availability of data impedes the robustness of the calculations.
8
programmes (e.g. fruit and vegetable sector) financed under the sectoral CAP support
for sectors, inclusion of the transport and conditioning costs in the calculation of the
Union compensation, removal of the condition relating to the share of market
withdrawals, removal of obligations relating to documentation on the side of producers
and recipients.
• Reduction of rules on marketing standards applying to withdrawn products
• Reduction of minimum control rate for hemp cultivation supported under CAP
Plans, and more flexibility for the eligibility of hemp varieties newly registered.
Impact of simplification concerning CAP support for transnational (associations of)
Producer Organisations
Of more than 1 600 (associations of) producer organisations recognised in the EU, 45 - all in
the fruit and vegetable sector - have members located in another/other Member State. Member
State where the head offices of these transnational organisations are located are responsible for
their recognition and administrative cooperation with other Member State(s), including on
controls. The simplification clarifies responsibilities of the Member States where head offices
are located by establishing that they are also responsible for approval of the operational
programmes of these organisations.
For producer organisations, the change reduces the uncertainty as regards expenditure,
administrative management and controls of the operational programmes. By avoiding
(potential) redundancies, it results in reduced paperwork linked to potentially multiple approval
procedures in different countries and multiple controls of transnational (associations of)
producer organisations. From national administrations’ perspective, this avoids also
redundant controls carried out by several Member States.
Impact of simplification concerning CAP support when it comes to market withdrawals
In case of market disturbance situations (e.g. oversupply), recognised producer organisations
implementing operational programmes may take the decision to withdraw part of their
production from the market. There are two types of market withdrawals, for free distribution
and for other destinations (e.g. compost, industry) and the support granted to those
organisations is based on different calculation methods (e.g. depends on the market withdrawal
type, on the products, transport and conditioning costs). The Union financial assistance of 50%
of the actual expenditure incurred is increased to 100% for market withdrawals for free
distribution of fruit and vegetables provided the withdrawn volume does not exceed 5% of the
volume marketed by the producer organisation. In all other cases, the Union financial assistance
is limited to 50%. The market withdrawals in the fruit and vegetables sector amounted to
EUR 28.3 million for both free distribution and other destinations. This represents less than 1%
of the total expenditure eligible for support in this sector.
This simplification provides the following: a simplified calculation method to compensate
production costs by organisations implementing market withdrawals, and a reduction of
administrative tasks for both producer organisations and managing authorities.
9
For producer organisations, the removal of this obligation results in:
• lower administrative burden stemming from: (i) not being subject anymore to the
presentation of supporting documents, not limited to a certain type of packages, (ii) no
more requirements on the recipients, (iii) simpler marketing standards to be complied
with.
• a simplified financial support, by (i) removing the Union conditioning costs; the costs
being calculated by Member States as transport costs; (ii) including the transport and
conditioning costs in the maximum Union compensation and increasing fixing at 90%
the percentage for compensation (since conditioning costs are now including in the
amount of compensation), and (iii) removing the limit of 10% of volume withdrawn
(not foreseen in the basic act)..
For national administrations, besides eliminating administrative costs linked to maintaining
records or checking documentation, standardisation of the calculation methods for the support
will help increase the efficiency and consistency in managing the support.
Impact of simplification concerning the minimum control rate for hemp
CAP support can be granted also when farmers cultivate hemp, provided the varieties used
have a tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) content not exceeding 0.3%. Therefore, the farmers have
to use certified seeds of hemp varieties which are listed in the Common Catalogue of Varieties
of Agricultural Plant Species19. The THC content of those varieties has to be verified and should
not exceed for two consecutive years the limit of 0.3%, which is a legal requirement set in the
basic act.
The current legislation establishes a minimum, 30% control rate in relation to cultivated area
under CAP support (or 20% in case the cultivation in question received a prior authorisation).
The main aim of these controls is not to detect illegal cultivations given that the farmer declares
the areas and provides the seeds label to the control authorities, but to verify the stability of the
THC content in a given variety in different territories of the same Member State and in relation
to changing climate conditions. Notably, during COVID, the rate was reduced to 10% without
significant impacts on the correctness of the results. Moreover, from 2023 the maximum THC
limit was raised from 0.2% to 0.3%, therefore the risk of exceeding the limit is very low for
the majority of varieties which proved to be traditionally below the 0.2%. The risk remains
with the new varieties with an average THC content comprised between 0.2 and 0.3%.
The simplification entails reduction of control rate from 30% to 15% (or from 20% to 10%) of
the area declared.
Assuming, based on the trend of cultivation data, about 40 000 ha, the number of hectares to
be controlled will be reduced by 5 000 hectares (from approximately 10 000), halving not only
19https://food.ec.europa.eu/plants/plant-reproductive-material/plant-variety-catalogues-databases-information-
systems_en
10
the number of field visits and samples taken, but also the number of laboratory analyses to
determine the THC. Based on the figures of one Member State relating a ratio of on-the-spot
controls to area (one control covering 7 ha on average), and extrapolating this data to all areas
under cultivation, one arrives at 1 406 total controls. Reducing by half the number of controls
would result in the reduction of 700 controls and associated laboratory analysis, annually.
Eliminating partially the controls, leads to reduction of enforcement costs on the side of
national administrations linked to preparing on-site-visits, attending them, taking samples
and performing the analysis. Assuming that each control and analysis takes one day for two
persons involved in sampling and analysis, the cost reduction is approximately EUR 366 240
annually, using average EU values for labour costs (EUR 32.7 per hour).
For farmers, this reduces the time spent on preparing, attending and following up a single
control and half a day spent on each by a farmer, translates into an annual reduction of
administrative costs in the range of EUR 31 500 to 92 000 (700 x 4 h x 11.25 or 32.7), using
data for labour costs from the Simplification study and average EU values for labour costs.

title: COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE EVALUATION of the 2019-2024 Protocol to the Agreement on a Sustainable Fisheries Partnership between the European Union and the Republic of Senegal
text:
EN
EN
EUROPEAN
COMMISSION
Brussels, 13.1.2026
SWD(2026) 6 final
COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE EVALUATION
of the 2019-2024 Protocol to the Agreement on a Sustainable Fisheries Partnership
between the European Union and the Republic of Senegal
{SWD(2026) 5 final}
1
Under the external dimension of the EU’s common fisheries policy (CFP)1, the Commission is
responsible for the negotiation of implementing protocols to sustainable fisheries partnership
agreements (SFPAs) with non-EU countries, and for the implementation of those protocols.
SFPAs create a legal, environmental, economic and social governance framework for fishing
activities carried out by EU fishing vessels in non-EU waters. In return, the EU pays financial
compensation to the partner country for access to its waters and provides it with financial
support for the implementation of a national strategy on fisheries and the blue economy. The
EU contribution is supplemented by fees payable by EU vessel owners.
Before submitting a recommendation to the Council asking it to authorise the opening of
negotiations for a successor protocol to a sustainable fisheries partnership agreement, the
Commission arranges for independent ex ante and ex post evaluations of each protocol, in
accordance with Article 31(10) of the CFP Basic Regulation1.
This staff working document (SWD) contains an ex post evaluation of the application of the
most recent implementing protocol (‘the implementing protocol’) to the sustainable fisheries
partnership agreement between the European Union and the Republic of Senegal (‘the
Agreement’). These evaluations are based mainly on an independent evaluation carried out by
an external consultant2. The external consultant undertook extensive consultations with
stakeholders in the EU and in Senegal. During the evaluation process, the consultant engaged
in discussions with the European and Senegalese authorities to gather their views on the
implementation of the 2019-2024 protocol.
The ex post evaluation covers the period up to March 2024, which is most of the period of
application of the 2019-2024 implementing protocol. It provides an overall assessment of the
implementing protocol, drawing conclusions on its effectiveness, efficiency, relevance,
coherence and acceptance and on the EU added value of the intervention. The detailed issues
raised by these evaluation criteria are set out in further detail in Section 4 of the evaluation
report.
The external contractor’s final report also presents an ex ante study evaluating the future of the
sustainable fisheries partnership agreement between the EU and Senegal. However, in keeping
with the EU’s zero tolerance policy on illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, and
considering the Commission’s decision to pre-identify Senegal as a non-cooperating country in
the fight against IUU fishing3, the Commission does not intend to recommend opening
negotiations for a successor protocol. The Commission therefore does not, at this point, need to
conduct and present its ex ante evaluation in this Commission staff working document.
This evaluation covers only the implementation of the 2019-2024 protocol to the sustainable
fisheries partnership agreement between the European Union and Senegal. It is independent of
the aforementioned Commission decision to pre-identify Senegal as a non-cooperating country
in the fight against IUU fishing and cannot pre-empt potential developments in connection with
that decision in the context of the application of the IUU Regulation.
1Regulation (EU) No 1380/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2013 on the Common
Fisheries Policy (OJ L 354, 28.12.2013, p. 22).
2 Évaluation rétrospective et prospective du protocole à l’accord de partenariat dans le domaine de la pêche durable entre
l’Union Européenne et la République du Sénégal – Rapport final, Publications Office of the European Union, 2024,
https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2771/806730.
3 Commission Decision of 27 May 2024 as regards the notification to the Republic of Senegal of the possibility of being
identified as a non-cooperating third country in fighting illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, C/2024/3319, OJ C,
C/2024/3277, 29.5.2024.

title: COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT […] Accompanying the document REPORT FROM THE COMMISSION TO THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT, THE COUNCIL, THE EUROPEAN ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COMMITTEE AND THE COMMITTEE OF THE REGIONS on the interim evaluation of the Fiscalis programme for cooperation in the field of taxation for 2021-2027
text:
EN
EN
EUROPEAN
COMMISSION
Brussels, 23.1.2026
SWD(2026) 9 final
COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT
[…]
Accompanying the document
REPORT FROM THE COMMISSION TO THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT, THE
COUNCIL, THE EUROPEAN ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL COMMITTEE AND THE
COMMITTEE OF THE REGIONS

INTRODUCTION
This staff working document (SWD) reports on the interim evaluation of the Fiscalis programme
(hereafter: ‘the programme’). The programme is one of the principal tools used to support the
implementation of European Union taxation policy. The programme provides a framework for
improving the functioning of the taxation systems in the single market by increasing cooperation
between participating countries, their tax authorities and officials. By ensuring the exchange of
information, supporting administrative cooperation and increasing participating countries’
administrative capacity, the programme supports: (i) the implementation of EU law in the field of
taxation; and (ii) the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive tax planning. The programme's
main beneficiaries are the EU Member States' tax administrations and its budget of EUR 269 million
for the period 2021-2027 supports three main types of activities, namely: (i) EESs, which have
accounted for over 80% of the budget so far; (ii) actions fostering collaboration among tax
administrations; and (iii) capacity-building actions.
The Fiscalis programme was set up by Regulation (EU) No 2021/847 of the European Parliament and
of the Council of 20 May 2021 establishing an action programme to improve the operation of taxation
systems in the European Union. In line with Article 15(2) of the Regulation establishing the
programme, the Commission must carry out an interim evaluation no later than four years after the
implementation of the programme is launched and must communicate the conclusions of the interim
[…and final] evaluations, including its observations, to the European Parliament, the Council, the
European Economic and Social Committee and to the Committee of the Regions.
1.1 Purpose and scope of the evaluation
Building on previous assessments, this evaluation focuses on the common components of the EESs
in the area of taxation, which account for most of the total budget allocated to the Fiscalis programme.
To a certain but lesser extent, the evaluation also covers the programme’s other core activities,
namely: (i) collaborative actions (which provide a platform for tax officials and other stakeholders to
cooperate and ensure, for example, uniform implementation of EU tax law); (ii) expert teams (a
relatively new bottom-up activity allowing the Member States to jointly develop specific initiatives);
and (iii) human capacity building. Since most of these activities were evaluated previously and have
been relatively stable over the years, the evaluation focuses on aspects that have recently been
introduced or have undergone recent changes. In this vein, when it comes to collaborative activities,
the evaluation also assesses the programme’s new monitoring and evaluation framework (MEF) and
takes into consideration follow-up measures arising from the evaluation of the previous iteration of
the programme.
The purpose of the evaluation is to assess the Fiscalis programme’s progress towards its main
objectives between 2021 and 2024, in terms of the five better regulation criteria of effectiveness,
efficiency (with a focus on costs and benefits), coherence, relevance and EU added value1.

Under the overall criterion of effectiveness, the evaluation examines first to what extent the Fiscalis
programme has been successful over the relevant period, and then, the possible reasons behind that.
The evaluation does this by focusing on the implementation and achievements of the different types
of activities and their relative contribution to the programme’s objectives. The efficiency of the
Fiscalis programme is evaluated by looking at the costs and benefits of the EESs and their
components, and the administrative burden for tax authorities and economic operators. The evaluation
then investigates the efficiency of the non-EES components, including training activities,
collaborative actions, the learning management system/platform, e-learning, and common learning
events. At this stage (i.e. halfway through the funding period) this will shed light on the extent to
which the programme’s budget (EUR 269 million between 2021 and 2027) has been spent efficiently
on the activities that it supports. The analysis also looks at the efficiency of the overall programme
management and governance.
The assessment of relevance covers two main aspects, namely: (i) the alignment of the programme’s
objectives with the EU's needs and challenges in the field of taxation; and (ii) the appropriateness and
fitness for purpose of the programme's features and set-up, specifically as regards its support for the
common components of the EESs and for collaborative activities, training and other actions. The
analysis of coherence will look at the extent to which the programme is coherent with other EU
initiatives/programmes with similar objectives, and at the internal consistency of the actions funded
by the programme itself. Thus, the evaluation will report on the implementation of the
recommendations regarding the Fiscalis programme's consistency with the Union anti-fraud
programme2, and its alignment with measures such as the instrument for pre-accession assistance
(IPA) and the instrument for technical assistance and information exchange (TAIEX) among others.
Lastly, the evaluation will examine the criterion of EU added value to report on the extent to which
the programme has brought about changes beyond those which could have been expected as a result
of national actions by the Member States acting alone. This aspect is assessed by looking at both the
EU added value of the different types of activities funded by the programme (i.e. IT systems, the
Customs & Tax EU Learning Portal, expert teams and collaborative actions) and the programme's
overall added value.
The overall evaluation methodology3 consisted of three main phases: (i) a structuring phase, which
included preparatory activities for designing and developing the evaluation, such as selecting an
external contractor and identifying relevant stakeholders to be consulted; (ii) data collection and
analysis, involving stakeholder consultations, legal and desk research, and analytical work to support
the assessment; and (iii) evaluation and insights, where the information collected was analysed to
produce the evaluation report by examining the five better regulation criteria and subsequently
drawing conclusions and lessons learned.
This evaluation is primarily based on the findings of an external study carried out over a 12-month
period by a consortium led by Economisti Associati4. In order to devise a suitable approach to the
evaluation, some critical elements had to be accounted for at the outset of the exercise. These

studies to investigate as deeply as possible the issues that are of most interest, while dedicating less
time and effort to assessing all the programme’s components (since previous evaluations have
covered this quite exhaustively)5.
Data for both the case studies and the programme-level assessment was collected via three main

information; (ii) 84 interviews with representatives of national tax authorities, economic operators
and the European Commission; and (iii) three separate targeted surveys, namely one for NFCs in
the national tax authorities of participating countries (27 respondents), and two short online user
surveys as part of two of the case studies (on VIES-on-the-web (1 248 respondents) and the LMS (62

2.
WHAT WAS THE EXPECTED OUTCOME OF THE INTERVENTION?
The predecessor to the current Fiscalis programme (Fiscalis 2020) ran from 2014 to 2020. The
findings of the final evaluation, published in 2022, indicate that the programme was broadly
successful in achieving its objectives6. The evaluation recognised that some limitations had affected
the analysis, but concluded that Fiscalis 2020 had delivered efficient and effective results for tax
authorities and businesses. There are examples that illustrate that specific activities carried out under
Fiscalis 2020, such as data sharing through the DAC1 and DAC2 systems, simplified both
communication between authorities and compliance with tax rules. Feedback gathered through
consultations also indicated that Fiscalis 2020 activities were perceived as useful by key stakeholders
and as having had an impact on their organisations’ working practices7. Specific initiatives also
provided evidence of the programme's value added, such as the development of the TNA system and
the excise duty calculator, which ‘might not have existed if Fiscalis 2020 did not provide funding for
expert teams’8.
2.1 Description of the intervention and its objectives
The current Fiscalis programme (for 2021-2027) aligns with the original objective of improving
cooperation among tax authorities. In the proposal for the 2021-2027 Fiscalis programme, the
Commission recognised the successes of previous Fiscalis programmes, while acknowledging that
more progress should be made in fostering cooperation among tax authorities9. The resulting
Regulation (adopted by the Council and the Parliament following the agreement on the MFF for 2021-
2027) allocates EUR 269 million in current prices to the Fiscalis programme, up from EUR 223.2
million in the 2014-2020 period10. In addition to the EU Member States, participation in the
programme (and in
some but not all of its activities and IT systems) is open to candidate and potential candidate countries,
with a view both to fostering convergence and supporting the programme's objectives.
The intervention logic of the programme hinges on three general objectives, namely:
• supporting tax authorities and taxation in order to improve the functioning of the internal
market;
• fostering the competitiveness of the EU and fair competition in the EU; and
• protecting (including from tax fraud, tax evasion and tax avoidance) the financial and
economic interests of the EU and its Member States.
In turn, these general objectives are reflected in three specific objectives, which comprise:

The activities of the Fiscalis programme are categorised in three main areas.
• EESs received 84% of the Fiscalis budget between 2021 and 202411 for developing,
maintaining and improving EESs to boost coordination and information sharing. The primary
aim of the EESs is to help implement EU tax legislation properly and to support tax authorities
in performing their tasks.
• Collaboration actions, including expert teams, provide a platform for tax authorities to
share their knowledge, experience and good practices, and to jointly develop operational
guidelines. This is achieved by supporting the setting up of meetings and project-based
collaboration. In most cases, the support consists of costs for travel, accommodation and
subsistence, while salary costs can also be covered for certain actions.
• Capacity building and human competency aims to improve performance across EU tax
authorities. Fiscalis supports capacity building through e-learning, workshops and training
sessions, ensuring that tax officials are equipped to manage modern taxation challenges. This
includes the development of a dedicated online portal, the Customs & Tax EU Learning
Portal12.

Several inputs underpin these activities, including financial resources (i.e. the programme budget)
that are used to: (i) obtain (primarily IT-related) services via public procurement; and (ii) provide
grants to enable stakeholders (mainly national tax administrations) to participate in the activities.
Human resources from both the European Commission and national levels are essential. The
multiannual work programmes (MAWP) (of which two have been produced so far, and the
multiannual strategic planning for taxation (MASP-T) provide direction for the programme.
While the form of the programme has been broadly stable across funding periods, the current
programme has some new features. The first new feature concerns the introduction of the MASP-T,
which sets out a strategic framework and milestones for managing the IT projects funded by the
programme13. Another new feature is the way in which collaborative activities are managed, with the
Commission no longer disbursing funding directly, but now awarding grants to a consortium
comprising tax administrations from participating countries. Lastly, dedicated ‘innovation activities’,
such as proof of concept, pilot projects and prototypes, can be funded under the Fiscalis Regulation.
The European Commission (DG TAXUD) is responsible for implementing Fiscalis under direct
management14. The programme is implemented on the basis of programming cycles in the form of
MAWPs, which represent the programme’s operational and financial framework. Two MAWPs (for
2021-2023 and for 2024-2025) have been produced so far. The Commission programme management
team (CPMT), which is part of DG TAXUD, ensures the strategic and overall management of the
Fiscalis programme, as well as providing oversight. The CPMT operates with the help of the Fiscalis
programme committee and national programme coordinators (NPCs) and their teams. The Fiscalis
committee was set up under Article 18 of the Regulation and is composed of delegates from all
participating countries. It plays a formal role in the programme's governance and decision-making
process, particularly concerning the legal endorsement of strategic documents, such as the MAWPs.
In contrast, the NPCs come together in a Commission expert group15, which also forms one of the
programme’s collaborative actions (see description of the actions below). The NPCs are designated
by each participating country and have a more operational function, involving the coordination and
day-to-day implementation of the programme, including the planning and monitoring of actions at
national level. The management arrangements for the different types of actions are as follows.
• For the EESs, DG TAXUD retains coordination functions, and develops and operates the EU
components of the systems, while (where relevant) the Member States develop and operate
national components.
• Collaborative actions are conducted via grant agreements with participating administrations,
represented by a grant coordinator (currently the Latvian tax authority for the collaborative
activities grant). Both the programme beneficiary countries and the Commission can initiate,
chair and lead such collaborative activities. Collaborative activities fall into two broad

2.2. Point(s) of comparison
The first version of the Fiscalis programme was launched in 1998 and has been followed without
interruption by subsequent versions since then. Therefore, it is rather limiting to compare the situation
under the current programme with a hypothetical scenario where no Fiscalis programme exists.
Subsequent versions of the programme have created a baseline of cooperation in the field of taxation
and have evolved gradually to address new and emerging challenges and priorities. Therefore,
comparing the developments in the last few years with the situation before 1998, or imagining a
sudden disappearance of the entire programme would not be overly instructive.
Relevant information that can act as a sort of ‘baseline’ can be draw from the final evaluation of
Fiscalis 202016, which concluded that the programme had been effective in achieving its objectives
and would probably continue to be a relevant tool at EU level for achieving the goals of supporting
the implementation of EU tax legislation and the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive
tax planning. The final evaluation of Fiscalis 2020 also identified some areas where there is room for
improvement, such as weak evidence on the costs and benefits of the IT systems, and the need for
non-EU countries to be able to participate in a wider set of activities.
Both assessments provide indications that can be used to: (i) contextualise and compare the
performance of the current programme with that of its predecessor; and (ii) assess to what extent
the conclusions of the previous evaluation continue to be valid, and whether the weaknesses identified
have been effectively addressed.
In addition to this, the following aspects also provide relevant points of comparison.
- An MEF for the current programme has been developed, and DG TAXUD has set targets and
collected data for the relevant indicators since the inception of the programme. Where possible
and appropriate, the evaluation considers how these indicators have developed over time, from
the ‘baseline’ in 2021 until 2024.
- The reliance on in-depth case studies to assess the effectiveness (including the costs and benefits
of selected IT systems) is a key element of the methodology for this evaluation. To facilitate a
robust analysis, each case study developed a counterfactual to consider what would have been

3.
HOW HAS THE SITUATION EVOLVED OVER THE EVALUATION PERIOD?
3.1 Current state of play
The current Fiscalis programme (2021-2027), which has a budget of EUR 269 million reflecting
recent EU policy developments, continues to pursue its original goal of improving cooperation
between tax authorities. The programme's budget supports the expansion and modernisation of IT
systems in the tax area to meet the growing need for more sophisticated digital tools. Guided by the
2021-2023 and 2024-2025 MAWPs, which outline the priorities and actions for each period, the
programme focuses on key components, such as developing and implementing EESs, establishing
expert teams and improving capacity building within tax administrations across the EU.
The MAWPs provide a clear roadmap for the Fiscalis programme by identifying priority actions that
address the changing needs of tax administrations in the context of cross-border cooperation,
digitalisation and tax compliance. Each of the programme’s components is designed to foster
collaboration, improve operational efficiency and build the necessary expertise to meet current and
future tax challenges.
After the Fiscalis 2020 programme, the funding cycle of the current Fiscalis programme began in
2021. However, as part of the transition, unused resources from the Fiscalis 2020 programme,
covering both IT projects and collaborative actions, were implemented in 2021 due to delays in the
adoption of the 2021-2027 MFF and the subsequent late adoption of the Fiscalis Regulation. Training
activities also continued to be funded through the Fiscalis 2020 budget until December 2021.
The budget allocation for the 2021-2024 period is distributed across several key categories, as
outlined in the MAWPs and detailed in Table 1 below. As with previous funding periods, most of the
budget has been committed to the EESs category. For collaboration activities, which include expert
teams, EUR 8.5 million (a large sum due to the fact that grants are multiannual as from 2021
(covering on average 2-3 years)) was allocated in 2021, with EUR 500 000 allocated in 2022. This
amount increased again to about EUR 1 million in 2024.
The ‘other service contracts category’, which covers areas such as training and consultancy, saw an
allocation of EUR 1.2 million in 2022, which increased to EUR 3.8 million in 2024. This expenditure
supports the operational activities, and the various external services needed to support the programme.
In 2021, EUR 70 000 was designated for external experts, but no funds were allocated to this category
subsequently from 2022 to 2024.
Overall, the total committed expenses for the Fiscalis programme have been relatively stable,
increasing gradually from just under EUR 34.5 million in 2021 to EUR 38.4 million in 2024.

Collaborative actions, including expert teams
The Fiscalis programme provides a framework for tax authorities to work together. It enables
cooperation through a variety of operational actions during which knowledge, experience and good
practices are exchanged, and practical outputs such as guidelines and recommendations are produced.
These activities all involve bringing together national tax officials, Commission officials and, in
specific cases, other stakeholders. Programme funding is mainly used to cover participants' travel,
subsistence and accommodation unit costs, although salary costs are also covered for one type of
action (expert teams, described below).
The programme has devoted 7.6% of its committed expenses for 2021-2024 to supporting
collaborative actions, as shown in Figure 3.

➢ Expert teams
Expert teams involve national tax specialists working on targeted policy areas. These teams
require a greater time commitment, a higher level of expert involvement, and a broader scope of
budget coverage, which includes both travel and salary expenses for national tax authorities. Expert
teams must bring together at least five participating countries and typically operate for 18 to 36
months, with the possibility of renewal. Their activities may blend virtual interactions with in-person
meetings. Although they lack legal personality, expert teams require a well-defined structure,
including roles for the project manager and grant agreement coordinator. DG TAXUD policy units
monitor the progress of deliverables, timelines and overall adherence to the expert team’s objectives.
According to the available APRs, seven expert teams were proposed under the current Fiscalis
programme, with the following five expert teams having either been launched or concluded by 2024.
• TNA: the TNA expert team, which was initially launched in 2020, has undergone several
iterations, of which only TNA III (2024-2027) is funded under the current Fiscalis funding
cycle. It aims to increase Eurofisc’s operational efficiency by: (i) improving fraud detection
tools; (ii) promoting inter-agency cooperation; and (iii) strengthening responses to complex
VAT fraud schemes, including VAT exemptions on imports and fraudulent vehicle
transactions.
• Managed IT Collaboration (MANITC V): launched in late 2021, the MANITC V expert
team continued its operations throughout 2023, providing support for IT collaboration in the
taxation domain, which included helping to integrate AI into tax operations.
17
• Development of data analysis tool (DATANA): launched in early 2022, the DATANA
expert team aimed to improve the handling of data exchanged under the DAC provisions on
automatic exchange of information (AEOI) that remained unmatched (i.e. that could not be
linked to taxpayers in national datasets). The expert team completed its work in January 2024,
delivering a prototype tool for the analysis of unmatched DAC data.
• Central Electronic System of Payment Information (CESOP): the CESOP expert team
helped the Commission to create a central system for processing payment data related to cross-
border e-commerce transactions. The first version of CESOP ran from February 2021 to May
2023, and the second version was launched in January 2024.
• Visits to Member States Directive on Administrative Cooperation (VISDAC): launched
in February 2023, the VISDAC expert team has helped Member States to implement the DAC

Two expert teams (the expert team for the EU cooperative compliance pilot project for larger
companies and the expert team on excise distance selling) that had initially been planned were

Capacity building
A range of training initiatives, such as CLEP events, e-learning courses, IT training sessions and
webinars, have been carried out since 2021. A key new feature introduced by the current programme
was the launch of the LMS in May 2021, along with its public interface, the Customs & Tax EU
Learning Portal. This platform serves as a centralised access point for all training materials and
capacity-building opportunities, offering e-learning courses, webinars, nano-learning modules and e-
books. It also acts as the place to register for CLEP training sessions, which include both in-person
and online learning events. While the total budget for all capacity-building activities combined was
unavailable (and indeed some actions are captured under the budget lines covered above), it is worth
noting that the LMS platform had received about EUR 1.5 million by the end of 2024, which is shared
between the Customs and Fiscalis programmes. About EUR 1 million of the cost was incurred during
the current funding cycle, while the rest came from the Customs 2020 and Fiscalis 2020 budgets. In
addition, EUR 540 000 were spent to fund tax officers' participation in IT training sessions and CLEP
events21.
The Customs & Tax EU Learning Portal is the primary training platform in the fields of customs
and taxation. It is specifically designed for tax and customs officials, but it also serves a broader
audience, including economic operators and academics. Many resources are accessible through an
EU login, while some specialised or technical courses are restricted to specific groups, such as tax
and customs officials.
Users can take the courses directly on the platform or download them for use via national systems. A
specific functionality, Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI), allows users to access courses
through their national LMS while still ensuring that data on engagement and completion is tracked

Box 1. Overview of the case studies
TNA
•
TNA is a centralised, automated risk analysis platform supporting Eurofisc’s fight against cross-border VAT
fraud, especially missing trader intra-community (MTIC) and carousel fraud (whereby illicit traders claim
repayments for input VAT that was never incurred). The system enables real-time data exchange and network
analysis among national tax authorities for the early detection of fraudsters and fraud facilitators. Operational since
2020, TNA replaced manual Excel-based data exchanges of information, which were time-consuming and affected
by quality issues (e.g. clerical errors in compilations, missing information, different formats). When it was
introduced, TNA covered only MTIC fraud, but its scope was subsequently expanded to include VAT fraud that
involves the violation of customs procedures (2021) and fraud related to means of transportation (2023).
•
Key findings: TNA was found to be highly effective in: (i) detecting VAT fraud; (ii) enabling early warnings;
(iii) improving the targeting of tax controls; and (iv) supporting real-time collaboration between Member States.
Between its introduction in 2020 and 2023, some EUR 37 billion in suspicious transactions were uncovered22,
with over 12 000 fraudsters being identified and 6 000 deregistered for VAT. TNA also achieved significant
success in preventing fraud by identifying fraudsters early and thus reducing their lifespan and, consequently, the
volume of their fraudulent activities. The system also led to significant cost savings for tax authorities (in the
order of EUR 1.7 million by 2024) by automating data collection and processing. Further (likely significant)
savings are generated by streamlining bilateral interactions, which can now be carried out on the system instead
of through lengthy administrative procedures.
DAC 6 Central Directory (CD)
•
The DAC6 CD is a central repository for exchanging information on reportable cross-border arrangements
that might have some tax avoidance consequences, in compliance with the obligation stemming from the fifth
amendment to the Directive on Administrative Cooperation23 (or DAC6). Under DAC6, information is collected
from reporting entities (tax advisers and other intermediaries or, as a last resort, taxpayers) through nationally
developed systems, and then transmitted machine-to-machine to the CD. The process is highly automated and
requires little or no human intervention. Similar processes are used to bulk download information on national
repositories to be used for tax controls and risk assessment by national tax officials.
•
Key findings: the case study suggests that DAC6 CD works well, and stakeholders only pointed out minor issues
or possible improvements. Most tax authorities believe that a centralised system (as opposed to bilateral
exchanges) is the right choice for these types of exchanges, although implementing a centralised system is not
necessarily less costly than bilateral exchanges. Tax authorities largely agree that DAC6 CD has three main
advantages. Firstly, it reduces the costs of follow-ups compared with bilateral interactions. Secondly, it
22 The suspicious transactions uncovered between 2021 and 2023 amounted to nearly 34 million.
23 Council Directive 2011/16/EU of 15 February 2011 on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation and repealing
Directive 77/799/EEC.
20
automatically generates statistics and monitoring data, which would otherwise need to be produced by national
tax authorities, with the consequent savings in terms of effort. Notably, these two categories of cost savings, while
not quantifiable, appear clearer for smaller or less automated administrations. Thirdly, the CD has advantages in
terms of transparency compared with bilateral exchanges. Overall, the DAC6 legislation has yet to yield
tangible benefits, which means that it is also too early to see the CD's quantitative benefits.
Vies on-the-web (VoW)
•
VoW is a web interface that is integrated with the VAT information Exchange System (VIES). Launched in
2001, VoW allows economic operators to verify business partners’ VAT numbers. Operating on a real-time
basis, each validation request made through VoW is instantly forwarded to the relevant administration's national
VIES system. If the entered VAT number is valid, the platform confirms its validity. If that is not the case, the
platform notifies users that the VAT number is invalid for cross-border transactions within the EU. Additionally,
it advises economic operators to reach out to the appropriate authorities for corrections or clarifications, providing
a useful link to the national tax authorities for further assistance. Before VoW became operational, the verification
of VAT numbers was cumbersome and varied significantly in different country-specific contexts. The process for
providing VAT details (including the VAT identification number of the buyer and the VAT amount due) was
manual and fragmented, often requiring the consultation of national VAT databases, direct communication with
tax authorities, or contact with trading partners. The launch of VoW marked a significant step towards centralising
and digitising the VAT number verification process, streamlining it for traders.
▪
Key findings: the case study found evidence that VoW has provided economic operators with a rapid, reliable and
centralised system for VAT number verification, dramatically changing the processes and tools available for
business and tax officials to verify VAT numbers. By standardising verification practices, VoW reduces national
disparities in data access and improves operational efficiency for businesses. Its main benefits include a
reduced administrative burden, and better VAT compliance and VAT enforcement. The centralisation of VAT
number verification delivers substantial cost savings, as tax authorities and economic operators would incur
higher costs in the counterfactual scenario. VoW allowed both tax authorities and economic operators to achieve
average cost savings in the order of EUR 62 million between 2021 and 2023, with a cost/benefit ratio of 7.524.
VoW also demonstrates significant EU added value by providing an EU platform for rapid, reliable and
centralised VAT number verification, which ensures interoperability with national VIES systems, brings
consistency and uniformity and lowers costs for tax administrations and businesses. Finally, the VAT in the Digital
Age initiative and the growing adoption of e-invoicing are expected to increase VoW’s capabilities and usage in
the future. The case study also identified significant areas for improvement, including improvements to the user
interface and platform accessibility, adjusting the daily limit on requests and modernising the API interface.
Excise Movement Control System (EMCS)
•
The purpose of the EMCS is to track the movement of excisable goods (alcohol, tobacco and energy products)
throughout the EU. It aims to improve the efficiency, safety, security and environmental footprint of the
monitoring of such goods. The system monitors several key types of information including: (i) the economic
operators; (ii) the consignors (the sender of the excisable good) and consignees (the recipient of the excisable
good), who have to be registered; (iii) the type of excisable good (listed in the EMCS code sheet); (iv) the details
of the provider of the mandatory movement guarantee; and (v) even the details of the transporter. Structurally,
EMCS is a complex, distributed system with both central and Member State components. The Commission is
responsible for developing and maintaining several components, including: (i) the SEED database, a central
registry which is used to automatically verify the validity of every movement against the trader records before the
goods are approved and moved; (ii) the SEED-on-Europa application, a data-searching tool, which allows
economic operators to check the validity of a SEED number in any Member State; and (iii) several other

accompanying explanatory paragraph, which can be found in Annex IV of the SWD.
21
components, such as the EMCS Core, EMCS ACO, ARC follow-up and the CCN/CSI. Since 2020, the
Commission has also developed key updates to the system that have added to its scope and functionality.
•
Key findings: EMCS is effective and fit for the purpose of helping Member State competent authorities and
economic operators to improve excise trade procedures and traceability/monitoring, and fight fraud. Despite being
difficult to quantify, the benefits of most of the components outweigh the costs (compared with the counterfactual).
The central SEED database (which, arguably, delivers the most significant added value) underpins much of the
automation (and benefits) of EMCS. Evidence shows that without the central SEED, both national authorities and
economic operators would have to redeploy resources for highly repetitive and manual tasks, such as verifying
electronic administrative documents (eADs). In contrast, although the SEED-on-Europa tool is widely used by
national authorities and economic operators, its usefulness is limited. This is because economic operators must
still carry out due diligence by other means, given that the tool only verifies SEED numbers, rather than providing
key information such as a company name or address. The case study found evidence that each of the updates
have been valuable to national authorities and certain economic operators, yielding tangible benefits (e.g.
reduced waiting times, business planning, possibility to redeploy resources) but that adjusting to the updates and
related process changes has also entailed significant costs for these stakeholders. Multinational operators
expressed some dissatisfaction due to inconsistent approaches to national implementation, which meant that they
had to operate different systems in which they were active (with significant cost implications), prompting calls for
more coherent implementation by the national administration.
LMS
•
The LMS, officially known as the Customs & Tax EU Learning Portal was launched in 2021 as a central location
for the e-learning courses developed as part of the Customs and Fiscalis programmes, as well as for the
organisation of events for the CLEP. The portal can be used for the e-learning courses in three different ways,
namely by: (i) taking a course directly on the platform; (ii) downloading and posting a course on a national LMS;
and/or (iii) using the LTI functionality, which allows courses to be embedded in a national LMS while still being
run from the EU LMS at the back end. This is important because LTI allows both DG TAXUD and national
administrations to collect detailed data on usage. The platform was developed and is managed by DG TAXUD
with the support of an external contractor, and the Member States have provided input throughout the process via
the TSG, a project group bringing together national training coordinators from tax and customs authorities. While
the main audience is customs and tax officials, economic operators and other stakeholders may use the LMS to
access certain publicly available material.
•
Key findings: regarding the rationale behind the LMS and how the LMS satisfies needs, the case study found
that it satisfies a strong need to collect and organise the e-learning catalogue in a single, easily searchable place.
It also aims to provide a platform for stakeholders to take the courses directly, although this need is peripheral for
most Member States due to the widespread existence of national LMSs. The design of the LMS was also assessed
positively, with stakeholders praising its user-friendliness, navigation, layout and organisation, and visual design,
as well as the quality and usefulness of its core functionalities. On usage and impact, the available metrics
suggest that the LMS is becoming increasingly established and serving its business function, with user numbers
continuing to grow. Overall, the LMS adds significant value at reasonable cost, fulfilling its role as the single
repository for e-learning courses and CLEP event registration. With a view to the future, several potential
incremental improvements have been identified, ranging from improvements to the search function, to efforts
to increase the uptake of LTI.
Source: study by Economisti Associati.

burdensome formal bilateral cooperation procedures.

collaborative actions funded by Fiscalis featured a number of ‘reinforced’ cooperation instruments,

or multilateral interactions among tax officers of different administrations, are regarded as flagship

(e.g. in dealing with data issues, or taxes on non-alcoholic beverages)34. The VISDAC expert team

➢ The programme's actions helped to implement EU tax law uniformly and, thus, to improve
the functioning of the EU single market
Fiscalis support for the common components of the EESs represents an essential element of EU tax
policy and its implementation. Since most of the recent EU tax policies and legislation require a
digital solution, IT capacity building is indispensable for the operationalisation of new initiatives
and actions. This is the case, for instance, for all DAC AEOI provisions. The Directive, in fact,
obliges the Commission to: (i) develop and maintain the central components of the infrastructure and
software necessary for the exchanges, which typically also provide access to horizontal infrastructures
(e.g. CCN/CCN2 and CSI); and/or (ii) develop central systems (e.g. DAC6). As discussed in the
dedicated case study, the IT solution conceived influenced the design of the policy, with the two being
completely intertwined.
In other cases, IT systems have improved and strengthened the implementation of existing or
evolving provisions. For instance, the introduction of the EMCS streamlined and improved the
processes related to the movement of excise goods, allowing the transition from paper-based to
electronic processes to be made. This helped not only to simplify and reduce the administrative
burden on economic operators, but also to strengthen tax authorities’ ability to monitor the
movements, thereby helping to implement the related policy fully.
The role of collaborative actions in implementing EU tax law uniformly is recognised across the
board by the stakeholders consulted, both in individual case studies and in the overall programme
assessment35. Those actions provide forums for national tax officials to exchange best practices,
develop common standards for the implementation of rules or the uptake of IT systems, and share
views and experiences across different legal, institutional and cultural backgrounds, in a way that
would not be possible without the programme.
35 See Annex V for a more in-depth overview of the consultation activities.
27
From an operational viewpoint, collaborative actions contribute to the implementation of EU law in
several different ways, some of which are set out below.
• There are structured activities, such as those carried out by project groups and expert teams
(including the TNA and the CESOP expert teams) that have engaged in the design,
development, roll-out and training of the IT systems funded by the programme. Those
structured activities are complemented by numerous events, such as IT training sessions,
CLEP events, workshops and seminars that aim to build the skills of tax authorities in using
the new or improved systems.
• There are also actions that aim to support uniform implementation through long-lasting
or permanent activities with operational functions. Such actions are carried out by
dedicated project groups, such as the EU Advanced International Administrative Cooperation
(AIAC) community, the standing committee for the implementation of Article 10 of the
Directive on tax dispute resolution mechanisms in the EU, or by the project groups supporting
the implementation of the GloBE minimum tax directive, the VAT OSS and the VAT scheme
for SMEs, as well as numerous workshops and seminars. Within these forums, tax authorities
can exchange best practices to strive for the harmonised implementation of EU tax law and to
ensure the adoption and uptake of the related IT systems.
• Other activities, such as MLCs and PAOEs, focus on compliance and correct
implementation. These activities allow Member States to concentrate on compliance with
the conditions of EU legislation, but they do not necessarily focus on differences between
countries. In a similar vein, most of the training actions, particularly the e-learning modules,
are focused on helping stakeholders to correctly implement or (in the case of economic
operators) comply with EU tax legislation.
Interaction between programme support for EESs and collaborative actions
While both IT systems and collaborative actions contribute to the implementation of EU tax law, and
thus to the functioning of the single market, they do so through different channels. IT systems are
an increasingly integral part of EU tax policies and law (often stemming from a requirement in
EU law) and thus contribute directly to the creation of a level playing field. In this respect, the role
of collaborative actions and learning activities is inextricably connected to the uniform
implementation of tax policies and laws, and to their uptake. This second aspect is essential for the
policies to produce the desired results.
➢ The programme supported the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive tax planning,
helping to protect the financial interests of the EU and its Member States
This evaluation confirmed the key conclusions of the final evaluation of the Fiscalis 2020 programme,
which found that the programme had supported the fight again tax fraud, tax evasion and
aggressive tax planning. This emerged also from the feedback collected from national Fiscalis
28
coordinators, who highlighted that all three types of activities, i.e. EESs, collaborative actions and
capacity-building activities, have continued to generate positive effects in this respect (see Figure 9)36.

Although secondary evidence on effects on tax fraud, tax evasion and aggressive tax planning is rather
scarce, the case studies considered for this evaluation provide more detail on how this impact has
been achieved in practice.
The detection of VAT fraud is the main objective of the TNA. The system helped to make fraud
detection quicker and more accurate, thanks to signals regarding potential fraudsters being more
targeted and precise than the manual exchanges that had occurred before the system was in place.
Evidence collected confirmed that since its introduction the system led to the identification of 12 000
fraudulent traders and to the de-registration for VAT of 6 000 suspicious traders. Furthermore, it
allowed the uncovering of nearly EUR 34 billion in suspicious transactions between 2021 and 2023,
and led to the prevention of fraud (unquantifiable but likely significant) thanks to the early
identification of fraudsters and to their reduced amount of time they can operate before being
discovered. These indicators have increased over the years since the introduction of TNA, likely
thanks to better targeting of the qualification activities and an increased number of overall
qualifications.
The DAC6 CD has the ultimate objective of providing tax authorities with high-quality and up-to-
date information on risky cross-border arrangements, with the threefold purpose of: (i) identifying
and closing legislative loopholes; (ii) feeding into audits and tax controls; and (iii) deterring tax
evasion and avoidance. Most tax authorities (23 out of 27) have started using the information received
for risk assessment and tax audits.
