Programme assessment
The five case studies were complemented by a broader programme assessment which aimed to gather
evidence on the Fiscalis programme as a whole and validate and to update the findings of the previous
Fiscalis programme evaluations. The analysis covers all evaluation criteria, with particular attention
to the EU added value, with the purpose of gathering any evidence indicating what the consequences
of discontinuing support to certain actions would be.
Data collection for the programme assessment focused on three elements: the desk review of a variety
of documents and sources of information (including the updated MEF, the Fiscalis programming
documents, previous evaluations and assessments, as well as other documentation monitoring the
programme (e.g. annual progress reports – APR)); an online survey of national Fiscalis coordinators;
and 14 interviews with EU and national-level counterparts, as well as exchanges with key DG
TAXUD stakeholders.
Final analysis and lessons learned
Part of the extensive analysis of both quantitative and qualitative data collected throughout the
programme was carried out by using statistical software for survey responses and programme
indicators to identify trends, correlations, and impact metrics. This included cost-benefit analyses (to
the extent possible, see discussion of limitations below) derived from the case studies. Qualitative
data were processed using coding techniques to reveal themes and patterns within interview
transcripts and survey responses. Triangulating data across multiple sources ensured the reliability
and consistency of conclusions.
The conclusions drawn from this comprehensive analysis addressed the five required evaluation
criteria of effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence, and EU added value. These highlighted the
achievements of the Fiscalis programme while also pinpointing areas for improvement, supported by
robust evidence. A stakeholder workshop was also organised by the contractor carrying out the
external supporting study to validate the preliminary conclusions and incorporate additional feedback
from representatives of Member State tax authorities, aiding in the refinement and completion of the
analysis.
Additionally, the analysis phase identified lessons learned, best practices, and areas for potential
improvement. These lessons are deemed relevant for enhancing future programming decisions and
increasing the programme’s overall impact and efficiency.
3. Limits to the evidence base and robustness of findings
Rather than aiming to cover a representative sample of the approximately 30 EESs, the case studies
sought, for several different types of system57, to go into more depth than has been possible in the
past, and thereby shed new light on the costs and benefits, and factors promoting and hindering
success. Previous evaluations found it very difficult to provide quantified estimates of the costs and
57 The sample was chosen in conjunction with DG TAXUD with a view to covering a range of the types of approaches to
IT systems (namely centralised vs decentralised), the different types of taxation (direct, indirect and excise), and both
long-established systems and systems that had been recently introduced.
66
benefits of the IT systems (and of the Fiscalis programme support for them), partly because the point
of comparison against which such costs and benefits should be assessed it is not always clear. One
reason for this is that IT systems typically go hand-in-hand with EU legislation that makes digital
data exchange mandatory, and so one cannot always simply assume that the absence of (the common
components of) the EES would imply a return to the previous situation of mostly paper-based
exchange of information. To address this issue, a new feature of this evaluation was to compare each
system to a hypothetical ‘counterfactual’ scenario – agreed with DG TAXUD – of what may have
been expected in the absence of EU funding.
The only ‘non-IT’ case study – which looked at the LMS – served to examine an aspect of the
programme that was new for the current funding period. The programme assessment, rather than
covering all remaining actions in detail, was a limited exercise aimed at confirming the validity of
previous evaluations and gathering new insight into issues of particular interest to DG TAXUD, most
importantly the EU added value of the collaborative actions and expert teams.
Overall, the methodology proved effective. The counterfactual approach to the case studies on EESs,
harvested insights of a different nature and scale than had been previously achieved, by pinpointing
the ways in which EESs – together with related collaborative actions – affect the work of national
administrations and economic operators and generate EU added value, compared to the most likely
alternative scenario. With some minor exceptions, it was possible to identify and engage with
stakeholders as hoped, ensuring that the case studies were able to build a solid evidence base. The
LMS case study and programme assessment were also implemented largely as planned and obtained
the expected input. That said, there are two key limitations that should be pointed out:
▪ Trade-off between depth and breadth: based on the considerations set out above, the
evaluation deliberately chose to go into more depth on specific IT systems, which necessarily
meant that other IT systems and aspects of the programme, particularly the collaborative
actions, could not be assessed in as much detail as for previous evaluations. For this reason,
the evidence for certain evaluation questions (particularly those not focused on the EESs) was
limited. In these cases, key findings and conclusions from previous evaluations were used as
a starting point, and either confirmed, refuted, or built on, based on the available data and
information.
▪ Fragmented IT cost data: the rationale for the approach based on in-depth IT case studies
was to include a detailed ‘cost-accounting’ exercise on the systems being studied. As part of
this, the study involved IT cost-accounting experts on the team, and developed a detailed
framework for EU-level costs in agreement with DG TAXUD. However a reduced data set
was available, covering fewer cost categories and a shorter timeframe than initially planned.
For this reason, while the IT case studies were able to generate significant and – in many
instances, quantitative – insight, it was not possible to conduct the full cost-accounting
exercise initially planned.

Summary response to evaluation questions on EFFECTIVENESS
The findings of the evaluation largely confirmed the key conclusions of the final evaluation of the
Fiscalis 2020 programme, which found that the programme contributed to the improved
functioning of the EU Single Market by supporting the fight again tax fraud, tax evasion and
aggressive tax planning. This emerged from the feedback collected from national Fiscalis
coordinators, who highlighted that all three types of activities, i.e. EESs, collaborative actions, and
human capacity-building activities, have continued to generate positive effects in this respect.
Table 8. IT systems contribution to the achievement of general objectives – evidence from case studies
Case study
Evidence of impact
VoW
While the primary objective of the system is to minimise the administrative burden for
economic operators when complying with this obligation, the system also aims to reduce
both involuntary mistakes and, ultimately, fraudulent behaviour. The reliability and the very
extensive and growing use of VoW by businesses shows its vital role in this task, which was
confirmed by interviews and large-scale survey (about 1 300 respondents) conducted for the
study. The tax authorities interviewed also agreed that VoW helps reduce VAT fraud and
further emphasised that the system helps them identify fraudsters.
EMCS
The latest innovation introduced to the EMCS fulfilled its purpose of reducing fraud and
illicit trade, although precise estimates are generally not available. The system had a pre-
emptive impact, acting as deterrent to fraudulent behaviour, as traders know that it allows
real-time verification of consignments. In addition, the direct experience of tax authorities
suggests that, particularly for duty-paid B2B frauds, the digitalisation of paper-based
procedures has had a noticeable – although hard to quantify – impact on fraud reduction.
TNA
Since its introduction the system has led to the identification of 12 000 fraudulent traders
and to the de-registration for VAT of 6 000 suspicious traders. It allowed the uncovering of
nearly EUR 34 billion in suspicious transactions between 2021 and 2023, and led to the
prevention of fraud (unquantifiable but likely significant) thanks to the early identification
of fraudsters and to their reduced amount of time they can operate before being discovered.
DAC6
Most tax authorities (23 out of 27) have started using the information received for risk
assessment and tax audits. However, tangible benefits have still not been identified from
DAC6 exchanged. On the one hand, the results of preventative measures are typically
extremely hard to measure. On the other hand, any results from audit (e.g. additional taxes
assessed or recovered) will take time to materialise, as complex cases take time – often years
– to conclude, while the cases that end quickly typically involve legitimate taxpayers.
Source: Economisti Associati study
More generally, several of the MEF indicators collected by DG TAXUD suggest an improvement
in the safeguarding of Member States’ tax bases through the reduction of tax fraud and tax evasion.
Macroeconomic indicators such as the VAT gap have continuously decreased over the years, while
total tax revenues increased in absolute value, and remained broadly stable as a percentage of GDP.
These indicators are a positive sign, even if, as also highlighted by the final evaluation of the Fiscalis
2020 programme, the contribution of the programme within these trends cannot be readily
isolated.

Summary response to evaluation questions on EFFICIENCY
The evaluation identified multiple benefits that the four EESs have brought to tax authorities and
economic operators. Process automation has led to notable efficiency gains, allowing tax
administrations both to save and to redirect resources from routine tasks to more productive,
strategic roles like fraud detection. Additionally, these systems have yielded several indirect
impacts such as fraud deterrence and a reduction in waiting times, which improves commercial
activity and protects the EU’s tax revenues. Economic operators also benefit from substantial
savings in resource allocation and VAT verification costs, particularly with VoW and EMCS.
Despite these successes, there remain areas for improvement. Enhancing the user-friendliness of
the systems and considering greater centralisation could deliver further efficiencies, although any
changes has to be analysed against the sensitivity of information and political priorities. There are
several other specific suggestions for simplification for each case study including: expanding TNA
data sources, using AI to increase efficiency, standardising data across Member States for VoW, and
addressing DAC6 manual input challenges in third countries. Overall, while the Fiscalis programme
has markedly improved the efficiency of the administration of and participation in the EU’s tax
regime, ongoing refinements and improvements could further optimise its impact.
It needs to be acknowledged that since this evaluation focused primarily on assessing (via in-depth
case studies) the effectiveness and efficiency of selected IT systems (EESs) supported by the Fiscalis
programme, it did not collect a very substantial amount of new evidence on the efficiency of other
(non-EES) activities. Nonetheless, the feedback collected and documentation reviewed confirm that
the conclusions in the final evaluation of Fiscalis 2020 programme on the efficiency of the non-EES
activities supported by the programme remain valid, namely that the collaborative and training
activities are broadly cost-effective. Their share of the overall Fiscalis programme’s budget is small,
but (as discussed under other evaluation questions) they add significant value by enabling national
tax administrations to work together and build their capacities and competencies on relevant topics
of interest; in many instances, they also support the effective and efficient development and
application of the EESs. In the absence of any major changes to the way collaborative and training
activities are implemented, there is therefore nothing to suggest the non-EES activities have become
any less efficient than under previous iterations of the Fiscalis programme.
In conclusion, the Fiscalis programme’s governance structure seems to be broadly efficient in
some respects with a relatively clear structure for decision-making as laid out in key documents.
However, stakeholders pointed out specific areas of improvement and the programme faces
challenges in terms of procedural complexity and transparency in decision-making. It remains to be
seen whether devolving responsibility for managing the collaborative actions to the Member States
will increase the efficiency of this aspect of the programme. Nevertheless, additions such as the
MASP-T framework have purportedly improved decision-making procedures and collaboration.

Summary response to evaluation questions on RELEVANCE
Since the relevance of the programme has been extensively assessed and substantiated by previous
evaluations, this evaluation focused on ascertaining the extent to which the conclusions of the
Fiscalis 2020 programme final evaluation are still valid. To briefly summarise, that evaluation
found that the underlying challenges and needs the programme aims to address were still present; that
the relevance of EESs in the daily operations of both tax authorities and economic operators was high
and growing; and that collaborative actions were also highly relevant.
Overall, there was no negative feedback from the stakeholders consulted in this study on the extent
to which the programme responds to EU policy needs and priorities in the area of taxation, nor of any
shortcomings or areas of misalignment between the two. Some noted that the Fiscalis programme
design is sufficiently flexible to provide support to address any new or emerging priorities, and
especially to fund digital solutions that may be needed. This is evidenced, for example, by the creation
in 2010 of the Eurofisc Network to combat cross-border VAT fraud in the EU and its continued
operation and evolution since then (supported by the Fiscalis programme via several project groups).
This includes its use since 2019 of the Transaction Network Analysis (TNA) electronic system, which
was also developed with programme funding. For details, see the case study on TNA.
On the IT systems specifically (i.e. the common components of the EESs), which is the focus of this
evaluation question, 86% of respondents agreed (almost half of them ‘fully’) that these correspond to
their needs. The remaining 14% gave a neutral response; none disagreed. This confirms that, overall,
the programme’s support for the common components of the EESs is fit for purpose; however,
the fact that the responses are less ‘enthusiastic’ than for the collaborative actions suggests that there
may be scope for some improvements in the way they are delivered, or that awareness of the
programme’s role in the EESs is still limited.
According to the national tax authorities that responded to the survey (see Annex V), the
collaborative actions correspond very closely to their needs. Nearly all respondents agreed with this
statement, and over 70% agreed ‘fully’. Some respondents explained that collaborative actions have
positive impacts on tax administrations, and that without them there would be a higher risk of
misalignment with EU legislation and less tax harmonisation across the EU. On the human
competency-building / training actions, again a clear majority (86%) of respondents agreed (a little
over half of them ‘fully’) that these correspond to the needs of EU tax administrations (with the
remainder giving a neutral response). This confirms such actions are also fit for purpose, although
perhaps not to the same extent as the collaborative actions referred to above. Competency-building
actions that were highlighted as especially well aligned with needs included the e-learning courses
(described by one respondent as ‘excellent’ in terms of completeness and depth, interactivity, ways
to track the progress of participants, and use of modern educational technologies), as well as, more
specifically, Common Event Learning Programme (CLEP) training and workshops for newcomers,
CLEP trainings on TNA, and CESOP. The case study on the LMS provides further evidence of the
relevance of this system, which was launched in 2021 as the single repository for the training and
capacity-building activities carried out under the Fiscalis programme (as well as the Customs
programme). It was created primarily to address the difficulty that tax administration staff faced in
locating and accessing training materials. Its centralised, searchable platform solved the problem of
76
scattered resources and improved awareness and uptake of EU training, particularly for training
coordinators who integrate courses into national curricula.

Summary response to evaluation questions on COHERENCE
The external coherence of the Fiscalis programme remains high and in line with the findings of
previous evaluations, despite the fact that the EU policy and programming context has evolved
significantly, particularly through post-pandemic measures such as the RRF and the European Green
Deal. Since the Fiscalis programme exists to support EU policy, this coherence stems mainly from
the broad alignment of EU tax policy with other policy areas. Yet, it is encouraging that all of the
initiatives identified showed little risk of overlap with the Fiscalis programme and considerable scope
for mutual reinforcement. While the evaluation’s focus on a limited number of IT systems – without
an in-depth examination of specific collaborative actions – means that some examples may not have
been captured, it is also positive that concrete instances of synergies were found for the European
Green Deal, RRF and TSI, often in the fields of digitalisation and green taxation. The absence of
concrete links with the SMP and IPA/TAIEX is not considered problematic, given the different target
audiences and implementation methods of these instruments. However, mechanisms for coordination
with the Hercule component of the UAFP (which were recommended in the previous evaluation)
have not been established.

Summary response to evaluation questions on EU ADDED VALUE
The survey feedback provided by national tax administrations on the overall added value of the
Fiscalis programme is overwhelmingly positive. The majority of respondents reported that the
programme builds trust and leads to convergence between participating tax administrations, that it
helps to apply EU rules more effectively, consistently and uniformly, and that it means EU legislation
is implemented more quickly than would be possible without the Fiscalis programme ‘to a great
extent’. A little more nuanced were responses to the question of whether the programme adds value
above and beyond initiatives at national level, without any duplication and overlap; even so, over
90% of respondents believed it does so to a greater or lesser extent. In response to follow-up
questions, respondents reported that the Fiscalis programme has had a significant impact on efficiency
and international cooperation, particularly through the development and implementation of IT
systems like VIES and projects such as VAT in the Digital Age, both of which were mentioned by
multiple respondents.
The conclusions of the final evaluation of the Fiscalis 2020 programme are still fully valid. The
programme, as well as all of the types of systems and activities it funds (see the previous evaluation
question), provide high EU added value. The Fiscalis programme supports the implementation of
EU taxation policy and legislation, enabling collaboration, coordination and information exchange
between national tax administrations that is vital to the effective, efficient and consistent application
of the former, and thereby helps to enhance the functioning of the internal market, and pursue a variety
of taxation policy objectives as outlined above (see assessment of Relevance). Without the
programme, national tax administrations would essentially be left to their own devices when it comes
to implementing EU taxation policy rules and mechanisms, which would be highly likely to be
detrimental to all of the aspects outlined previously.

ANNEX V. STAKEHOLDERS CONSULTATION – SYNOPSIS REPORT
This section of the report presents the stakeholder consultation activities performed within the context

methods, topics covered, as well as the associated limitations.
1. Overview of consultation activities
For the purpose of this study, two main stakeholder consultation activities were conducted:
1. Interviews: a total of 84 in-depth interviews were conducted with representatives of national

provided qualitative insights into the experiences and perspectives of stakeholders directly
involved in or impacted by the case studies and the Fiscalis programme. The interviews
covered various aspects of the Fiscalis programmes, and when direct participation was not
possible, written responses were secured to ensure full coverage and input from all relevant
parties.
2. Targeted surveys: three distinct surveys were conducted to gather quantitative data and

coordinators within the national tax authorities of participating countries. Additionally,

2. Programme assessment surveys and interviews
This section presents an analysis of the responses provided by Member States on experiences with
and views on the Fiscalis programme.
The initial input was gathered through a survey developed by the contractor performing the external
study and refined with feedback from DG TAXUD. The survey was launched on 8 November
2024and remained open beyond the original deadline of 6 December 2024, with 15 responses received
by 13 December. It covered 13 Member States and two other participating countries. While this earlier
86
survey formed the foundation for the consultation, it has since been complemented by follow-up
interviews. These interviews were carried out with national Fiscalis coordinators (NFCs) from seven
of the countries who had completed the questionnaire – allowing for deeper exploration of their
responses – as well as with stakeholders from seven Member States who had not participated in the
initial survey. The analysis presented in this section draws on both sources.
Visibility of the Fiscalis programme and dissemination of information
The focus of this section is on the visibility of the Fiscalis programme within tax administrations,
based on the insights provided though both the initial survey and the follow-up interviews.
According to the feedback collected, awareness of which IT systems are funded by the Fiscalis
programme was generally ‘moderate to low’ among tax officials. Nine participants indicated that
officials in their administration are aware ‘to some extent’, while eight described awareness as being
only ‘to a small extent’. A smaller group – four participants – described a higher level of awareness.
One participant was uncertain.
When asked about the broader visibility of the Fiscalis programme within their administrations,
several participants noted that awareness tends to be concentrated among senior management or
officials involved in international activities, while regular staff often have limited exposure. Some
administrations have internal structures or dedicated coordinators that help promote the programme,
but others reported gaps in communication and a lack of clarity about which initiatives are funded by
the Fiscalis programme. While a few participants did not view low awareness as problematic, others
suggested that better internal information sharing (such as brief statements, info sessions, or clearer
messaging) could strengthen engagement and improve the overall impact of the programme.
Awareness of collaborative actions funded by the Fiscalis programme tends to be higher among those
directly involved but still remains limited for those officials not engaged in these activities.
The next question was on sources of information about the Fiscalis programme. A key role is played
by NFCs: in fact, the majority of respondents highlight that dissemination activities by coordinators
are one of the main means to receive information on the programme. The PICS platform and direct
interaction with colleagues in their own administration were cited as frequent sources by over half of
respondents (respectively 15 and 20 out of 22), together with direct interaction with colleagues within
one’s own administration (12 out of 22). Other sources seem comparatively less important.
87
Figure 15. Sources of information about the Fiscalis programme and its activities
Source: NFC consultations (no of respondents: 22).
All in all, the moderate level of awareness reported within tax administration about the role of the
Fiscalis programme in funding IT systems does not diminish the level of satisfaction on dissemination
activities carried out by the Fiscalis programme as a whole, with 20 out of 22 respondents reporting
that they were fully or mostly satisfied. While most respondents appreciate the clarity, efficiency, and
timeliness of the information shared via the PICS platform and video conferences, some suggestions
for improvement were made, such as the need for clearer communication strategies, better
coordination with national coordinators, and more centralised communication efforts, particularly in
smaller countries. These responses indicate that while there is room for improvement, overall
satisfaction with how information is disseminated is generally positive.
Programme management
The second section of the questionnaire and interviews focuses on management aspects, particularly
the effort and administrative burden required across different types of activities.
In general terms, most respondents (19 out of 22) find the overall administrative burden related to the
Fiscalis programme to be moderate or significant. Significantly, three respondents pointed out how
the change in programme management, with a shift of management responsibilities from the
Commission to participating countries, has significantly increased the administrative burden, which
is reportedly particularly challenging for smaller (and under-resourced) national administrations.
Issues with the registration process and key implementation challenges were explored in more depth
through follow-up questions. Respondents pointed out that registration remains more complex than
necessary, with overlapping systems (e.g. ART, CLEP, emails), manual steps, and a lack of
harmonisation. While some tools are still seen as helpful, most respondents expressed a clear desire
for simplification and better integration. More broadly, the financial aspect emerged as the most
88
significant concern. The rigid budget rules, requiring 80% of the budget to be spent before additional
funding can be requested, were frequently cited as a key obstacle. Combined with staffing shortages
and complex financial procedures, these factors have placed increasing pressure on national teams,
making it harder to plan and manage events effectively.
The survey then assessed more in detail the burden related to (i) collaborative activities (other
than expert teams), and (ii) expert teams. The tax administrations of 18 of the 22 interviewees had,
since the start of the current Fiscalis programme, initiated at least one collaborative action (not
including expert teams). Of those, nine said that the burden connected to initiating a collaborative
action was moderate, one that it was minor, and another eight that it was significant, but would not
discourage them from initiating other actions in future. Of the four administrations that did not initiate
any collaborative action over the period reviewed, one reported that the main reason for this was the
lack of human resources, while other two are non-EU participating countries.
The administrative effort required for long-term participation can be a significant motivating factor,
but the lack of human resources and time is often a key challenge. Tasks like selecting the appropriate
action policy and engaging relevant Member States can be complex, and many smaller
administrations struggle with the increased workload. Experts in these administrations are often
overwhelmed by their existing responsibilities, which limits their capacity to initiate or lead new the
Fiscalis programme activities. While some administrations, such as those hosting groups, can manage
specific tasks, they are not generally in a position to initiate large-scale events. Despite the
considerable administrative burden, the process can be managed effectively once personnel become
familiar with it, with the NFC playing a crucial role in guiding colleagues through the process.
The feedback is overall similar when it comes to participation as a member of the consortium for
collaborative actions. The feedback provided is generally in line with the previous answer – most
respondents (14 out of 22) believe the administrative burden to be moderate or significant, but none
of them believed that it was to a level that would discourage them from doing it in the future. Similar
considerations were in evidence when it comes to the administrative burden connected to officers’
participations in the actions. Nine out of 22 respondents believe that the administrative burden is
significant, other nine believe it is moderate and four consider it minor.

three indicated that, although the burden was significant, it did not discourage them from taking the
lead in future expert teams. However, one participant noted that the burden was significant enough to
discourage them from assuming the leadership of future teams.
Of the 17 tax administrations that had never acted as grant coordinator or project manager, nine
identified insufficient human resources as one of the main reasons. Six pointed to the excessive
administrative burden as one of the key factors, while four highlighted a lack of operational need for
initiating expert teams. Additionally, two reported insufficient support or lack of interest at the
national level (hierarchy). A few respondents mentioned that the complexity and engagement required
to lead an expert team were deterrents, particularly for smaller administrations with limited resources.
Others preferred initiating project groups or workshops due to the lower administrative burden and
costs. Additionally, a few highlighted the lack of a specific topic as the main reason for not initiating
or participating in expert teams, though they would consider it if a pressing issue arose.
The number of tax administrations whose officials participated in expert teams is instead higher (19
out of 22). The feedback on this is possibly the most negative, with two out of 19 respondents
reporting that the burden was so significant that it would discourage participation in further expert
teams. The process of reporting in the activity report tool, ART, is indicated as the most complex and
burdensome aspect. The administrative burden, however, was not indicated as one of the reasons for
not participating by the three tax administrations not having taken part in any expert team; instead,
this appears related to a lack of interest or specific expertise.
Finally, respondents were asked to compare the overall administrative burden under the current the
Fiscalis programme funding cycle with the arrangements of the previous cycle. Just over half of the
respondents (12 out of 22) believe that the current management process is more or much more
onerous than the previously, while another seven did not experience any change, and only three
reported improvements. Additionally, respondents noted that NPCs handle more responsibilities in
the current cycle, including budget management and reporting, which were previously managed by
the Commission. The introduction of the grant coordinator role has increased national coordinators’
independence but also created coordination challenges. As their role becomes more operational,
NPCs face a heavier workload with fewer resources.
Overall added value of the Fiscalis programme
The third section of the questionnaire focused on the extent to which respondents believe that the
programme has contributed to achieving results that could not have been achieved by national
administration acting on their own, i.e. generating EU added value. Most respondents find
collaborative actions useful or very useful (21 out of 22), while 20 out of 22 respondents find expert
teams useful, though they were slightly less enthusiastic on them than on collaborative actions.
Respondents specifically emphasised the significant value of collaborative actions and expert teams
in promoting cooperation, sharing best practices, and harmonising the implementation of EU laws.
In particular, the CESOP expert team was highlighted for its role in enabling countries to contribute
to and benefit from these efforts, fostering a unified approach to issues like fiscal fraud and VAT
90
implementation across the EU. These actions are seen as crucial for improving national
implementation processes and encouraging collaboration among tax administrations.
The feedback on the overall added value of the Fiscalis programme was also overwhelmingly
positive, with the majority of respondents finding that the Fiscalis programme contributed to a faster
implementation of EU legislation and application of EU rules. The area with the most positive
responses was the extent to which the Fiscalis programme contributed to building trust and to
convergence among tax administrations. However, there was some difference in opinion regarding
whether the Fiscalis programme adds value beyond national-level initiatives, with a few respondents
expressing uncertainty or differing views on this aspect.
Through follow-up questions, respondents reported that the Fiscalis programme has had a significant
impact on efficiency and international cooperation, particularly through the development and
implementation of IT systems like VIES and projects such as VAT in the Digital Age, both of which
were mentioned a couple of times. Additionally, respondents highlighted the value of workshops, IT
training, and collaborative networks, including those focused on e-invoicing, which have greatly
supported tax administrations in implementing EU legislation and sharing best practices.
Figure 17. Fiscalis programme added value for national administration
Source: NFC consultations.
Finally, respondents were asked to estimate the extent to which they would still be able to participate
in collaborative actions under two possible budget scenarios for the programme: the first, entailing a
reduction in the coverage of expenses, and the second, a reduction in the total elimination of funding
for collaborative actions. Under a partial reduction scenario, tax administrations would still reportedly
participate in at least some actions, but in most cases (12 out of 22) with a major reduction, while a
smaller number of respondents indicated only a minor reduction in participation. In the absence of
Fiscalis programme funding, three out of 22 respondents would not be able to participate in any
action, while another 12 would need to majorly cut back on participation.
Participants were also requested to indicate which types of action and topic they would prioritise if
Fiscalis programme funding were reduced. In their responses, several highlighted that they believe
91
extended collaboration activities (such as project groups) have a higher return on investment than
workshops, and so they would tend to privilege the former. Some respondents mentioned that they
would prioritise topics and actions based on national and EU priorities, with some highlighting the
importance of IT systems and multilateral controls (MLCs). Additionally, some noted that prioritising
would be on a case-by-case basis, taking into account specific needs at the time. Furthermore,
Member States would reportedly reduce the number of participants by adopting a more selective
approach and by participating more in online-only events.
Validation of and reflections on the previous evaluation
This final section of the survey investigated the extent to which the conclusions drawn in the final
evaluation of the Fiscalis 2020 programme (2014-2020) were still valid in the context of the current
Fiscalis programme (2021-2027).
The feedback provided by the 22 respondents suggests that the majority strongly agreed that the
impact of the Fiscalis programme was positive across various areas. Specifically, most respondents
highlighted the programme’s significant contribution to enhancing authorities’ administrative
capacity, the reduction of administrative burdens, and the fight against tax fraud, tax evasion, and
aggressive tax planning. While the consensus was overwhelmingly positive, some respondents were
neutral, particularly regarding the alignment of IT systems and collaborative actions with the specific
needs of EU tax administrations, which indicates some uncertainty.
Figure 18. Extent to which the conclusions of the previous evaluation are still valid under the current Fiscalis funding cycle
Source: NFC consultations.
92
Building on the previous responses, participants were asked to elaborate on their experiences and
reflections regarding the Fiscalis programme. In their replies, respondents consistently highlighted
the importance of training actions funded by the programme, with several specific systems and
training initiatives being frequently mentioned. CESOP and TNA were noted as key IT systems that
contribute significantly to the fight against tax fraud and support operational efficiency. EU AIAC
(Advanced International Administrative Cooperation), AIAC training and Eurofisc networks were
also emphasised for their role in enhancing collaboration and sharing best practices, particularly in
cross-border tax matters.
In comparison to previous Fiscalis programme cycles, respondents noted improvements in flexibility
– with Member States now able to initiate their own project groups – and increased use of hybrid
meetings. However, some respondents highlighted the growing administrative burden placed on
national coordinators and the complexity of financial rules, particularly the 80% pre-financing
threshold. Moving forward, suggestions for improvement included simplifying the funding process,
improving communication, and ensuring timely and sufficient funding to better support tax
administrations. Additionally, respondents recommended enhancements to IT systems like PICS and
emphasised the need for more targeted working visits to address specific national challenges and
further improve international cooperation.
3. Case study consultation activities
Each case study included the collection of documentary evidence and interviews with stakeholder
directly involved in the technical aspects of the Fiscalis EESs but also with policy officers. The
stakeholder consultations were adapted to each case study’s EES. Additionally, concise online user
surveys were conducted for two of the case studies, namely VoW and the LMS. More specifically for
each case study:
Transaction Network Analysis system (TNA)
Stakeholders consulted included representatives from DG TAXUD, as well as 15 Eurofisc liaison
officers, including (i) the Eurofisc chair and grant coordinator for the TNA expert team; (ii) the
current and former WF1 coordinators; (iii) the current WF2 coordinator; (iv) the Europol, EPPO and
OLAF contact point within Eurofisc; (v) other ENLOs and ELOs, including members of both WF1
and WF2, and members of the TNA expert team.
Directive on Administrative Cooperation (DAC6)
Consultations were conducted with Administrative Cooperation on Direct Taxation (ACDT)
delegates representing 13 Member States58. Participants held a range of roles within their national tax
administrations, covering both policy and operational dimensions of DAC6. These included
representatives of the competent authority responsible for implementation, IT specialists involved in
system development and management of the central directory, and coordinators or analysts supporting
58 Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, Estonia, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Spain,
Sweden.
93
the day-to-day application of DAC6 requirements. Some also worked across multiple DAC
frameworks or broader areas of administrative cooperation, providing a wider perspective.
VIES-on-the-web (VoW) system
In-depth interviews were conducted, each lasting around an hour, with officials of the tax
administrations (members of SCAC and SCIT – the standing committees on administrative
cooperation and on information technology) of six different MS. Where administrations were unable
to participate in interviews, they provided input through written responses to the interview questions.
The participants included representatives from Bulgaria (SCIT), Denmark (SCAC), Germany (SCIT,
written answers), Hungary (SCAC, written answers), Lithuania (SCIT) and Slovenia (SCIT).
A short survey was launched on the VoW interface to assess the added value of the system, and of
the ability to check VAT numbers at the pan-European level compared to national interfaces (the
counterfactual scenario). This survey was designed to capture economic operators’ perspectives on
the costs and benefits of VoW. Access was provided through a link on the VoW website59, and the
survey ran for four weeks, from 10 March to 6 April 2025. The questionnaire clarified that VoW is
not a centralised database of VAT numbers but rather functions as an interface forwarding requests
to national VIES systems; the clarification was intended to prevent economic operators mistakenly
attributing blaming the VoW system for issues with national databases and their updates to the VIES.
A total of 1 248 survey responses were received. Most survey respondents were from Italy (21%),
Germany (10%), Poland (11%), and the Netherlands (7%), with the remaining respondents more or
less evenly distributed among the other 23 EU MS. Among the companies surveyed, 36% were micro
enterprises, 27% were small enterprises, 18% were medium enterprises, and 19% were large
enterprises.
In addition to the survey, six interviews were conducted. They were with a key business association
(one interview) as well as with specific member companies nominated by the association (three
interviews with medium and large enterprises in the retail, online platforms and energy sectors). Two
of the interviews were held with large companies, including a digital platform. This interview
approach complemented the survey and allowed for cross validation of survey results.

Survey respondents and interviewees consistently highlighted speed and reliability60 as primary
benefits of VoW61. Survey data shows that 70% of economic operators are satisfied with the speed of
VAT number verification, and 64% appreciated the platform’s ease of use (see Figure 19).
Significantly, 53% of survey respondents indicated that verifying VAT numbers took less than one
minute62, with an additional 36% stating it takes between one and three minutes. To the question
‘what would you say are the main benefits of VoW for your business’, respondents consistently
mentioned the platform’s speed: ‘quick check’, ‘fast action’, ‘rapid verification’63. Respondents also
emphasised the reliability of the platform and its vital importance in ensuring tax compliance64. In
interviews, some economic operators expressed confidence in the accuracy of information from
VoW, including on company address details. VoW’s availability rate of 99.92% in 2024, consistent
since 201465, underscores its dependability. Tax authorities also reported that VoW operates
effectively, receiving few complaints from national taxpayers, which indicates its stability.
However, in interviews, some large enterprises, who conduct over 100 000 VAT verifications daily,
raised concerns about the service’s reliability. These operators reported experiencing periods of
unavailability and highlighted inadequate communication from the European Commission regarding
scheduled service downtimes, noting instances where planned downtimes were not announced or did
not align with the provided schedule.
Excise movement and control system (EMCS)
Several interviews were conducted to help build the evidence base of the case study. Multiple policy
officers from DG TAXUD, each with direct and in-depth experience of EMCS, were interviewed to
help refine the team’s understanding of this complex IT system. These EU-level insights were further
complemented by three consultations with MS competent authorities. These discussions helped
assess both the costs and benefits of the current system and the potential implications under the
counterfactual scenario–for example, the impact if Member States could no longer verify excise
information via a central SEED. Finally, the team also spoke with 11 economic operators and
industry associations from the alcohol and tobacco sectors. These stakeholders shared their views
on the overall functioning of EMCS, the EU-level applications like SEED-on-Europa, and their
perspectives on recent system updates such as EMCS phase 4.

Learning Management System (LMS)
For this case study, the stakeholder consultation consisted of two main parts:
• A series of interviews with DG TAXUD, the contractor responsible for developing and operating
the LMS, and tax officials taking part in the TSG from five Member States. The sample took into
account diversity in terms of both geography and varying levels of engagement with the LMS
based on the statistics provided by DG TAXUD, and covered Germany, Greece, Ireland,
Lithuania and Spain66. Eight interviews were conducted in total, based on a semi-structured
format that used pre-defined questions agreed with DG TAXUD, while also allowing interviewees
to go into more detail on issues of particular importance to them. While a few additional Member
States declined to participate due to limited experience with the LMS, the sample was sufficient
to gather significant insight into the LMS and in line with the approach originally proposed.
• A survey of LMS users was promoted on the LMS site itself as well as by TSG members. The
survey was conducted together with the parallel case study on the LMS for the Customs platform
and garnered 62 replies, of which 10 mentioned an interest in taxation only and 19 mentioned an
interest in both taxation and customs; the remaining 33 respondents expressed an interest in
customs only and are not referred to in this report. Of the respondents interested in tax, 15 were
from tax authorities and 10 from customs authorities, while two represented both tax and customs
administrations, and just two were from private organisations. Given the relatively small sample
size, and the fact that most respondents seem likely to have been TSG members rather than course
participants as such, the survey cannot be deemed representative of all LMS users, but it
nonetheless adds value by providing structured input on a wide range of issues of interest, thereby
serving to corroborate and expand on the interview findings. In addition, the case study also drew
on the findings of the survey and interviews conducted for the programme assessment part of the
evaluation, which included several questions on the LMS in addition to other topics.
Overall, the methodology was implemented as planned and collected sufficient insight for a robust
and meaningful analysis. A limitation that should be noted is that very little input was collected
directly from economic operators / private stakeholders, an important secondary target audience for
the LMS. In addition, no formal usage targets were set prior to the LMS launch, limiting the extent
to which it has been possible to gauge success in terms of initial expectations for the platform. Instead,
the findings have been contextualised based on the views and perceptions of stakeholders, and the
judgement of the evaluators, transparently explained.

with the LMS.

INTRODUCTION
PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THE EVALUATION
The purpose of this ex-post evaluation is to assess the outputs and outcomes achieved by the
Consumer Programme 2014-20201 (hereinafter ‘Programme’), and the progress made towards
the set objectives and its longer impact. It focuses on the five evaluation criteria: effectiveness,
efficiency, relevance, coherence, and the EU added value of the actions funded. Where
applicable, further evaluation criteria were applied: utility, complementarity, equity,
coordination, sustainability, and acceptability.
It covers the period between 2014 and 2020, while building up on the findings, conclusions,
and recommendations of the mid-term evaluation2. The mid-term evaluation covered the period
between 2014 and 2017. It considers the implementation of the Programme in all EU countries,
as well as in Norway and Iceland3. The evaluation exercise provides the necessary space for
reflection on whether the Programme had been flexible to respond to the needs of its
stakeholders, i.e. consumer organisations, Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC)
authorities, European Consumers Centres (ECC) who are its direct beneficiaries, and
consumers who benefit from a better implemented and enforced consumer law. It identifies the
main problems in its implementation and lessons learned.
This retrospective evaluation meets the legal obligation set out in Article 34 of the Financial
Regulation (EU) No 2018/10464. The Financial Regulation requires an evaluation of all
programmes and activities that entail significant overall spending. While it does not define the
level of the ‘significant spending’, the Better Regulation guidelines set an indicative threshold
at least at EUR 5 million. The Programme was a continuation of the Consumer Programme
2007-2013. It is closed now, while most of its activities continue to be funded under the Single
Market Programme 2021-2027, albeit with some necessary adaptations5. To the extent possible
the evaluation findings will feed into the design of the Multi-annual Financial Framework
2028-2034.
The evaluation applied a mixed-method approach, including desk reviews of literature,
programme documentation, and a sample of grants and procurement files. Stakeholder input
was gathered via a call for evidence, an online survey of beneficiaries (n = 57), targeted
1 Regulation (EU) No 254/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on a
multiannual consumer programme for the years 2014-20 and repealing Decision No 1926/2006/EC
2 Report from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social
Committee and the Committee of the Regions. COM(2019) 490 final, and Commission Staff Working
Document. SWD(2019) 382 final.
3 According to Article 7 of the Programme Regulation, participation in the Programme shall be open to the
countries of the European Free Trade Association participating in the European Economic Area, i.e. Norway,
Iceland and Liechtenstein.
4 Regulation (EU) No 254/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on a
multiannual consumer programme for the years 2014-20
5 Only two actions of the Consumer Programme 2007-2013 do not feature in the Consumer Programme 2014-
2020, namely the financial contribution to ANEC, which represents consumer interests in standardisation,
and was transferred to Regulation (EU) No. 2015/2012 on European Standardisation, and financial
contributions for the development of integrated European master’s degree courses in consumer issues. This
Programme also took into account new priorities under the Juncker Commission, including new focus on
sustainable consumption and circular economy.
2
interviews, and five focus groups covering each Programme objective and one cross-cutting
theme. The evaluation was supported by an external 6￼ and drew limited additional7.￼ Further
methodological information is detailed in Annex II and Annex III. The structure of this report
follows the five evaluation criteria and answers the evaluation questions per Programme’s
specific objective.
The evaluation faced several methodological and data-related challenges, which were mitigated
to the extent possible through triangulation and additional data collection. These limitations
include:
•
Data governance issues: Administrative changes during the Programme period led to
incomplete or inconsistent programme management data, particularly in project
tracking.
•
Data accessibility and quality concerns: Funding and performance data, especially for
procurement contracts, were manually recorded, often lacking standardisation, which
affected reliability and comparability across actions.
•
Stakeholder participation deficits: The overall response rate to the consultation tools
was low. The online survey had only 57 responses, mainly from beneficiaries, which
limits the generalisability of the findings.
•
Methodological limitations in indicator design: The Programme relied heavily on
output-based indicators as set in Annex II of the Regulation. These were not
systematically complemented by outcome or impact indicators, limiting the capacity to
assess behavioural or systemic effects.
Despite this multi-source approach, the evaluation encountered major data limitations.
Baselines for several outcome and impact-level indicators were missing or poorly defined at
the outset of the Programme. For example, there was no shared baseline for consumer detriment
beyond the one-off Consumer Detriment Study, no standardised data on whether businesses
changed their compliance behaviour because of Programme-funded actions. While awareness
and reach of campaigns were tracked, behavioural follow-up was rare, and longitudinal data to
assess sustained effects were absent. Business-side data were also lacking, except for proxy
indicators from CPC sweeps or RAPEX reactions. Inconsistencies in Member State reporting,
especially within the CPC system, further limited the ability to assess cross-country effects.
The ODR platform itself lacked integrated monitoring of user satisfaction, case quality, or
reasons for complaint attrition, making it difficult to assess outcome quality.
Mitigation included use of external Scoreboard data, case studies, and a theory-of-change
approach to assess causal links. Triangulation of qualitative and quantitative data supported the
analysis, although the lack of baseline and counterfactual data prevented econometric

relevance, and added value. It found that many organisations were unaware of the Programme or its broader
objectives, though some achievements, such as RAPEX/Safety Gate, the CPC Network, and support to
policymaking, were recognised. The Programme was seen as flexible and responsive. Future programmes

interpreted cautiously due to selection and recall bias. These constraints informed the careful
framing of conclusions and lessons learned.
2.
WHAT WAS THE EXPECTED OUTCOME OF THE INTERVENTION?
2.1 Policy context
Article 169 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union requires the EU to
contribute to protecting the health, safety, and economic interests of consumers through actions
in the field of consumer protection and also to take consumer protection requirements into
account in defining and implementing other Union policies and activities. Besides the
possibility to adopt legislative proposals in the context of completion of the internal market,
the EU may adopt measures to support, supplement and monitor the policy pursued at national
level to promote consumers’ rights to information, education and to organise themselves. The
Commission outlined its strategic vision for EU consumer policy in the European Consumer
Agenda8. To support the European Consumer Agenda and to cope with the challenges outlined
in it, the Commission adopted a multi-annual Consumer Programme for the years 2014-2020.
The Programme contained targeted policies that contributed to the 2030 Agenda for
Sustainable Development9, concretely to its Goal 12 on Sustainable Consumption and
Production and Goal 3 on Ensuring Healthy Lives.
2.2 Description of the intervention and its objectives
Key challenges that the Programme was meant to address were identified in its 2011 impact
assessment10:
1. Product safety: Uneven enforcement across Member States and the lack of a pan-European
framework compromised the safety of the Single Market. Global supply chains increased risks,
while the absence of EU-level coordination reduced the value of co-financing.
2. Consumer information and education: Inadequate data on consumer behaviour, weak
capacity of consumer organisations (especially in newer Member States), and lack of clear,
comparable information hindered consumer decision-making, particularly in cross-border
contexts. EU tools were not adapted to digital developments.
3. Consumer rights and redress: Consumer protection remained weak in cross-border
situations, with low confidence in online shopping and limited awareness of redress
mechanisms. There was also a need to better integrate consumer interests into EU policies,
including digitalisation, sustainability, and social inclusion.
4. Enforcement: the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network was underutilised, with
untapped potential for coordination. Moreover, the European Consumer Centres Network
(ECC-Net) lacked visibility, and needed strengthening to more effectively support cross-border
complain resolution.
The Programme’s intervention logic (see Figure 1) illustrates how its objectives, resources,
and outputs are expected to generate results, based on key assumptions for success. It responds
to a context of weak market monitoring, under-resourced consumer organisations, and limited
8 COM(2012) 225 final
9 https://sdgs.un.org/2030agenda
10 COM(2011) 1320 final
4
consumer awareness, factors that contribute to higher consumer detriment from unsafe
products and non-compliant business practices.
To address these challenges, the Programme aimed to ensure a high level of consumer
protection, empower consumers, and place them at the centre of the internal market, in line
with the Europe 2020 strategy (Article 2 of the Programme Regulation). It sought to protect
consumers’ health, safety, and economic interests, promote their rights to information and
education, and support the integration of consumer interests into other policy areas. The
Programme complemented and supported Member State policies and was structured around
four specific objectives and 11 action types (Article 4 and Annex I), further detailed in 40
activities (see Table 1). Funded actions addressed digitalisation, information complexity,
sustainability, and diverse consumer vulnerabilities.

internal market, through a sequence of actions organised under four specific objectives. This
logic linked inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and long-term impacts, while also making
key assumptions about how and why the intervention would work. The evaluation used this
logic to systematically test whether causal links materialised and whether these assumptions
held in practice.
The intervention logic followed a theory-of-change structure:
→ If the Programme funded cross-border cooperation and enforcement tools (e.g. CPC,
ECC-Net),
→ Then Member States would better enforce consumer protection rules,
→ Which leads to greater consumer confidence and protection in the Single Market.
Objective I: Funding for coordinated actions on product safety → better market surveillance
→ fewer unsafe products.
Each of the Programme’s specific objectives followed a distinct causal pathway. Under
Objective I, the Programme funded activities such as scientific risk assessments, data-sharing
mechanisms, and market surveillance coordination, particularly through the Safety
Gate/RAPEX system. The underlying assumption was that more timely and accurate
information would enable national authorities to respond more effectively to unsafe products,
while at the same time providing for cost saving, as testing did not have to be repeated across
Member States. This was explored in the evaluation using Safety Gate/RAPEX data, which
indicated that the proportion of reactions to alerts increased substantially, from 39% at baseline
to over 70% by the end of the Programme. The Coordinated Actions for the Safety of Products
(CASP) provided complementary evidence through coordinated testing, joint risk assessments,
and market surveillance campaigns. Results of all activites can be found in Safety Gate/RAPEX
and ICSMS, but most importantly trust and methods of cooperation between MSAs was
fostered, and common risk assessment methodologies were developed. Complex or novel
products that provided a challenge to MSAs were also addressed in CASP. Despite those
actions being a step towards improved product safety across the EU, enforcement responses
varied considerably across Member States, reflecting differences in administrative capacity and
prioritisation. The available evidence suggests that the causal link between alerts and consumer
protection was stronger where authorities acted promptly, and weaker in Member States with
limited resources or follow-up mechanisms.
Objective II: Consumer education tools → increased knowledge of rights → more confident
and empowered consumers.
Objective II addressed consumer awareness, education, and support for civil society actors such
as consumer organisations. Activities included Europe-wide awareness campaigns, market
studies, and capacity-building support to national and EU-level organisations. The underlying
assumption was that better-informed consumers would make more confident and rational
decisions, thereby reducing the incidence of detriment and improving trust in the market. The
evaluation tested this logic through Consumer Conditions Scoreboard data and campaign
metrics. Within this logic, campaigns like #YourEUright aimed to reach large audiences across
the EU to increase knowledge of rights, while capacity-building support to organisations such
as BEUC sought to strengthen their ability to advocate for consumers and engage in
3
policymaking at both EU and national levels. The causal pathway therefore linked large-scale
information provision and enhanced organisational capacity to intermediate outcomes such as
higher consumer awareness, stronger representation, and ultimately more informed consumer
choices and improved market trust.
Objective III: Development and promotion of ADR/ODR mechanisms → better access to
redress → reduced need for court procedures.
Under Objective III, the Programme aimed to improve access to redress through actions such
as the development of the Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) platform and support for national
Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) schemes. The assumption was that increasing access to
easy, low-cost dispute mechanisms would reduce unresolved complaints and increase
consumer satisfaction. This assumption was tested using ODR usage statistics and ADR uptake
data. Within this logic, the ODR platform was intended to offer consumers and traders a simple,
multilingual entry point for resolving cross-border disputes online, while support to ADR
schemes aimed to expand their availability, improve quality standards, and ensure consistent
coverage across the EU. The causal pathway linked the availability and accessibility of these
mechanisms to higher resolution rates, greater consumer confidence in seeking redress, and
ultimately improved market trust.
Objective IV: Support for ECC-Net and CPC sweeps → improved enforcement and consumer
support → higher trust in cross-border commerce.
Objective IV focused on enforcement, supporting joint actions between national authorities,
coordination through the CPC network, and the work of the ECCs. The Programme assumed
that better cooperation tools and training would lead to faster, more consistent enforcement of
consumer law across borders. Within this logic, CPC cooperation mechanisms, shared IT tools,
and targeted training were intended to strengthen cross-border case handling, facilitate timely
information exchange, and enable coordinated market surveillance actions. Support to ECCs
was designed to enhance assistance to consumers in cross-border cases, feeding intelligence
back into enforcement networks. The causal pathway linked these measures to intermediate
outcomes such as more efficient resolution of enforcement requests, greater consistency of
enforcement actions across Member States, and ultimately higher levels of consumer protection
in the internal market.
The evaluation tested these assumptions and causal links using a mix of quantitative and
qualitative methods. Indicators from Annex II of the Regulation were used to assess outputs,
including the number of RAPEX alerts, ECC contacts, ODR complaints, and grants awarded.
To evaluate outcomes and impacts, the assessment relied on the Consumer Scoreboard, ECC
and CPC network data, and key studies such as the 2017 research on measuring consumer
detriment. Focus groups, interviews, and project reporting also provided insights into
behavioural effects and enforcement practices, helping to validate or challenge the assumptions
embedded in the logic model.
Beyond its internal logic, the Programme’s outcomes were shaped by external factors. The
COVID-19 pandemic increased consumer vulnerability and accelerated digitalisation,
highlighting the need for flexible, digital-first tools while disrupting some enforcement
activities. Rapid growth in e-commerce introduced new challenges not foreseen at design stage.
Regional disparities in consumer awareness and institutional capacity also influenced
implementation success. Additionally, interaction with other EU initiatives (e.g. LIFE, Rights
4
and Equality, Consumer Agenda) created both synergies and attribution challenges. To assess
the effectiveness and coherence of the Programme, the intervention logic was not only
reconstructed but also used systematically throughout the evaluation as an analytical
framework.

HOW HAS THE SITUATION EVOLVED OVER THE EVALUATION PERIOD?
3.1 Programme management
The Programme was managed by DG Justice and Consumers and implemented by the
Consumer, Health, Agriculture and Food Executive Agency (CHAFEA) until its closure in
2021, after which responsibilities were transferred to the European Innovation Council and
SMEs Executive Agency (EISMEA). The transition affected the accessibility of data storage,
and documentation, creating challenges for the evaluation.
3.2 Programme implementation
The Commission implemented the Programme via annual work programmes. Funding was
provided through operating grants, action grants (including joint actions between Member
States), event grants, enforcement grants, and procurement contracts for studies, IT tools,
training, and awareness campaigns. Co-financing rates ranged from 50% to 95% (Article 8 of
17 Average 2007-2010; no data available for 2011-2013.
9
the Programme Regulation). Funding was awarded through competitive procedures, including
calls for proposals, tenders, reimbursements, and indemnities.
3.3 Budget overview
The Programme was allocated a budget of EUR 188.8 million, with an additional EUR 5.6
million from EFTA countries (Norway and Iceland), bringing the total to EUR 194.4 million.
Of this, EUR 175.5 million was for operational commitments and EUR 18.9 million for
administrative and support costs, 64% of which went to executive agencies. Annual
commitments were stable, with a notable increase in 2019. Payments lagged behind
commitments, with no disbursement in 2014. From 2015 to 2024, EUR 169.9 million was
spent, yielding an absorption rate of 87.4%, higher than comparable programmes like LIFE
(64.1%) and Rights, Equality and Citizenship (84.2%).
Grants amounted to EUR 62.2 million, supporting 270 projects across 30 countries and 130
beneficiaries. Most funding went to Objective IV (69%), followed by Objective II (21%),
Objective I (8%), and Objective III (2%). Only seven projects were cross-border. Funding was
concentrated in Belgium, Germany, and the Netherlands, which received 47% of total grant
funds. Grants typically covered half of project costs. Procurement totaled EUR 107.7 million,
financing 573 contracts with 116 entities. While many contracts were under EUR 100,000,
large projects like RAPEX/Safety Gate, CASP, the ODR platform, and consumer campaigns
absorbed nearly half the budget. Procurement levels were steady (EUR 11 million/year) except
in 2019, when funding nearly doubled due to a shift from grants to procurement in key areas.
The total cost of the Programme is estimated at EUR 230 million. This includes EUR 194.4
million from the EU budget, and an estimated EUR 41.5 million in co-financing provided by
grant beneficiaries. The actual co-financing rates varied between 50% and 95% depending on
the type of action and beneficiary. Therefore, a weighted average co-financing rate of 60% was
applied to estimate the overall contribution from stakeholders. By objective, Objective II and
IV received the largest shares of funding (32% and 35%, respectively). Under Objective II,
Action 4 (evidence base) and Action 5 (support to consumer organisations) received the most
funding, while Action 7 (consumer education) saw notable growth. Under Objective I, Action
2 (market surveillance coordination) accounted for 86% of funding, with a 58% increase
between 2018–2019 following a strategic shift to procurement. Table 3 and Annex V provide
further detail on funded projects by year and activity.

EVALUATION FINDINGS (ANALYTICAL PART)
To what extent was the Consumer Programme successful and why?
4.1 Effectiveness
This section assesses whether activities funded delivered the expected outputs and contributed
to outcomes and impacts in line with the intervention logic. The evaluation found that the
Programme has been broadly effective in achieving its objectives.
Objective I: Product Safety
Objective I aimed to ensure a high level of product safety across the EU through activities
funded under Actions 1 to 3: provision of scientific advice, coordination of market surveillance
and enforcement, and risk analysis. Over 80% of the objective’s operational budget was
allocated to Action 2, especially via the Safety Gate/RAPEX system and CASP (Coordinated
Activities on Safety of Products).
The mid-term evaluation found that the funded activities were largely effective. Safety
Gate/RAPEX became a central pillar of EU market surveillance, enabling rapid cross-border
communication and information sharing between national authorities. Between 2014 and 2020,
over 14 000 alerts and 30 000 follow-up actions were recorded, demonstrating its expanding
reach18. However, achievement levels were influenced by limited staffing and financial
resources in national market surveillance authorities. Stakeholders noted the continued
18 Safety Gate Reports 2014-2020.
11
presence of unsafe products, especially due to e-commerce, cross-border trade, and the rising
complexity of items like connected devices and wearables. These trends demanded more agile
enforcement, straining existing capacities. Nonetheless, the Programme demonstrated strong
effectiveness through sustained investment in CASP and ongoing development of Safety
Gate/RAPEX, including new business reporting tools and better integration with national IT
systems19. The Safety Gate/RAPEX enables the rapid exchange of information between
national authorities on measures taken against products, thus facilitating coordinated actions
across the single market. It also provides accessible information to the wider public via its
online portal.20
Table 2 above presents progress under Objective I, based on two key indicators from the
Regulation. The percentage of Safety Gate/RAPEX notifications triggering follow-up actions
rose steadily from 2014 to 2018. A dip to 51%)21 was due to a surge in COVID related alerts
with limited traceability, but by 2020 the rate climbed to 72%, far exceeding the 47.5% target
set. The reactions-per-notification ratio also improved from 1.28 in 2014 to 2.69 in 2020,
showing stronger cross-border cooperation. Safety Gate/RAPEX demonstrated its
effectiveness and agility, especially during the pandemic, for example, 25 million unsafe masks
were flagged in June 2020. In 2019–2020, alerts covered about 41.8 million products,
averaging 77,900 per notification, with 97% classified as serious risks22. Most notifications
concern serious risk (97%), highlighting the system’s focus on preventing the most dangerous
threats to consumer health and safety. Data quality also improved over the Programme period,
with fewer notifications missing key manufacturer details like batch numbers or barcodes.
However, gaps remain regarding product identification (e.g. model type), pointing to a need
for further improvements23. The steady volume of dangerous goods reported and followed up
through Safety Gate/RAPEX indicates that coordinated action and rapid communication have
helped reduce unsafe products in the EU market.
Focus group participants confirmed Safety Gate/RAPEX’s critical role in consumer protection
but identified areas for improvement. A key gap is the lack of linked accident or injury data,
which limits the ability to fully assess consumer safety impacts. Participants also stressed the
need for more harmonised risk assessments and regular training for national authorities.
Ongoing efforts, mainly through CASP, are addressing these challenges. Limited product
traceability, especially in complex global supply chains, remains a barrier to effective
enforcement. Participants suggested that allowing trusted external bodies (e.g. consumer
organisations) to submit structured alerts could enhance responsiveness. Some also noted that
they rarely receive follow-up from authorities after submitting product concerns, which
undermines feedback loops and system trust. Improved interoperability between Safety
Gate/RAPEX and ICSMS allowed faster data sharing and reduced duplication; by 2020, over
90% of national authorities used ICSMS to upload surveillance findings.

Joint cooperation and enforcement actions and the Coordinated Activities on the Safety
of Products (CASP) significantly enhanced national-level market surveillance. These
initiatives supported implementation of the General Product Safety Directive (Directive
2001/95/EC) through coordinated testing, risk assessment, surveillance operations, awareness
campaigns, and customs cooperation. In CASP 2019 and 2020, 17 product categories were
assessed. In 2019, 652 products were tested, with a 75% non-compliance rate, generating 170
RAPEX alerts. In 2020, 775 products were tested across 12 activities, with unsafe or non-
compliant products ranging from 12% to over 80%, depending on the product group.
Specialised labs carried out risk assessments that often triggered RAPEX activity.24 25
Stakeholders, including national surveillance authorities, CSN members, and EU officials,
stressed that joint tools like guidelines and handbooks improved coordination and capacity,
especially for smaller Member States. 26 CASP also piloted innovative cooperation methods,
such as mystery shopping in e-commerce, joint communication campaigns, and rapid risk
assessments during COVID-19. These activities strengthened technical capacity and promoted
a more harmonised and proactive surveillance culture across the EU.
The Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) provided essential risk assessments
that shaped EU safety regulations. During the term 2016-202127, it adopted 66 final opinions,
including on hair dyes (14), cosmetic ingredients (30), nanomaterial in cosmetics (9), and
statements and other outputs (13). The important output documents of the SCCS are the ‘SCCS
Notes of Guidance for the testing of the cosmetic ingredients and their safety evaluation’ (9th28,
10th29 and 11th revisions30), as well as a memorandum on the use of In Silico Methods for
Assessment of Chemical Hazards. These opinions have had major impact on legislation of
cosmetic products, by providing the risk assessment on which the risk management decisions
were taken.31 The 11th revision also aimed to make findings more accessible to non-experts,
including regulators and businesses. Beyond cosmetics, the SCCS contributed to the EU-wide
debate on nanomaterial safety, extending its impact to other regulatory areas.
