Objective II: Consumer information and education, evidence base and support to
consumer organisations
The mid-term evaluation found that, by the end of 2017, the Programme delivered mixed
results. It was effective in developing the evidence base, with Scoreboards and market studies
influencing consumer policy at both EU and national levels. It also successfully supported EU-
level consumer organisations, notably BEUC. However, consumer information and education
measures, such as the Consumer Champion training and Consumer Classroom, were less
effective. Although awareness campaigns met engagement targets, they had limited long-term
impact on consumer awareness. Key challenges included limited resources, lack of curriculum
integration, and the inability of training alone to overcome organisational capacity gaps. The
evaluation concluded that information campaigns had mixed results in contributing to the
Programme’s objectives. Despite earlier challenges, more recent campaigns showed improved
reach and engagement. Fully funded by the Programme, these educational efforts aimed to
boost awareness and confidence, particularly in cross-border online shopping. According to
interviews and literature, they helped inform consumers about their rights. The #YourEUright
campaign, targeting 18–35-year-olds, used social media, influencers, and interactive events
(e.g. escape rooms), reaching over 319 million contacts and generating 94 million
interactions38. Other specific campaigns included an information campaign to raise consumer
awareness on their rights39, a campaign targeting young consumers between 18 and 35 years
old about what rights they have when they take out a credit, and an awareness raising on energy
efficiency targeting energy poor households40. An ‘ex-ante evaluation for awareness raising
and promotion campaign for energy efficiency in households’ was conducted to guide decision-
making on the use of the Programme resources for communication campaigns. An evaluation
of the campaign on consumer credit rights among young consumers concluded that the
campaign’s objectives were relevant, given low financial literacy levels in Austria and Czechia,
however, the age range was too broad for effective communication. The campaign had limited
impact, raised only low awareness. Focus group and survey results showed no significant
increase in knowledge. Media coverage was modest, mostly found in financial sections
unlikely to be read by young adults.41 While the campaigns' targets in terms of hits or
impression were typically achieved, little long-term impact on consumer awareness was
discernible. Although ECCs and CSN made considerable efforts to reach vulnerable consumers
through dedicated campaigns and educational materials, evaluation of the campaign
suggested42 that more tailored communication strategies are needed to ensure these groups are
adequately informed and protected, particularly in the digital marketplace. This finding aligns
with that of the EESC, according to whom several communication initiatives under the
Programme, although well-intentioned and broadly disseminated, lacked precision in their
targeting and sustainability of impact. The Committee highlighted that without long-term

Despite efforts to improve consumer awareness, achieving tangible educational outcomes—
particularly among young people, remained difficult. Consumer Classroom, launched in 2013
as a multilingual EU platform for secondary school teachers (students aged 12–18), provided
resources on consumer rights, sustainable consumption, and financial literacy. While it offered
a rich library and collaborative tools, uptake was limited. Focus group participants attributed
this to low school interest, largely because consumer education is not integrated into national
curricula. This highlights the ongoing challenge of embedding consumer topics in formal
education systems across Member States.
Consumer Champion, launched in 2014, aimed to build the capacity of consumer
organisations through training, networking, and resource sharing. Managed by BEUC until
2018, the programme aligned with Digital Single Market goals and featured an online platform
as a collaborative hub. However, it struggled with user engagement, especially with its e-
learning modules. Stakeholders noted the need for more localised content tailored to national
contexts and sectors like telecoms, digital services, and e-commerce. The impact of the 2019
transition from BEUC to the Commission could not be assessed, due to the absence of
consistent performance data before and after the shift. Consumer PRO is a train-the-trainer
programme implemented by BEUC from 2019 to July 2021, focused on equipping consumer
professionals with comprehensive knowledge of consumer law to facilitate peer training. The
programme successfully conducted 28 planned and 14 additional national training sessions,
reaching over 735 professionals and six European workshops attended by 178 participants.
Satisfaction rates were notably high, ranging from 90% to 100%. Follow-up surveys showed
18
that most participants were able to transfer the knowledge (80% for national trainings, 73% for
workshops) and apply the resources (77% and 76% respectively). The majority reported a
positive impact on themselves or their organisations (94% and 93% respectively).46 Consumer
Law Ready, launched in 2016 by the Commission in partnership with BEUC, Eurochambres,
and SMEUnited, aimed to improve SMEs’ understanding of EU and national consumer law
and thereby fostering consumer trust. Initially coordinated by BEUC, the project later
transitioned to Eurochambres. Since 2017, it has built a network of 24 national lead trainers
and around 2,500 local trainers across 24 Member States, training around 3,000 SMEs. The
programme covered topics like pre-contractual information requirements, right of withdrawal,
guarantees, unfair contract terms and unfair commercial practices. It also showed adaptability
by updating content to reflect legislative changes, creating targeted content on emerging issues,
and moving online during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In the stakeholder survey, most Objective II activities scored around "effective", while areas
such as representative actions, financial services awareness, and consumer education tools
scored between "neutral” and “effective". These findings, supported by interviews and focus
groups, suggest a need for more targeted and context-specific approaches to education and
awareness efforts.

It focused on enhancing understanding of consumer behaviour and market dynamics through

Stakeholders in the mid-term evaluation confirmed these studies were effective and
recommended more targeted, smaller-scale research, a practice now adopted in the 2021–2027
SMP. According to focus groups, the studies directly shaped EU and national policymaking,
and supported legislation and enforcement. They also influenced how consumer vulnerability
is understood, reinforcing the concept of bounded rationality, and moving away from the
assumption of fully rational consumer behaviour.
Despite substantial efforts, the Programme did not significantly improve consumer access to
simple, low-cost redress mechanisms, particularly ADR. The ODR platform, launched in 2016
and fully funded by the Programme, aimed to provide a single EU entry point for online
consumer disputes. While communication efforts were highly effective, actual use remained
limited. Backed by a 2015 ex-ante evaluation, the ODR campaign exceeded expectations: it
reached 21 million users on Facebook, 9 million on Twitter, and generated 13 million video
views, four times the forecast. The platform saw 2.8 million visits in 2019, with 200,000
monthly users, and a Christmas campaign achieved 6.2 times more clicks than expected.
Activities also included branding, communications support, and outreach to traders, but these
efforts did not translate into widespread platform use.
Despite high visibility and traffic, the ODR platform saw very low conversion rates. Between
2016 to 2021, only about 1% of submitted complaints, fewer than 200 annually, were resolved
20
via ADR48. This remained unchanged despite technical upgrades and improved guidance. In
response, the Commission proposed repealing the ODR Regulation in October 2023, with the
repeal adopted in December 2024 and set to take effect in July 2025, citing the platform’s
persistent underperformance and limited added value.
Barriers to effectiveness extended beyond the ODR platform. While the Programme funded its
launch and extensive awareness campaigns, its overall impact on access to redress was limited
by the fragmented transposition of the ADR Directive across Member States. Compliance with
ODR obligations varied significantly by country, sector, and trader size, with larger traders and
some Member States engaging more, while smaller traders often lacked awareness or
willingness to participate. Inconsistent implementation, complex cross-border procedures, and
limited monitoring further weakened ADR reliability. Despite improvements to the platform’s
interface and communications, these systemic issues remained unresolved during the
Programme period.
Some stakeholder responses to the Call for Evidence expressed critical views on enforcement
and redress mechanisms under Objective IV. Organisations such as Next Energy Consumer
(NEC), DECO (Portugal), ITM (Poland), MSPCA (Malta), and individual citizens (e.g. from
Germany) raised concerns about limited access to justice and ineffective ADR mechanisms,
especially for vulnerable consumers. NEC cited structural barriers such as low trader
participation and lack of trust in redress tools. DECO and ITM noted slow and inconsistent
enforcement, while MSPCA highlighted a lack of responsive authorities in cross-border cases.
These concerns indicate that while the Programme provided tools like CPCS and ECC-Net,
some stakeholders found practical redress outcomes lacking, particularly in high-risk sectors
or for underrepresented consumers. They underline the need to clarify the Programme’s role
versus Member State responsibilities and highlight persistent gaps not reflected in indicator
data. Funding for ADR activities also underperformed. While 50 ADR grants were awarded
between 2018 and 2020, the budget was not fully absorbed. Key barriers included the 50% co-
financing requirement and administrative burden, especially for smaller ADR bodies.
Simplification efforts had limited effect. However, from 2022, the successor funding
programme, the SMP increased the EU co-financing to 90% and streamlined applications,
leading to a notable increase in uptake. ECCs also contributed to the Objective III by informing
consumers about ADR options and ODR platform. They did so through awareness-raising
campaigns on their national websites and social media channels, or physical stands in major
European cities e.g. around Black Friday, Christmas period or summer sales, etc. Many ADR
entities were awarded grants to raise awareness on out-of-court dispute resolution e.g.
conferences, TV and radio slots, etc.
The analysis of Objective III indicators shows mixed performance in facilitating consumer
redress. Of the three core indicators, only Indicator 1 (number of ODR complaints) met its
target, with 147,000 submissions by 2020, showing high initial uptake. However, Indicator 2
(proportion of unresolved ECC cases referred to ADR) reached just 24%, well below the 75%
target, and Indicator 3 (proportion of consumers acting on a problem) remained at 67%, missing
the 90% target (see Table 7). The broad definition of “complaint” in Indicator 3 (e.g. contacting
the seller, not just formal redress) limits its relevance for assessing ADR/ODR effectiveness.

increased, trust, visibility, and practical usability did not. These results underscore the need for
stronger trader engagement, better incentives for ADR participation, and clearer, targeted
indicators to assess the real-world impact of funded redress tools.

The Consumer Conditions Scoreboard 202149 provides a useful summary of how consumers’
perception of consumer rights evolved over the period of 2014-2020. Highlights from this
report, in terms of the average proportion of EU consumers with a stated perception in the year
2020, all representing a significant improvement, were: 70% trusted public authorities to
protect consumer rights; 80% agreed that retailers and service providers generally respect
consumer rights; 66% trust non-governmental consumer organisations to protect consumer
rights; 63% feel confident purchasing goods or services via the internet from retailers or service
providers in their country; and 43% feel confident purchasing goods or services via the internet
from retailers or service providers in an/other EU country.
In the area of consumer redress, the 2021 Consumer Conditions Survey reported that in 2020,
47% of consumers agreed that it is easy to settle disputes with retailers and service providers
through an out-of-court body (a significant increase during the survey years 2014-2020). In
contrast, only 35% agreed that it is easy to settle disputes with retailers and service providers
through the courts (no significant change during the survey years 2014-2020). Additionally,
27% of respondents in 2020 reported a high level of knowledge of consumer rights, though no
comparable data were available for earlier years, limiting longitudinal analysis. However,
persistent barriers remain. While 77% of consumers did not experience any problems with
online purchases in 2020, consistent with previous years, there was a notable increase in the
proportion of consumers who encountered a problem but did not act to resolve it. Among the
main reasons cited were perceptions that it would take too long (50%), the amount at stake was
too small (43%), or that a satisfactory outcome was unlikely (38%). These findings suggest
that despite improved trust and legal frameworks, perceived inefficiencies and low expected
returns continue to discourage consumers from pursuing redress, particularly for minor
disputes. Taken together, Scoreboard results confirm that the Programme helped build
consumer trust and awareness, but its impact on redress behaviour remained limited, hindered
by structural issues such as complexity, delays, and low trader accountability.
The Citizens’ Energy Forum, co-organised by DG JUST and DG ENER, plays a strategic
role in promoting transparency and consumer participation in EU energy policy. Established in
2008, it brings together 200–300 stakeholders, including citizens, regulators, and industry
representatives. The Forum supports the development and enforcement of consumer rights in
the energy sector by fostering informed consumer engagement, facilitating dialogue between
regulators and industry, and helping to ensure that consumer perspectives are integrated into
energy market rules and redress mechanisms, particularly in the energy transition. The 2018
edition in Dublin focused on themes such as energy poverty, renewables, and consumer
protection, in line with the 'Clean Energy for All Europeans' and 'New Deal for Consumers'
packages.

under the Programme to ensure that the perspectives of users, particularly consumers, SMEs,
and civil society, are reflected in EU financial services policymaking. It directly contributes to
the Objective III by strengthening consumer rights in financial services by providing expert
advice that informs regulatory frameworks, and redress provisions. Composed of
representatives from consumer organisations, trade unions, academics, and other non-industry

Stakeholder feedback from the Programme’s online survey placed the effectiveness of
Objective III activities just below “effective” but above “neutral”, the lowest average score
across the four objectives. This suggests that while activities under Objective III were viewed
positively, their impact may have been less visible or more uneven than others. An exception
was the Citizens’ Energy Forum, which received a “very effective” score. Four activity types
were rated close to “effective”, while two scored nearer “neutral”: communication campaigns
and studies, training, actions or events, indicating scope for improvement in these areas. When
asked about the benefits of Objective III in their own countries, respondents rated most impacts
around “mostly achieved,” with three areas closer to “neutral”: awareness of financial services,
teacher resources for consumer education, and information on national consumer markets.
Overall, while Objective III strengthened EU-level frameworks for consumer redress and
improved coordination among ADR bodies, its practical impact at national level was uneven.
Persistent barriers, such as low trader participation in ODR, fragmented implementation of the
ADR Directive, and varying national commitment, limited improvements in consumers’ ability
to resolve disputes quickly and at low cost. These findings point to the need for more consistent
national implementation, targeted measures to increase trader engagement, and stronger
monitoring of ADR performance in future programming.
Objective IV: Enforcement
According to the mid-term evaluation, the Programme was successfully achieving Objective
IV by enhancing cooperation among national enforcement bodies and improving access to
enforcement-related advice for consumers. The CPC Network significantly expanded its
activities, becoming a cornerstone of EU consumer law enforcement. Mechanisms such as
mutual assistance, information exchange, and coordinated sweeps became more effective,
although handling times remained lengthy in some cases. CPC enforcement sweeps between
2014 and 2020 addressed sectors such as e-commerce, travel services, online reviews, and
misleading green claims, with non-compliance rates ranging from 42% to 78.7%. Most traders
corrected identified issues voluntarily, with enforcement action required in fewer than 18% of
cases. These actions contributed to notable improvements in compliance in targeted sectors.
Consumer trust in authorities and retailers increased, while reported consumer problems
slightly declined.
However, challenges remained. Stakeholders highlighted limited staffing and financial
resources in national authorities and the increasing complexity of products, services, and online
marketplaces as key obstacles. The CPC Network provided EU-wide added value by promoting
harmonised enforcement, supporting less-resourced authorities, and enabling best practice
exchange. Stakeholder support was strong: 15 of 19 responding national enforcement
24
authorities rated joint actions as “effective”, and sweeps were similarly well-regarded. Survey
and interview feedback confirmed the CPC’s relevance and the value of coordinated EU-level
enforcement. Capacity-building efforts were also central. Tools like the CPC Knowledge
Exchange Platform (CPC Wiki) and CPC Market Watch enhanced cooperation and risk
monitoring. The E-Enforcement Academy, launched in 2016, trained enforcement officials on
digital investigation skills through a mix of online and scenario-based modules. Performance
monitoring via the Single Market Scoreboard showed positive results: 66% of enforcement
requests were handled within 12 months (exceeding the 60% target), and 79% of information
requests were processed within three months (vs. a 50% target). These results demonstrate
improved efficiency and responsiveness across the CPC Network.
Enforcement cooperation and capacity building under Objective IV were core components
of the Programme’s effectiveness. From 2014 to 2020, a total of 859 exchanges of enforcement
officials took place, promoting standardised enforcement practices and cross-border
knowledge sharing. Survey responses from 7 participating national authorities rated the
exchange programme as effective (4) or very effective (2), with one neutral. While participation
varied by country, feedback confirmed its value.
Training for enforcement officials and the judiciary also received moderate to high
effectiveness ratings, reinforcing the importance of capacity-building. Other networking
activities, such as Presidency events and policy conferences, supported coordination efforts:
23 out of 24 respondents rated them as effective or very effective. The CPC Regulation (in
force since 2020) further strengthened enforcement coordination mechanisms. According to
the mid-term evaluation, two-thirds of retailers believed that public authorities actively monitor
compliance with consumer legislation, an observation confirmed by national and EU-level
interviews and stakeholder feedback. Sweeps were widely seen as effective by CPC
stakeholders, although some noted uneven implementation across countries. Capacity-building
tools, such as peer exchanges, training modules, CPC Wiki, and IT systems, were credited with
reinforcing enforcement capabilities and enabling cross-border cooperation.
Interviews with enforcement stakeholders (including CPC authorities, CSN, ECCs, BEUC,
ADR bodies, and Eurochambres) highlighted significant progress in capacity building, joint
enforcement, and knowledge sharing. However, gaps remain, especially in tackling complex,
evolving issues like greenwashing, where additional training and coordination are needed.
Survey respondents gave an average score of 4.2 ("Effective") for enforcement-related
activities. ECCs were rated closest to "Very Effective", and most respondents indicated that
intended benefits were “mostly achieved” in their country, showing strong alignment with the
Programme’s objectives.
Performance indicators under Objective IV present a mixed picture of enforcement cooperation
within the CPC Network (see Table 2). The number of information exchange requests dropped
from 132 (2014) to 25 (2020), despite a brief rebound in 2018. Enforcement measure requests
peaked at 198 (2017) but fell to 113 (2020), indicating limited net progress. Alerts shared
within the CPC network consistently remained below the annual target of 82. Timeliness
indicators also underperformed: enforcement requests handled within 12 months fell short of
the 60% target and were later removed under the revised CPC Regulation (EU) 2017/2394.
Similarly, information requests handled within 3 months never reached the 50% target, ranging
between 23% and 38%. While the Programme supported training, coordination, and CPC
25
operations, it did not fund operational enforcement, limiting its direct influence on these results.
The worsening of some indicators reflects structural challenges across Member States,
particularly limited staffing, uneven prioritisation, and legal fragmentation.
In terms of wider impacts, consumer trust in public authorities rose slightly from 60% to 64%
(2014–2018), though overall market functioning remained stable, with 20–25% of consumers
reporting issues warranting complaints (see Table 8). Retailers’ perception of enforcement
declined, with only 66% in 2018 believing authorities monitor compliance, down from 75%
(2011–2013 baseline). These results underscore the need for stronger national capacity, better
CPC coordination, and improved data monitoring under the new regulatory framework.

The European Consumer Centres (ECCs) played a key role in advancing Objectives II, III,
and IV, supporting consumers with cross-border issues through advice, complaint handling,
and referrals to ADR procedures. Their communication efforts also included newsletters, social
media, and public outreach. Performance indicators show growing engagement: targets for
consumer contacts have been met since 2018, and website visit targets since 2014. Complaints
26
handled nearly doubled between 2014 and 2020, with over 60,000 COVID-related cases
addressed in 2020 alone. Stakeholders, including CPC authorities, ECCs, DG JUST, and
consumer organisations, consistently rated ECCs as very effective, a view echoed in the online
survey, where ECCs received the highest effectiveness rating of all actions evaluated.
Respondents also confirmed that ECCs had mostly achieved their national-level benefits. ECCs
contributed to knowledge sharing and networking via participation in strategy groups, ECC-
Net events, and international conferences, reinforcing their role in consumer and enforcement
support. However, coordination gaps persist. While ECC intelligence triggered CPC actions
(e.g. on subscription traps), feedback remained one-way: ECCs rarely received updates on
follow-up actions. Cooperation with ADR bodies also lacked structured interaction. Despite
participation in the Consumer Policy Network, ECCs had limited influence on policy or
enforcement strategy. Recommendations include establishing formal feedback mechanisms
and increasing joint CPC–ECC actions to close coordination gaps.
4.2 Efficiency
The evaluation assessed the costs of financing various activities under the Programme and
attempted to compare these with monetised benefits where such data was available. The
absorption rate stands at 87.4% indicating a relatively high level of budget execution,
particularly considering the diversity of implementing entities (e.g. consumer organisations,
enforcement authorities, and research bodies) and the cross-border nature of many activities.
This strong absorption rate reflects the Programme’s capacity to allocate funds, though some
variations existed between objectives and funding instruments. Notably, grants required co-
financing and were subject to administrative complexities, which sometimes limited
participation or delayed implementation. Both quantitative and qualitative benefits were
identified as part of the effectiveness criterion. However, due to limited quantified data on
benefits, both the mid-term evaluation and this evaluation have faced constraints in analysing
the Programme's efficiency. Funded activities were not subjected to econometric evaluations
to establish causal links between their outputs and the actual benefits produced, relying instead
on the assumption that they contributed to some extent to the Programme's overall impacts.
This section highlights a selection of activities to illustrate the Programme's efficiency. The
absence of harmonised cost/output tracking limited the possibility of calculating benefit-cost
ratios. However, proxies such as alerts triggered, resolved cases, and stakeholder-reported time
savings were used to estimate relative efficiency.
Simplification measures introduced in the Programme aimed to increase efficiency and reduce
administrative burden, especially for recurrent and large-scale activities. A key measure was
the shift from grants to procurement contracts, particularly under Objective I (Product Safety).
From 2019 onward, funding for coordinated market surveillance and testing activities—
previously supported via grants, was implemented through procurement mechanisms,
including high-value contracts under the CASP framework. This shift enabled the Commission
to achieve greater centralisation, faster implementation, and better control over deliverables,
while also reducing the co-financing and reporting burden on national authorities. Other
simplification efforts included: centralising IT infrastructure development and maintenance
(e.g. for RAPEX/Safety Gate, the ODR platform, CPCS, and ECCNet2) under procurement
contracts, allowing for multi-annual planning and more efficient supplier management;
27
streamlining awareness campaigns; focusing grant funding on EU-level capacity-building (e.g.
BEUC, ANEC) and essential operating support for the ECC-Net
Objective I: Product safety
Safety Gate/RAPEX notifications, which alert national authorities and the public about
dangerous non-food products found on the EU market, have proven to be cost-effective. This
is because of these notifications’ impact on the number of accidents and ill-health consequences
avoided thanks to Member States follow-up actions upon receiving the notification. While it is
not possible to estimate the overall avoided detriment for consumers due to the lack of detailed
data on number and severity of avoided accidents, benefits would likely outweigh the costs of
Safety Gate/ RAPEX. This conclusion is further supported by the broader estimate from
product-related accidents, which amounts to approximately EUR 76.6 billion per year. Of this,
about 15%, equivalent to EUR 11.49 billion annually, is deemed preventable through improved
product design, safety features, or better usage instructions50. This highlights the significant
potential of preventive systems like Safety Gate/RAPEX in reducing avoidable harm.
More than 2 000 notifications of products posing serious risk were reported each year between
2014 and 2020, alerting other Member States about dangerous products and thus enabling them
to undertake follow-up action. The study supporting this evaluation estimated the cost-benefit
ratio of Safety Gate/RAPEX notifications51. Using an illustrative example of an unsafe item
having a 4:100 000 likelihood of causing injuries of any severity, the cost of avoided accidents
from the items withdrawn in other Member States as follow up to the annual number of
notifications (2 000 notifications x 109 000 items52) results in an estimate of annual number of
8 700 injuries of any severity being prevented. The monetary cost of these accidents being
prevented can be estimated at EUR 61 million per year. It is estimated that on average around
EUR 1.2 million per year was spent on Safety Gate/RAPEX from the Programme.53 This
suggests that the avoided costs of injuries caused by unsafe products is likely to have exceeded
the Programme’s annual contribution to Safety Gate/RAPEX (the cost/benefit ratio for the

Safety Gate/RAPEX has also led to increased efficiency of product safety enforcement
throughout the EU by enabling Member States to share alerts about products posing a serious
risk and follow-up notifications. The costs beyond the direct costs of implementation of the
activities, such as the costs of recalling products notified through Safety Gate/RAPEX are
deemed by this evaluation as generally affordable, considering the stakeholder categories,
market surveillance authorities and manufacturers. For national market surveillance
authorities, the removal of unsafe products from the market is their core activity which is made
more efficient by receiving alerts from other Member States. For economic operators, it
levelled the playing field with regard to compliance and safety standards, such as in reduction
in differences between Member States).
Some activities improved collaboration between the Member States resulting in resource
savings due to improved information sharing and prevention of duplication. Safety
Gate/RAPEX, joint actions and Coordinated Activities on the Safety of Products (CASPs)
helped deal with lower capacity of Member States, administrative burden (through the
development of templates and procedures), and the avoidance of duplication of effort, thus also
increasing the quality of notifications. Interviewees comprising representatives from national
market surveillance authorities, EU-level officials involved in product safety coordination, and
members of the Consumer Safety Network agreed that funded joint actions and collaborative
projects, such as CASPs have proved valuable in areas such as surveillance, especially for
Member States with limited budgets for product testing. CASPs support Member States by
reducing the administrative burden of testing procedures with the role of a cross-Member State
coordinator. CASPs offered a high return on investment. For example, CASP 2019 tested 652
toys, with 75% being found unsafe or non-compliant, resulting in 170 Safety Gate/RAPEX
alerts. The average EU contribution per tested product was estimated at EUR 450, making
CASP a cost-effective intervention when considering the potential harm prevented55. CASP
testing (activity) directly generated outputs in the form of laboratory-verified unsafe products,
which fed into Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts (output), contributing to market withdrawals,
consumer warnings, and long-term behavioural adjustments in supply chains (outcomes and
impacts). While the improved indicators and increased trust align with Programme activities,
causality cannot be definitively established due to the lack of a control group and the influence
of external market and regulatory dynamics. Nonetheless, triangulated evidence supports a
credible contribution claim.

Objective II: Consumer information and education, developing the evidence base and
support to consumer organisations
BEUC has contributed across a wide range of consumer protection areas, including policy
development, consumer education, and enforcement coordination. It has also supported
national consumer organisations, particularly those with limited resources, by providing know-
how and facilitating their input into EU-level policymaking. While a detailed cost-effectiveness
analysis was not carried out, stakeholders consulted in the evaluation, such as representatives
of BEUC, national consumer organisations (some of which are BEUC members), officials of
DG JUST, and national authorities engaged in the programme, considered the level of funding
allocated to BEUC to be broadly proportionate to the scope and scale of its activities and
outputs. This perception was based on BEUC’s visible role in representing consumer interests
at EU level, its contribution to legislative and policy files, and its capacity-building work with
national organisations. As such, the assessment of proportionality reflects a qualitative
judgement informed by interviews and programme documentation rather than a quantified cost-
benefit analysis. BEUC receives funding from membership fees, EU budget (funded projects
and operating grant), foundation funded projects and other income. Interviewees noted that
external donors allow BEUC to increase the impact of the activities, for example, by
contributing to sustainability issues, energy efficiency of buildings, and clean energy. In 2020,
BEUC’s income was EUR 5 899 806, of which around EUR 4 million covered staff costs. A
third of that income (33%) was from an operating grant from the Programme, which is its
primary source of income. Based on project documentation, the main activity funded by the
Programme operating grant is representation of member consumer organisations, policy input,
and undertaking ‘enforcement actions’. Furthermore, the operating grant funds some topical
activities which are chosen on the basis of market concerns, e.g. payment fraud and abuse. The
majority (90%) of BEUC’s work involved preparation and dissemination of position papers;
press releases and press briefings in order to raise public awareness; and active participation in
conferences and hearings.56 An increase of the BEUC’s operating grants from 201857 onwards
allowed BEUC to expand and develop several workstreams. For instance, in 2018, a BEUC
project contributed to developing, implementing and sharing reinforced IT tools and platforms
at the disposal of the less affluent members to reach out to consumers in their countries. BEUC
also supported and coordinated its members in developing strategies to enhance their
enforcement activities.
Other consumer awareness and education activities, including Consumer Champion and
Consumer PRO have resulted in outputs (e.g. consumers being trained or consumer
organisations’ capacity building), but evidence of lasting impacts is lacking. For the first two
years of the of the Consumer PRO (2019-20), EUR 1.47 million was committed to activities
such as needs analysis, train-the-trainers, local and regional trainings and an exchange of best
practice seminar.

to the policy development process. The average project budget for behavioural studies was
relatively large compared to other procurement projects (in the range EUR 279 000 to EUR

The 2023 Impact Assessment of the proposed ADR Directive58 noted the difficulty in
quantifying costs to stakeholder groups but concluded that ADR remains the most cost
advantageous system both for traders and consumers, but also for Member States if going to a
court. The same report also identified potential cost savings. Facilitating digitalisation of ADR
and the use of modern technologies and exchange of good practice funded by ADR grants
contributed to increasing the cost-effectiveness of the funded entities. The cost-effectiveness
of ADR grants as a whole, however, was hampered by the Programme’s inability to disburse
the full allocations. Low uptake of ADR grants was primarily due to the 50% co-financing rate
and complex administrative requirements. In addition, many eligible entities lacked dedicated
fundraising or project staff, limiting their capacity to apply. This mismatch between funding
design and stakeholder reality severely reduced the efficiency of Objective III grant delivery.
The low success rate of the ODR platform remained broadly constant between 2016 and 2021,
regardless of the technical/design improvements and information campaigns with only around
1% of all claims made through the ODR platform proceeding to ADR, i.e. on average less than
200 cases per year. For this reason, the ODR platform was assessed as not cost-effective. Still,
some of the activities may have been cost-effective with regard to their specific objectives. For
example, ODR platform awareness campaigns were effective and evidenced in terms of cost
per click generated, compared with similar campaigns. Therefore, with an average of only ~1%
of 147,000 ODR complaints resulting in an ADR outcome between 2016 and 2020, and
operational costs exceeding EUR 2 million over the period, the platform's cost-effectiveness
remained very low, estimated at over EUR 1,300 per resolved case. The evaluation concluded
that due to structural limitations in the ODR design (e.g., double opt-in and low trader
coverage), the system could not deliver proportional value relative to its operational cost, even
after technical improvements.

Objective IV: Enforcement
A significant share of Programme funding was committed to activities related to actions under
Objective IV. EUR 60.7 million (35% of funds) was split between activities under action 10
(EUR 16.2 million), which includes the CPC Network, and ECC-Net (EUR 44.5 million),
funded under action 11. The Programme funding committed to action 10 increased from EUR
0.98 million in 2014 to a peak of EUR 4.35 million in 2019. Funding allocated to the CPC
authorities for CPC capacity-building was through grants. The grants were used to cover costs
related to personnel and training, equipment and infrastructure, operational costs, such as travel
and meeting expenses and studies, surveys, and other research activities. Overall, a mix of large
and small value grants were awarded, the latter awarded since 2018. While the Programme did
not perform a dedicated cost-benefit analysis for CPC capacity-building grants, qualitative data
and stakeholder feedback indicate that the CPC Network's interventions were, after the
simplification measures, considered cost-effective. This model also enabled more direct
Commission oversight and facilitated the development of standardised tools and services,
reducing administrative burdens and increasing consistency.
A cost-benefit analysis of the ECCs confirmed a high level of efficiency and proportionality
under the Programme. ECCs were predominantly funded by grants, with EU co-financing
averaging 55, with those MS of low GDP receiving 67%. Annual EU funding rose from EUR
5.2 million in 2015 to EUR 7 million in 2020, supporting 29 ECCs, including centres in Iceland,
Norway, and the UK (until its withdrawal in 2020). France and Germany received the highest
total allocations (EUR 7.7 million each), due in part to their leadership of joint projects. Iceland
received the lowest funding (EUR 29 977–38 845). While most countries received a similar
number of grants, grant values varied considerably. Operational costs were generally co-
financed equally with national authorities, with higher co-financing rates for lower-GDP
Member States and joint projects (renamed ‘EU Dimension Activities’ in 2024) benefiting
from a 54% co-financing rate. From 2014 to 2020, the ECC caseload nearly doubled, from 94
000 to 168 000 contacts. Efficiency improvements included ECC-Net 2 (streamlining case
handling), expanded social media outreach, and partnerships with media outlets. As a result,
the average cost per case declined from EUR 70 in 2014 to EUR 40 in 2020, demonstrating
strong and growing cost-efficiency, even before the COVID-related demand surge.
The level of ECC funding did not always align with caseloads or resolution times. For instance,
the UK ECC had a high caseload but was not among the top five funded centres, likely due to
contextual rather than efficiency differences. In contrast, France and Germany ranked high in
both funding and caseloads, partly due to their leadership in high-value joint projects that
attracted additional co-financing. To assess proportionality, the evaluation estimated the
monetised value of ECC services. Using findings from the Commission’s consumer detriment
study, which identified financial loss, time lost, and psychological stress as key factors, a
simplified estimation was developed. Although ECC data do not perfectly match these
categories, the number of complaints handled between 2014 and 2020 allowed for a reasonable
approximation.
32
During this period, ECCs dealt with 130 781 complaints59. Applying an average financial
detriment value of EUR 46.90 per problem60 results in an estimated EUR 6.13 million in
avoided or recovered financial losses. In addition, the average consumer reportedly spends 5.8
hours dealing with such issues. Assuming this time was saved through ECC support and
applying an average EU hourly wage rate, the estimated time-saving benefit amounts to
approximately EUR 17.3 million. Although psychological stress was not monetised in this
calculation, it remains a significant factor. Approximately 57% of respondents to the consumer
detriment study reported experiencing ‘quite a lot’ or ‘extreme’ stress due to problematic
purchases. Extrapolating from this proportion, around 74 000 of the consumers supported by
ECCs during the evaluation period likely benefited from reduced psychological stress as a
result of receiving assistance. Taken together, the monetised benefits to consumers, financial
recovery and time saved, are estimated at roughly EUR 23.4 million over the evaluation period.
When compared to the EUR 44.5 million in Programme funding committed to ECCs, this
suggests a substantial return, though not a one-to-one financial match. Importantly, the estimate
does not capture the full range of benefits delivered by ECCs, such as improvements to cross-
border enforcement, trust-building among consumers, and institutional development through
shared tools and practices. In particular, joint projects helped generate efficiency gains by
reducing duplication and allowing ECCs to leverage common infrastructure and
methodologies. Overall, ECCs are considered a success story within the Programme, delivering
both tangible consumer benefits and broader systemic value that support the case for continued
EU-level investment.
4.3 Coherence
The Programme was designed to be internally coherent across its four specific objectives.
Activities funded under each objective were intended to support complementary tools, data
flows, or actions, thereby reinforcing the broader goals of consumer protection, enforcement,
and information. Internal coherence was evident in several cross-cutting initiatives—for
example, how behavioural studies under Objective III were informed by research funded under
Objective II, or how data collected by ECCs (Objective IV) supported enforcement actions
under the CPC Network. Training tools such as the e-Enforcement Academy were designed to
serve multiple objectives, including product safety, market surveillance, and redress. Overall,
the evidence confirms the mid-term evaluation’s conclusion: the Programme was both
internally and externally coherent. While isolated areas showed room for improvement,
particularly in better linking networks like ECCs and the CPC, there were no significant
contradictions or overlaps identified. The Programme’s priorities and funded actions were
viewed as complementary and synergistic.

Objective I: Product safety
Safety Gate/RAPEX was well integrated with broader enforcement and surveillance efforts.
For example, the online marketplaces that are signatories to the Product Safety Pledge have
committed to regularly check Safety Gate/RAPEX and remove dangerous products from their
websites61, a model now embedded in the General Product Safety Regulation. CASP activities
further operationalised Safety Gate/RAPEX insights through joint surveillance activities (some
of looking at cooperation with the customs authorities or online market surveillance), risk
assessments and communication campaigns.62 Initiatives such as Safety Gate/RAPEX
improvements, and international workshops work together to enhance the overall effectiveness
of consumer safety measures. The collaboration between Safety Gate/RAPEX, Member States
and Consumer Safety Network was also highlighted by interviewed stakeholders, including
representatives from national market surveillance authorities, members of the CSN, and EU-
level officials, as essential for improving data gathering, streamlining risk communication, and
aligning national surveillance efforts. For example, CASP 2019 and 2020 generated 170 and
218 Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts, respectively, illustrating clear functional linkage. In parallel,
the Information and Communication System for Market Surveillance (ICSMS) ensured that
test results, surveillance actions, and Safety Gate/RAPEX notifications could be linked and
tracked by authorities across Member States. By 2020, over 90% of Member State authorities
were using ICSMS in connection with Safety Gate/RAPEX notifications. These systems
worked synergistically to avoid duplication in testing, consolidate findings, and streamline
responses.
Capacity-building tools such as the e-Enforcement Academy further reinforced this coherence
by providing training modules on risk assessment and surveillance techniques. Several smaller
or newer national authorities noted that CASP participation and training improved their ability
to report into Safety Gate/RAPEX and use ICSMS effectively, thereby improving consistency
in surveillance quality and enabling common enforcement responses. The alignment between
CASP, Safety Gate/RAPEX, and market surveillance also ensured that alerts triggered
coordinated withdrawals across Member States, enhancing the systemic efficiency of the
product safety framework.

covering consumer rights and enforcement, digital rights, financial services, food safety and

synergies between BEUC and other activities, particularly those under Objective IV on ECCs.
BEUC and ECCs work on similar topics and frequently exchange expertise and information.
BEUC’s role in bridging national and EU-level consumer priorities was supported by regular
coordination with CPC authorities and participation in the Consumer Policy Advisory Group

Objective III: Consumer rights and redress
Objective III supported the other three objectives of the Programme by generating policy-
relevant evidence and facilitating consumer access to ADR mechanisms. A key tool in this
regard was the series of behavioural and market studies, which provided insights into consumer
behaviour, market functioning, and regulatory needs. These studies not only underpinned legal
and policy proposals (e.g. the revised Consumer Credit Directive), but also had cross-cutting
impacts, informing product safety communications (Objective I), feeding into awareness
campaigns and training modules (Objective II), and supporting enforcement coordination
(Objective IV). Their influence extended across EU-level networks. Interviews conducted
during the evaluation, including with representatives from national consumer organisations,
EU policymakers, and members of the Consumer Policy Network, confirmed that the
dissemination of behavioural evidence played an important role in initiating discussions,
raising awareness, and shaping enforcement priorities across objectives. While the proposed
amendments to the ADR Directive in 2023 fall outside the evaluation period, its content reflects
continuity of themes identified during the 2014–2020 Programme, notably the need for closer
coordination between ECCs and ADR bodies. This coherence was also reflected in the
Commission’s proposal to designate ECCs as ADR contact points, a move seen by stakeholders
as building on the groundwork laid by the Programme. Feedback from stakeholders further
revealed that improved sharing of best practices, especially where complaints handling,
enforcement referrals, or consumer rights education overlapped, was necessary. For example,

Objective IV: Enforcement
Activities funded under Objective IV, particularly the CPC Network and ECC Net, were found
mutually reinforcing and contributed to a coherent enforcement system that addressed both
collective consumer interests and individual assistance needs. While the CPC Network pursued
systemic infringements of EU consumer law, ECCs provided direct, cross-border support to
consumers. Their collaboration helped bridge the gap between policy enforcement and day-to-
day consumer redress. Cooperation between the ECC-Net and the CPC Network included joint
actions, such as coordinated response during the Covid-19 pandemic, when rogue traders
marketed fraudulent health products. Similar collaborations were reported in areas subscription
traps and other unfair commercial practices, where consumer complaints gathered by ECCs
informed CPC sweeps and investigations, linking Objective IV and III effectively. Synergies
also existed with BEUC, particularly in organising regular meetings and aligning advocacy on
enforcement gaps or systemic issues. Coherence in training and capacity building was
supported through initiatives such as the e-Enforcement Academy, which was also relevant to
Objective I, especially regarding product safety enforcement. The Academy provided market
surveillance and consumer enforcement authorities with access to harmonised training
materials, tools, and practices that strengthened cooperation and consistency across borders.
Despite these achievements, several stakeholders, particularly from ECCs, indicated that
synergies with the CPC Network could be further strengthened. Suggestions included
increasing the number and scope of joint activities, such as joint monitoring of emerging
commercial practices or coordinated responses to pan-European scams. The flow of
information between ECCs and ADR bodies was also seen as suboptimal, with feedback loops
often described as one-directional. During focus groups, ECC representatives noted that while
they regularly share intelligence with CPC and ADR bodies, they rarely receive systematic
updates or coordinated follow-up, limiting the potential to close the policy-practice loop.
Overall, Objective IV demonstrated solid internal coherence and contributed to enhancing the
overall enforcement ecosystem, yet further integration and feedback mechanisms between
networks and actors could significantly improve its impact.
External coherence
External coherence assesses the complementarity and alignment of the Programme with
broader EU consumer policy objectives and other relevant Union initiatives. Throughout the
2014-2020 period, the objectives and eligible actions of the Programme were coherent with
Article 169 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and with Article 38 of the
Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union which enshrines the right to a high level
of consumer protection, reinforcing the Programme’s role in safeguarding consumer rights and
promoting fair market practices across the EU. It supported the practical implementation of the
vision outlined in the Consumer Agenda 2012 and Digital Single Market Strategy 2015. There
was also a significant degree of coherence between the objectives of the Programme and the
2018 New Deal for Consumers. Since the last set of commitments under the Programme were
36
made in 2020 and their implementation thus goes beyond 2020, the evaluation assessed
coherence with the 2020 Consumer Agenda66 that builds on the 2012 agenda and addresses
new and emerging challenges, including the Covid-19 pandemic, digital transformation and
green transition.
The Programme contributed to the EU's strategy for smart, sustainable, and inclusive growth
by improving consumer confidence, market transparency, and regulatory coherence—all
essential enablers of competitiveness. By reinforcing trust in digital and cross-border
transactions, supporting informed decision-making, and enabling dispute resolution, the
Programme reduced friction in internal market functioning and stimulated both consumer and
business activity.
Several Programme elements were directly conducive to smart, sustainable and inclusive
growth by strengthening the position of consumers as informed, empowered and protected
actors in the internal market: 1. Actions supporting digital transition (e.g. consumer education
on digital rights, ODR, BEUC’s work on platform regulation) improved digital market
confidence. 2. CASP and RAPEX helped create safer product markets, thereby fostering a fair
competitive environment. 3. ADR and ECC-Net contributed to business competitiveness by
reducing costly litigation and improving customer satisfaction. 4. Capacity-building for SMEs
through Consumer Law Ready reduced compliance burdens and increased trust in SME offers.
Less growth-relevant areas included awareness campaigns with limited long-term behavioural
effects and the underperforming ODR platform, which had lower practical uptake by
consumers and traders.
Overall, the aims and objectives of the Programme complemented those of the other EU
funding programmes, contributing to a comprehensive approach to consumer protection,
environmental sustainability, social equality, and market integration within the EU. This also
suggests that the activities funded under the Programme were coherent with broader EU
policies. In relation to broader EU policies, Article 12 of the TFEU commits the EU to taking
consumer protection requirements into account in ‘defining and implementing other Union
policies and activities’. A significant degree of coherence between the Programme and the
following programmes has been identified:
• With the LIFE Programme, coherence was found in environmental goals, particularly
in promoting sustainable consumption practices and eco-labelling, though LIFE’s focus
is broader and more environmentally anchored.
• With the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF), coherence emerged particularly in the
digital domain, where CEF funded digital infrastructure while the Programme
supported digital consumer empowerment, such as through ODR and consumer
education on digital rights.
• With the Rights, Equality and Citizenship (REC) Programme, coherence was
ensured through internal coordination within DG JUST, avoiding duplication despite
thematic overlap. While REC covered broader social issues, it included a specific
objective on consumer rights. Funded actions, averaging EUR 1.3 million annually,
were small-scale and complementary, focusing on digital consumer protection, capacity

building, and analysis. Examples include a study on digital content products67, updates
to the Consumer Law Database, and SME training on consumer and marketing law.
In addition, there was documented coherence with international obligations, particularly
through cooperation with OECD and participation in ICPEN (International Consumer
Protection and Enforcement Network) via the CPC Network. These partnerships helped ensure
that EU consumer protection standards contributed to and benefited from global best practices.
The mid-term and final evaluations both concluded that the Programme’s actions were
generally well coordinated with national and EU-level interventions, supporting shared goals
such as high consumer trust, effective enforcement, and alignment with the Single Market’s
digital and green transitions.
Objective I: Product safety
The external coherence of coordinated market surveillance and alerts was high, as these actions
supported enforcement of, and disseminated data relevant to, on a wide range of EU product
safety legislation, including GPSD and various sectoral directives. The Safety Gate/RAPEX
system served as a key instrument in sharing information on dangerous non-food products
across Member States and with external partners, thereby supporting consistent
implementation of EU law and enhancing market surveillance coordination. The exchanges of
enforcement officials, through joint actions and CASP projects, contributed to a more
harmonised and coherent approach to surveillance across the EU. International cooperation
reinforces the external coherence of the Programme by ensuring that EU actions in product
safety and market surveillance are aligned with broader international frameworks and partner
initiatives. The Commission’s active participation in global fora such as the OECD Global
Recall System and International Product Safety Week not only supports the exchange of best
practices, but also ensures complementarity with global efforts. Examples such as the
reciprocal data-sharing with Health Canada and the adoption of EU-led product safety pledges
by other jurisdictions underscore the Programme’s alignment with international norms and its
contribution to globally coherent consumer protection frameworks. These efforts help avoid
duplication, enhance trust, and ensure consistent standards in an increasingly interconnected
global marketplace.
Objective II: Consumer information and education, developing the evidence base and
support to consumer organisations
The support provided to BEUC, as the main grant beneficiary under Objective II, significantly
enhanced the external coherence of the Consumer Programme. BEUC acted as a key interface
between EU consumer policy and both internal and external policymaking arenas. At the EU
level, it ensured alignment between consumer protection priorities and broader strategies such
as the Digital Single Market, the Green Deal, and the Capital Markets Union by actively
contributing to legislative processes and coordinating the input of its national members.
Externally, BEUC represented EU consumer interests in global fora including the OECD,
ICPEN, and the Trans-Atlantic Consumer Dialogue, ensuring consistency between the
Programme’s objectives and evolving international consumer policy standards. Its cooperation
with ANEC and regular interaction with ECCs and CPC authorities further reinforced policy
alignment across standardisation, enforcement, and redress mechanisms. Other activities under
Objective II also demonstrated a high degree of external coherence. Programmes such as

cross-cutting EU priorities related to digital rights, SME engagement, and sustainable

Objective III: Consumer rights and redress
Behavioural studies were initially pioneered in consumer policy and are now used by a range
of other policies within the Commission, demonstrating strong external coherence and cross-
policy relevance. Support for ADR provides practical and efficient means for consumers to
enforce their rights without resorting to the often costly and time-consuming court system, thus
reinforcing the overall coherence with the EU consumer rights acquis and contributing directly
to EU goals of access to justice and effective enforcement. Moreover, ADR grants provided
under the Programme were coherent with other EU policy frameworks, such as the Small
Business Act for Europe68, which encourages the reduction of administrative burdens for
SMEs. By promoting effective and fair resolution of consumer disputes, ADR mechanisms
helped foster trust in the Single Market, ensure a level playing field, and support sustainable
growth.69 Feedback from interviews and focus group discussions with stakeholders, including
ADR bodies, European Consumer Centres (ECCs), BEUC, national consumer organisations,
and officials from DG JUST, confirmed that Programme’s actions are well-coordinated with
national consumer policies. In particular, national-level decisions on ADR implementation
were reinforced by EU-level funding, visibility, and knowledge exchange, improving the
consistency and reach of ADR solutions across Member States.
Objective IV: Enforcement
The funding provided under Objective IV was externally coherent with the overall EU legal
framework. The activities of ECCs contributed to key Single Market goals, by enhancing
confidence in cross-border trade. Certain ECCs led joint activities (now known as EU
Dimension Activities) benefiting the whole of ECC-Net, while others produced policy position
papers on pressing consumer issues, including geo blocking (2019), the right to repair, roaming
charges, and aggressive timeshare sales tactics. These papers informed and influenced key
pieces of legislation, such as the revised Timeshare Directive (Directive 2008/122/EC) and the

during consultations by the European Parliament on the Digital Services Act, which resulted
in the Digital Services Regulation (entered into force in 2022). ECCs also contributed to
consultations on the repeal of the ODR Regulation and the review of the Package Travel
Directive. At the national level, ECCs demonstrated external coherence by collaborating with
sector-specific actors, such as civil aviation authorities on passenger rights, travel and hotel
agents, trade unions, and major e-commerce platforms. These efforts complemented the work
of national consumer organisations, reinforcing the EU’s consumer protection architecture.

online and cross-border commerce, were externally coherent with broader EU priorities, such

4.4 How did the EU intervention make a difference and to whom?
The mid-term evaluation of the Programme highlighted that funded activities, such as Safety
Gate/RAPEX, the CPC Network, ECC-Net and support to BEUC, have generated clear EU
added value. This was particularly evident where actions complemented national measures by
addressing cross-border challenges, enabling economies of scale, or creating synergies that
could not have been achieved by Member States acting alone. The Programme facilitated more
effective collaboration among national authorities, enabled the sharing of best practices, and
allowed resources to be pooled to achieve common goals, contributions widely recognised as
valuable by stakeholders responding to the survey and other consultations.
The EU intervention through the Programme made a tangible difference to European
consumers, especially in cross-border contexts where national measures alone would have been
insufficient. It provided tools, networks, and enforcement mechanisms that ensured consumers
could shop more safely, resolve disputes more easily, and access reliable information,
regardless of where they lived. Activities such as Safety Gate/RAPEX, ECC-Net, CASP, and
the CPC Network helped to harmonise protection levels across the Single Market, supporting
trust in product safety, e-commerce, and redress. Quantitative and qualitative evidence
confirms that consumers were the primary beneficiaries. For instance, the ECC-Net is
estimated to have generated at least EUR 23.4 million in direct consumer benefits through
complaints handled and guidance offered. Nevertheless, quantifying the difference or impact
of the Programme on consumers remains challenging, quantifying the difference or impact of
the Programme on consumers is challenging, as the Programme was not designed with a strong
counterfactual evaluation framework, and many of its broader effects were not directly tracked.
Equally, the Programme’s impact on competitiveness and economic growth was primarily
indirect and not always quantifiable. While it likely contributed to a fairer business
environment and more efficient markets, especially in cross-border trade, the evaluation
acknowledges the difficulty in attributing specific macroeconomic outcomes (e.g. increased
GDP or innovation) directly to Programme actions.
Stakeholders consistently emphasised that EU support was essential to ensuring consistent
services across the Single Market and building consumer confidence, particularly in areas such
as product safety, cross-border trade, the digital economy, and e-commerce. Specific
achievements, such as the promotion of ADR mechanisms in sectors like telecommunications
and postal services, were viewed as directly dependent on EU-level intervention. EU funding
was also seen as critical for enabling capacity-building, training, policy development and
enforcement actions. Many stakeholders noted that, without sustained EU support, national
public resources would likely have been insufficient to achieve similar outcomes, potentially
resulting in fragmentation and weakened consumer protection, especially in Member States
with more limited capacity. However, some stakeholders expressed more critical or nuanced
views. These included concerns about uneven access to consumer protection tools across
Member States, the limited practical reach of certain actions, particularly in redress and
enforcement, and the underperformance of specific initiatives, such as the ODR platform. Civil
society and consumer organisations also pointed to areas where enforcement could be
strengthened, and consumer education further enhanced. These perspectives underline the
40
importance of ensuring that future actions are both inclusive and adaptable to national contexts,
and that they respond to gaps in impact, especially in domains with weaker infrastructures.
Compliant businesses also benefitted through improved legal clarity, a more level playing field,
and increased consumer trust in cross-border transactions.
Objective I: Product safety
Sharing and streamlining information on unsafe consumer products through Safety
Gate/RAPEX identified by a Member State with other Member States avoided duplication in
the identification and investigation of unsafe products and enabled a co-ordinated approach to
market surveillance and enforcement. This system, coupled with harmonised market
surveillance, ensured that products met the same safety standards regardless of where they were
sold, reinforcing the integrity of the Single Market. By pooling resources and expertise, by
sharing risk assessment practices and building trust between authorities, CASP projects
reduced the administrative burden of testing, allowing for comprehensive testing and efficient
market surveillance while avoiding duplication of efforts - achievements that would be difficult
for Member States to attain individually. CASP also facilitated development of methodologies
and ways of working that are based on good practices from around the EU through its horizontal
activities.
Objective II: Consumer information and education, developing the evidence base and
support to consumer organisations
EU-funded awareness initiatives, such as campaigns on online shopping and travel or e-
learning platforms, delivered stronger results than national efforts alone by ensuring a
harmonised approach and avoiding disparities in information quality across Member States.
Centralised coordination also enabled more efficient use of resources. Interviewees, including
representative from national consumer organisations, BEUC, and DG JUST officials noted that
these initiatives improved consumer access to reliable information and support. BEUC’s cross-
border activities added clear EU value by supporting national consumer organisations,
coordinating collective redress, and contributing to high-profile cases such as Dieselgate and
the Google Shopping antitrust appeal. Its policy input helped shape key initiatives like the New
Deal for Consumers and informed EU rules on digital markets, financial services, and green
claims. BEUC also supported enforcement by helping national organisations act on large-scale
consumer harm and by contributing expertise to international forums. This strengthened the
capacity of national organisations, particularly in smaller Member States, and ensured more
consistent consumer protection across the EU.
Within Consumer PRO and Consumer Law Ready the national level activities benefited
from European level support and coordination, ensuring a consistent level of service across
MS, while maintaining topics and training tailored to the MS. The Consumer PRO European
workshops were well-received, with feedback noting that companies are international, and can
use their resources more effectively by learning from other countries70. While EU interventions
in the field of consumer education and information contributed to some improvement, it cannot
be argued that the changes resulted directly from EU interventions, rather than other factors.
Arguably, the impact of EU interventions is higher in the Member States with lower budgets
