dedicated to consumer education and information. However, this finding would have to be
validated in further studies.
Objective III: Consumer rights and redress
Analysis of evidence related to Objective III confirms the added value of EU interventions.
Persistent disparities in the results of the Consumer Conditions Scoreboard71 highlight the
ongoing need for EU-level action. Behavioural studies contributed to this by sharing findings
with Member States that lacked the capacity to conduct such research themselves, thereby
supporting evidence-based policy and regulatory improvements. Additional EU added value
came through the commissioning of consumer market analyses, legal gap assessments, and
application reports, which informed policy development. A citation analysis showed that
behavioural studies were frequently referenced in documents supporting legislation and that
some recommendations were incorporated into EU initiatives. While direct evidence of
behavioural studies influencing enforcement or voluntary practices remains limited, there are
indications that some enforcement actions, such as sweeps in the areas of consumer credit and
online travel websites, have followed themes identified in behavioural studies. Similarly, the
updated Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) guidance72 includes enforcement
examples relevant to online platforms and social media.
The Programme supported the implementation of the ODR Regulation and the ODR platform,
by providing the necessary infrastructure and accompanying measures to promote their use.
While the ODR platform established a unified, centralised channel for dispute resolution,
particularly useful for Member States with less developed systems, the low success rate of
resolved cases limited its overall EU added value73. The Programme also supported the
implementation of the ADR Directive by funding activities that promoted access to quality out-
of-court resolution for consumers across the EU, especially in cross-border contexts. Grants to
ADR entities typically ranged from EUR 10 000 to EUR 60 000, co-financing up to 50% of
eligible costs. These grants supported awareness-raising activities, case handling
improvements, staff training, and exchanges of best practices. In 2020, and again under the
2024 call for proposals, the Programme allocated dedicated budgets (e.g. €1 million in 2024)
to enhance the capacity of ADR entities and qualified consumer organisations. Interviewed
stakeholders, including representatives of ADR entities and national competent authorities,
highlighted that Programme-funded networking and training initiatives helped improve
consistency and visibility of ADR mechanisms across Member States. Given that nearly half
of complaints submitted via the ODR platform concerned cross-border cases, the Programme’s
support for ADR capacity and cooperation provided meaningful EU added value, particularly
in Member States where national systems remained underdeveloped.
71 Consumer Conditions Scoreboard, Editions 2015 -2020
72 Commission Notice – Guidance on the interpretation and application of Directive 2005/29/EC of the European
Parliament and of the Council concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal
market,
available
at:
https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-
content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52021XC1229%2805%29&qid=1640961745514
73 Only about of 1% (i.e. on average less than 200 cases per year) proceeded to ADR and the low success rate
remained broadly constant between 2016 and 2021, regardless of the technical and design improvements to
the ODR platform and information campaigns. See European Commission, 2023e.
42
Objective IV: Enforcement
Activities funded under Objective IV related to the CPC Network have provided significant
EU added value, which is widely acknowledged by stakeholders, including CPC authorities,
ECCs, consumer organisations, ADR entities, DG JUST officials in both mid-term evaluation
and this ex-post evaluation. The Programme enhanced EU value by complementing and
strengthening national measures, through joint actions, networking and training of enforcement
officials. In addition, the Commission’s coordination activities and support of enforcement
against international companies, ensured an improved level playing field across the Single
Market. Stakeholders explained that as e-commerce had been steadily growing and exploded
in 2020, it made the Commission’s coordination and tools like web crawlers even more
essential for CPC authorities to respond effectively. They also emphasised that without
financing and developing these tools, it would have been very difficult for Member States to
react to the rapid changes in e-commerce and technological advancements.
The ECC-Net played a crucial role in cross-border trade by assisting with disputes and
ensuring consistent service across all centres. Better-resourced ECCs supported those with
fewer resources, allowing for a uniform level of service regardless of location. This
collaboration ensured that consumers, wherever they were, received reliable assistance with
cross-border issues, demonstrating the added value of the EU's support. ECC-Net's contribution
to consumer confidence extended to the digital economy. By helping consumers trust the
internal market, the network enabled cross-border purchases of goods and services, benefiting
both consumers and businesses. This was validated by ECC representatives, who emphasized
the importance of the network in building trust in cross-border trade and supporting the Single
Market. Prior to joining ECC-Net, some centres74 only dealt with national complaints, but the
network's resources allowed them to expand their support to cross-border issues. Thanks to the
CPC Regulation, many ECCs were designated to send external alerts related to existing and
potential infringements which were made directly available to the CPC network; hence
contributing to a more robust EU enforcement toolbox.
4.5 Is the intervention still relevant?
The evidence from this evaluation confirms the ongoing relevance and appropriateness of the
Programme’s objectives. These objectives remain aligned with the needs of consumers across
the EU, especially in light of the continued digitalisation, globalisation, and emergence of new
market risks related to AI, sustainability, and cross-border digital commerce. Activities, such
as market surveillance, consumer education and cross-border dispute resolution, continue to
address systems risks and ensure fair treatment of consumers in an evolving internal market.
The increasing demand for cross-border dispute resolution and the need for stronger
cooperation among enforcement stakeholders highlights the continued relevance of the
Programme, particularly in light of emerging e-commerce and AI-related safety concerns. The
mid-term evaluation found the Programme addressed the needs and problems identified at the
Programme’s outset, with the exception of limited targeting of vulnerable consumers. The
Programme’s actions were able to adapt to the changing consumer needs, particularly as
74 For instance, the European Consumer Centre in the Czech Republic, operating under the Czech Trade Inspection
Authority, began providing assistance with cross-border disputes following its inclusion in ECC-Net.
Similarly, the European Consumer Centre in Lithuania, established in 2005, started offering support for cross-
border consumer issues as part of the network's mission to enhance consumer confidence in the internal
market.
43
challenges evolved in digital and green policy areas. Results from the Consumer Conditions
Scoreboard75, the thematic breadth of consumer complaints76 across the scope of Programme’s
actions, as well as views of stakeholders, including national consumer organisations, consumer
authorities, market surveillance officials, and representatives of the Commission show that all
four objectives of the Programme were appropriate and still relevant. Further, the 2020
Consumer Programme Statement, an annual programming document accompanying the EU
draft budget for the year 202077, highlighted the continued relevance of the Consumer
Programme’s objectives under the new consumer strand of the Single Market Programme,
which retains the same four objectives.
Product safety continues to be important due to structural shifts in consumer markets, including
globalisation and digitalisation, which introduce new safety risks and enforcement challenges.
Funding facilitating joint testing and coordinated enforcement, e.g. CASP, improved the
knowledge and capacity of inspectors and strengthened continued cooperation between
Member States in market surveillance, monitoring products and ensuring compliance with
safety regulations. CASP was adaptable and able to focus on products important at a given
moment. For instance, CASP Corona2020 highlighted the relevance and the agility of the
Programme, such as improving market surveillance of Covid-19 related products. CASP also
produced an EU wide communication toolkit on Product Specific Activities (PSA) and
Horizontal Activities (HA), further contributing to effective testing and exchange of best
practices. Furthermore, scientific advice provided by the SCCS committee guided risk
assessments, and Safety Gate/RAPEX78 addressed dangerous products and informed and
enforced safety regulations. While consumers generally lack awareness of Safety
Gate/RAPEX, it does influence consumer organisations, who use Safety Gate/RAPEX
information when planning their product testing (such as selecting priority areas for the year
ahead). Further, the EU product safety awards recognise best practices in consumer protection
and the Product Safety Pledge was signed by five major online marketplaces and also
encourages proactive monitoring of SafetyGate.
BEUC played a crucial role in ensuring consumer representation and adapting to crises
encompassing a wide range of cross-cutting consumer needs – from digital rights, financial
services, energy markets, to sustainability. BEUC’s annual reports reflected the priorities of
their members and their in-depth knowledge of their needs, expectations, difficulties and
complaints. The relevance of BEUC’s work also results from working across the Consumer
Agenda, thus covering a broad range of consumer needs, while also bringing new issues and
topics to the agenda. Examples of such topics that BEUC worked on in 2018 concerned issues
such as Internet of Things and connected products, big data and Dieselgate79, while in 2020,
BEUC continued to address emerging and complex consumer challenges, including digital
fairness, greenwashing, the right to repair, and the consumer impacts of the Covid-19 crisis80.
75 Consumer Conditions Scoreboards, editions 2015-2020.
76 DFR, IPSOS, 2019 and IPSOS, 2020.
77 European Commission, Draft General Budget of the European Union for the financial year 2020 – Working
Document Part I: Programme Statements of Operational Expenditure, COM(2019) 400, pp. 101–104.
https://commission.europa.eu/document/download/a2cd479f-980d-4927-9863-
0d029b67eac6_en?filename=draft-budget-2020-wd-1_2019_en.pdf
78 Economisti Associati, 2016; DG JUST, 2021. SafetyGateRAPEX was used to report products claiming to
protect consumers from viral infection during the COVID-19 pandemic.
79 BEUC, Annual Report 2018, available at: https://annualreport.beuc.eu/year-2018/.
80 BEUC, Annual Report 2020, available at: https://annualreport.beuc.eu/year-2020/.
44
The relevance of capacity building initiatives, Consumer PRO and Consumer Law Ready
demonstrated adaptability (e.g. transitioning to online formats during the pandemic) and high
satisfaction rates. Tools such as training sessions, pre-tasks, and modular learning formats
allowed for tailored national implementation and supported professional capacity-building.
Behavioural studies were cited in the mid-term evaluation and in interviews for this evaluation
as a key source of evidence for new trends and potential consumer detriment, including on
online marketing and pricing techniques and dark patterns. The studies were either directly
cited in Commission policy documents and served as reference material in legislative drafting.
Examples include the study on the digitalisation of the marketing and distance selling of retail
financial services81, which was cited in the evaluations of the Directive on Distance Marketing
of Financial Services (DMFSD)82 and the Consumer Credit Directive (CCD)83 undertaken in
2020 and the study on strategies to improve the effectiveness of product recalls84, which was
cited in the Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for the General Product Safety
Regulation (GPSR)85. Notably, the behavioural study on commercial practices in the digital
environment had a significant impact on legislation under the New Deal and the consumer
agenda. The Commission was seen as a pioneer in behavioural studies, also considering the
influence of these studies on Member States and organisations such as OECD. Interviewees
indicated that the supranational nature of behavioural studies meant their findings could be
shared and help initiate discussion and raise awareness, as well as inform future policy and
actions.
The ODR platform and ADR entities addressed persistent cross-border redress gaps.
However, the ODR platform proved less effective due to structural limitations and overlap with
private dispute resolution systems. ADR grants contributed to capacity-building, training, and
awareness-raising activities, proving relevant especially in Member States with limited
national resources for redress. According to the 2011 Impact Assessment of the Programme,
one of the key challenges in the enforcement of consumer legislation was the underutilisation
of the CPC Network, with persistent gaps in cross-border enforcement. In this context,
activities under Action 10 were highly relevant for achieving Objective IV of the Programme.
The Programme also directly supported the implementation of legal obligations set out in the
CPC Regulation, notably by maintaining the CPC IT tool, an essential infrastructure for
coordinated enforcement. High levels of non-compliance by online traders emerged as a
particularly pressing problem at the Programme's inception and remained so throughout its

European
Commission,
Directorate-General
for
Justice
and
Consumers,
2019.
https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/9c891010-e88c-11ea-adf7-01aa75ed71a1

Marketing of Consumer Financial Services (Directive 2002/65/EC), SWD(2020) 254 final, Brussels, 10
December 2020. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020SC0254

(Directive 2008/48/EC), SWD(2020) 253 final, Brussels, 10 December 2020. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-
content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52020SC0253
84 Civic Consulting and London Economics, Behavioural Study on Strategies to Improve the Effectiveness of
Product Recalls, European Commission, Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers, June 2021.
https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/1a695500-9e31-11ed-b508-01aa75ed71a1
85 European Commission, Commission Staff Working Document – Impact Assessment Accompanying the Proposal
for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on General Product Safety, SWD(2021) 169
final, Brussels, 30 June 2021. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52021SC0169
45
implementation. As focus group participants, comprising representatives from BEUC, ECCs,
DG JUST, Member State enforcement authorities, and legal experts, emphasised, the growing
complexity and cross-border nature of markets, especially in e-commerce, has made EU-level
infringements increasingly frequent. In this regard, EU-wide action was deemed more
appropriate than national responses alone. Annual coordinated actions by CPC authorities
targeting specific sectors proved especially relevant in addressing these widespread breaches.
Further, improvements to the mutual assistance mechanism and the development of common
enforcement guidelines strengthened cross-border enforcement capacity. The ECCs also
remained highly relevant, providing frontline support to consumers involved in cross-border
transactions and contributing to policy alignment through their role in stakeholder
consultations.
Stakeholder engagement and civil society participation were also important aspects of the
Programme’s coherence. However, as noted by the EESC, there is a need to further simplify
procedures to enhance the participation of civil society actors, improve transparency in
communication, and ensure consultations are genuine opportunities for input86. Feedback
received during the Call for Evidence in 2023 further underlined the Programme’s importance
to a wide range of stakeholders. Several respondents, including consumer organisations and
national authorities, reiterated the relevance of EU-level funding for maintaining robust
consumer protection systems and enabling knowledge-sharing. Feedback also supported better
integration of consumer needs into digital and green policies and advocated for targeted
measures to reach vulnerable groups more effectively. Respondents called for strengthening
tools like Safety Gate/RAPEX, increasing transparency in ADR and ODR mechanisms, and
improving enforcement capacity at Member State level, all aligning with the objectives and
achievements of the Programme.
4.6 Further evaluation criteria
Utility: The evidence supports the continued usefulness of the Programme’s objectives and
actions, across all four objectives. In particular, the Programme adapted to emerging challenges
faced by consumers in the context of digitalisation and globalisation. It successfully addressed
product safety concerns, benefiting vulnerable groups, including children. Tools such as Safety
Gate/RAPEX and CASPs strengthened market surveillance, contributed to improve the safety
of products placed on the market. While information sharing, awareness-raising campaigns,
and educational initiatives remained essential, they were often seen as less useful for consumer
groups due to how they were designed and implemented. Nevertheless, the growing demand
for cross-border dispute resolution and for enhanced cooperation among enforcement
authorities underlines the ongoing utility of the Programme, especially in the context of e-
commerce and AI-related safety concerns. These are increasingly being addressed 87revised
legislation￼ and initiatives funded under the Single Market Programme. The utility of the
cooperation networks was evident, for example, in the activities of the CPC and ECC networks.
Overall, the Programme was largely useful, with room for improvement in addressing
stakeholder concerns and better responding to consumer needs.
86 European Economic and Social Committee (EESC). (2024). Final evaluation of the Consumer Programme
(2014–2020). INT/1053-EESC-2024.
87 Such as the new General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR) (Regulation (EU) 2023/988), discussed further in
the case study on e-commerce in Annex VI.
46
Complementarity: The Programme was, to a great extent, complementary to other EU and
national policies and interventions. Funded actions, such as Safety Gate/RAPEX, BEUC, CPC-
Network and ECC-Net are widely recognised to be valuable and complement national
measures. Collaboration with consumer associations played a crucial role in enforcing
consumer protection rules at both EU and national levels, complementing the efforts of the
Programme by providing valuable insights and advocacy. Secondly, the Rapid Alert System
aided national authorities in implementing consumer protection regulations by providing
timely information on dangerous products. Thirdly, EU-level risk assessments and scientific
opinions informed the development of consumer policies at the Member State level. Finally,
the Programme's actions contributed to broader policy objectives such as the Europe 2020
Strategy and Sustainable Development Goals, aligning with overarching policy agendas and
enhancing its impact on societal and environmental goals.
Coordination: To assess coordination, the evaluation examined the extent to which the
Programme's actions were strategically organised to maximize their collective impact,
including by mobilising resources and harmonising measures. This was analysed in relation to
two specific objectives: improving consumer services safety and enhancing enforcement
coordination. Thanks to its centralised coordination and support mechanisms, the Programme
enabled Member States to collaborate more effectively, share best practices and pool resources
to achieve goals. The judgment criteria included the coordination of market surveillance and
enforcement actions on product safety, as well as support provided to bodies recognised by
Union legislation for the coordination of enforcement actions between Member States. By
pooling resources through platforms like Rapid Alert System, the Programme ensured a
comprehensive approach to identifying and addressing dangerous products. Harmonisation
efforts, such as EU-wide follow-ups and coordinated activities, like joint sweeps aimed to
establish consistent consumer protection standards and enforcement practices.
Equity: was assessed by examining how equitably the Programme’s effects were distributed
across regions, stakeholders, and vulnerable consumers. The evaluation revealed disparities in
Member State participation, partly due to language barriers. Efforts to improve accessibility,
such as translating Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts into all EU languages (since 2018) and
simplifying user interfaces, helped mitigate this. Despite continued regional differences,
particularly in consumer conditions across eastern and southern EU countries, progress toward
narrowing the gap was observed. The Consumer Markets Scoreboard showed that financial
status influenced consumer experiences, with financially struggling individuals reporting lower
satisfaction and less likelihood to seek redress. BEUC addressed some vulnerability issues,
such as energy poverty, payment fraud, and vulnerable borrowers, but broader attention to
vulnerable groups was limited. Children were primarily mentioned in the context of unsafe
toys, and one cosmetics risk assessment lacked adequate consideration of vulnerable users.
Overall, Programme outputs addressing vulnerable consumers were limited and concentrated
in 2017–2020, mainly via behavioural studies. In a sample of 97 funded projects, only five
explicitly targeted vulnerable groups. These findings partially align with EESC concerns,
which called for earlier and more systematic integration of vulnerable consumer needs across
all Programme objectives88.
88 European Economic and Social Committee (EESC). (2024). Final evaluation of the Consumer Programme
(2014–2020). INT/1053-EESC-2024.
47
Sustainability: The sustainability of the effects of interventions showed a mixed picture, but
on the whole most funded actions will have long lasting results. Regulatory measures supported
by the Programme have resulted in enduring structural changes. Ongoing alert services, such
as the Rapid Alert System, ensure continuous monitoring of product safety. Risk assessments
and scientific opinions remain relevant until updated due to new discoveries. Platforms like the
ODR platform provided a foundation for sustained consumer protection in online transactions.
Although a decision to discontinue the ODR platform has been made, useful elements of it such
as the database of ADR bodies will continue to be used. The impact of the Programme on
international systems was not well documented in the literature reviewed.
Acceptability was assessed based on how well the Programme’s interventions aligned with
consumer needs, higher alignment typically signals greater acceptability. The Programme
demonstrated strong alignment, as seen in BEUC’s advocacy during Dieselgate, enforcement
actions addressing penalty gaps, and the emphasis on product safety and authority cooperation.
Internally, actions were implemented with a high degree of coherence. The evaluation also
examined the Programme’s role in ensuring a consistent level of consumer protection across
the EU and EEA. Despite some coordination challenges for EU-level associations and varying
national collective redress procedures, mechanisms like Safety Gate/RAPEX and CPC joint
actions significantly contributed to harmonised enforcement and responses. To identify shifts
in perception, historical and current stakeholder and public views were compared. Public
perception was influenced by several factors, including high-profile product safety incidents
such as the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 overheating issue.
5.
WHAT ARE THE CONCLUSIONS AND LESSONS LEARNED?
5.1 Conclusions
The ex-post evaluation demonstrated that the Programme has been broadly effective with
regard to its main objective and the four specific objectives, efficient and had EU added value.
It was coherent and relevant. However, while the available indicators provide evidence of
outputs and immediate results, their fitness for tracking long-term impact remains limited.
Several indicators remained output-focused, and few were linked to baseline or target values,
making it difficult to measure changes in consumer detriment or business compliance. The
evaluation relied on triangulated qualitative data, interviews, focus groups, stakeholder
surveys, to fill these gaps, but acknowledged the limitations of these sources, particularly the
non-representative nature of the 57-survey responses and the likely selective memory bias.
Where observational data (e.g. Scoreboard trust metrics, market outcomes) were available, they
were used to reinforce the conclusions, but cannot be interpreted as directly attributable effects
due to the absence of a counterfactual.
Regarding effectiveness, the evaluation demonstrated that the Programme has been broadly
effective in achieving its objectives. Under Objective I, Safety Gate/RAPEX significantly
improved cross-border product safety coordination, reduced disparities in market surveillance,
and contributed to greater consumer confidence in cross-border shopping. The Coordinated
Activities on the Safety of Products (CASP) benefited national authorities, businesses, and
consumer organisations—particularly in recall effectiveness and informing legislation.
However, challenges remain due to unequal enforcement resources among Member States and
ongoing difficulties integrating scientific advice into regulatory processes. Maintaining
consistent standards and coordination across Member States continues to require attention.
48
Under Objective II, BEUC’s activities effectively coordinated national consumer
organisations and ensured their input into EU policymaking on digital, environmental, and
financial issues, including those affecting vulnerable consumers. In contrast, other consumer
awareness and education initiatives, despite achieving outreach metrics, had limited long-term
impact on consumer knowledge and trust, as reflected in Consumer Scoreboard data. Structural
challenges, including low integration into national curricula and declining NGO trust, hindered
broader effectiveness. Programmes like Consumer Law Ready and Consumer PRO performed
strongly, meeting targets and adapting well to online delivery during COVID-19, with reported
improvements in knowledge and behaviour. However, Consumer Champion and Consumer
Classroom underperformed due to low engagement, lack of localisation, and weak alignment
with national systems.
Under Objective III, the Programme was moderately effective in supporting consumer rights
and access to redress. Behavioural and market studies were a key strength, informing major
policy initiatives (e.g. Consumer Credit Directive, UCPD) and cited as good practice
internationally. However, their direct enforcement impact was limited. The ODR platform
reached visibility and usage targets, but its resolution rate remained extremely low (~1%),
mainly due to limited trader participation. While ADR structures benefited from grants and
training, uptake and awareness remained uneven across the EU, and key performance
indicators were not achieved. Progress was made in strengthening redress infrastructure, but
systemic and legal limitations undermined its full potential.
Under Objective IV, the Programme effectively supported cross-border enforcement through
the CPC Network and ECC-Net, though with mixed results. ECCs consistently exceeded
targets for consumer contacts and website visits, proving effective especially in countries with
fewer resources. Conversely, CPC Network performance indicators showed declining
effectiveness, notably in the timeliness and number of enforcement actions. Nonetheless,
stakeholder feedback strongly supported the added value of EU-level coordination, the CPCS
IT platform, and joint enforcement actions—particularly for tackling online infringements. The
Programme helped maintain a minimum level of enforcement capacity across Member States,
but uneven national commitment and resourcing continued to constrain outcomes.
With regards to efficiency, under Objective I, the Programme demonstrated high efficiency
by pooling resources and coordinating market surveillance activities. CASP projects were cost-
effective, enabling joint product testing at significantly lower average costs compared to
national testing. The integration of Safety Gate/RAPEX with ICSMS further enhanced
efficiency by improving information flows and avoiding duplication. However, efficiency
varied across Member States due to differences in administrative capacity and levels of national
funding.
Under Objective II, efficiency outcomes were mixed. Initiatives like Consumer Law Ready
and Consumer PRO achieved strong economies of scale and consistent training quality across
Member States, making effective use of EU coordination. In contrast, digital outreach tools
such as Consumer Champion and Consumer Classroom showed limited efficiency due to low
uptake and weak sustainability, despite considerable resource inputs. The BEUC operating
49
grant was generally considered efficient given its broad coordination role, but limited
availability of detailed cost and output data prevented a full assessment.
Under Objective III, efficiency was undermined by the low cost-effectiveness of the ODR
platform, which incurred substantial investment but resolved only a small number of disputes.
By contrast, ADR mechanisms—when used—proved more cost-efficient for consumers,
traders, and Member States. Grants supporting the digitalisation of ADR and the exchange of
best practices improved efficiency at the organisational level. However, the full potential of
these grants was not realised, as funding uptake was limited and the Programme was unable to
disburse its full allocations.
Under Objective IV, ECCs showed high efficiency by consistently meeting increasing
consumer demand without significant increases in EU funding. Their collaborative structure
enabled more resourced centres to assist others, boosting overall network performance. CPCS
activities were more variable: while joint enforcement actions and training helped reduce
fragmentation, several performance indicators declined or stagnated. This was partly due to
uneven national investment and administrative burdens. Stakeholders highlighted the
importance of Commission coordination, which was viewed as a necessary and efficient
enabler, though returns on investment varied by Member State.
On internal coherence, the Programme’s four objectives were broadly complementary and
mutually reinforcing. Actions funded under different objectives (e.g. behavioural studies under
Objective III informing campaigns under Objective II, or ADR capacity-building supporting
ECC work under Objective IV) demonstrated functional synergy. Internal coherence was
evident in the alignment between educational initiatives, enforcement coordination, and
consumer information. However, some gaps persisted, particularly in the underexploited
collaboration between ECCs and the CPC Network, and the limited integration of ECCs with
ADR entities in sharing practices and feedback mechanisms.
On external coherence, the Programme was well aligned with EU consumer law, notably
Article 169 TFEU and Article 38 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, which require a high
level of consumer protection. It supported implementation of the 2012 Consumer Agenda and
ensured coherence with EU strategies such as the Digital Single Market, the Green Deal, and
sustainability policy. Its tools and funding filled important implementation gaps in EU
consumer acquis, and complemented other EU programmes, such as the Rights, Equality and
Citizenship Programme and the LIFE Programme, without duplication.
With regards to EU added value, the Programme demonstrably enabled actions that Member
States or stakeholders could not have undertaken independently. This includes coordinated
enforcement actions through CPC and CASP, cross-border complaint handling via ECCs,
supranational behavioural research, and harmonised training platforms like Consumer Law
Ready. Interviewees and focus group participants confirmed that EU-level intervention was
essential for scale, consistency, and legitimacy, particularly in cross-border contexts, digital
markets, and areas where national capacity was weak.
On relevance, the Programme remained well aligned with consumer needs throughout the
2014–2020 period, adapting to key structural shifts such as digitalisation, the rise of online
50
platforms, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Its focus areas, product safety, redress, information,
and enforcement, addressed persistent and emerging risks. While the needs of vulnerable
consumers were not always sufficiently targeted, the Programme overall retained its policy
relevance, as confirmed by both stakeholder feedback and independent evidence (e.g.
Scoreboards, complaint data, Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts). The continued inclusion of the same
objectives in the SMP 2021–2027 reflects this enduring alignment.
5.2 Lessons learned
Throughout the evaluation several areas for improvement have been identified:
• Ensure consistent data collection and record keeping, so as to enable evaluations
of funding programmes: a consistent, systematic, comprehensive and accurate
method for recording documentation, including a list of all funded projects and a
comprehensive set of project data records required for evaluation shall be established.
Data consistency across all funded activities, including data on outputs, and results shall
be improved.
• Further develop indicators to better monitor impact: Develop outcome and impact
indicators that focus on the quality of deliverables and achieved results. Measurement
should expand beyond the simple numerical indicators and should also focus to capture
quality, e.g. the quality of BEUC’s interactions with policy makers in terms of influence
they have had, rather than just the number of meetings or presentations. For ECCs and
the CPC network, for example indicators should focus on the nature and extent of the
actions taken or results for consumers.
• Streamline campaigns, and information and education provision: Strengthen the
role of BEUC and national consumer organisations in information and education
activities to enhance the impact and reach of consumer protection initiatives across the
EU. Limit EU communication campaigns to key topics targeting consumer awareness.
Enhance consumer education through diversified communication channels and
strengthen school programmes to include consumer-related information.
• Maximise the use of behavioural studies to support policy-making and
enforcement: Continue conducting studies supporting policy-making and initiate
studies to support CPC authorities. Conduct both large and smaller studies to ensure
more flexibility and keep them supra-national to address common concerns across
Member States. Increase access to data supporting policy-making, particularly for
academic scholars and consumer organisations.
• Strengthen co-operation and communication between national actors to further
build capacity: Promote networking and collaboration and creating further synergies
by joint planning of and outreach about activities and encourage greater sharing of
knowledge, data and expertise, as well as tools and approaches. Revise how impacts of
joint working are captured. Continue with joint training initiatives to build capacities at
national level.
• Strengthen the Safety Gate/RAPEX: Continue ensuring that Safety Gate reflects the
new General Product Safety Regulation by, amongst others, enabling direct consumer
reporting of unsafe products through the Consumer Safety Gateway, facilitating closer
interaction between online marketplaces and national authorities through the Safety
Business Gateway, and improved interoperability between systems like the Information
and Communication System on Market Surveillance (ICSMS), Safety Gate, etc.
51
Continue providing opportunities for common risk assessments through CASP or other
formats, and keep the CASP framework agile and responsive to emerging risks and
unexpected situations such as COVID-19.
• Streamline support for and obligations to participate in ADRs: Further simplify the
funding application process ADR bodies, especially for smaller organisations, to reduce
administrative burden and improve funding access, and closely monitor the uptake of
the programme’s funding for ADR. Strengthen collaboration among Member States to
improve the fragmented ADR landscape across Europe and encourage sector-specific
networks of ADR bodies to collaborate, helping to alleviate administrative challenges
through shared resources, exchange of best practices and enhance information flow.
• Strengthen enforcement: Increase utilisation of the mutual assistance mechanism and
improve handling times for enforcement requests within the CPC network. Expand and
upgrade IT tools to enhance coordination and response times across Member States.
Continue investing in e-enforcement training to equip authorities for the challenges of
digital marketplaces. Strengthen cross-border enforcement efforts through joint actions
and peer-to-peer meetings. Foster increased cooperation between the CPC Network and
ECC Net. Also in the area of product safety, make use of all enforcement options that
the GPSR provides for, including for example sweeps.

title: COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT IMPACT ASSESSMENT REPORT Accompanying the documents Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), European cybersecurity certification framework, and ICT supply chain security and repealing Regulation (EU) 2019/881 (The Cybersecurity Act 2) And Proposal for a Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Directive (EU) 2022/2555 as regards simplification measures and alignment with the [Proposal for the Cybersecurity Act 2]
text:
EUROPEAN COMMISSION
Strasbourg, 20.1.2026
SWD(2026) 11 final
COMMISSION STAFF WORKING DOCUMENT

1. Introduction: Political and legal context
In today’s interconnected world, technology is the backbone of Europe’s economy, society, and sovereignty. From energy grids and hospitals to financial systems and transport networks, digital infrastructure powers every critical sector. With this transformation comes a reality which by now is widely acknowledged: cybersecurity is no longer optional. It is a political, economic, and strategic imperative.   The EU’s Preparedness Union
1
and ProtectEU
2
strategies have placed cybersecurity at the heart of Europe’s resilience agenda. These strategies recognise that persistent cybersecurity threats are not just technical challenges, but strategic risks to our democracy, economy, and way of life. The  revision of the Cybersecurity Act (CSA)  is an important contribution to reinforc e   EU preparedness and mak e the EU cybersecurity framework more eff ective and effi cient.
The  2019 CSA empowered the EU Agency for cybersecurity (ENISA) and established the European Cybersecurity Certification Framework (ECCF) to ensure trust and consistency across the internal market. At the time, the EU cybersecurity regulatory and policy framework was rather limited. However, since 2019, the cybersecurity threat landscape has significantly evolved
3
in an increasingly complex geopolitical reality and subsequently triggered a more comprehensive European regulatory and policy approach.
Cyberattacks have surged and became more sophisticated, targeting critical infrastructure, businesses, and citizens. Emerging technologies like AI and quantum computing are reshaping the tools of defence and the tactics of adversaries. The overall cost of cybercrime in the global economy was estimated at amounting to EUR 5.5 trillion in 2020
4
. Projections show that by 2031, ransomware will strike every 2 seconds down from 11 seconds today
5
.   S upply chain incidents , either caused by criminals for financial gain or State actors for disruption, espionage, disinformation or warfare   have intensified .   Nowadays , the impacts of a c yber incidents do no t just stop at stolen data or financial losses . As part of a wider hybrid strategy, t hey ripple outward, disrupting essential services, undermining trust in institutions, and affect ing our defence readiness. The aval anche effect s of cybersecurity incidents onto the real worl d can have impacts from disruption of services and economic activity , financial instability   to existential consequences , with a risk on citizens’ lives . I ncidents, such as the 2020 Solar W inds attack , which im pa cted more tha n 18 , 000 organisations worldwide incl uding EU defence actors, or the recent attack on Collins aerospace which disrupted air traffic in several EU airports, show the magnitude of impacts from single incidents
6
( see Annex 7 , Parts 2, 3 and 4 ) .
Th e   EU has expanded its legal and policy tools with the adoption of the NIS2 Directive to strengthen cyber security for critical infrastructure , complemented for physical security by its ‘sister directive’ CER, the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) to enhance the cybersecurity of products , the Cyber Solidarity Act (CSoA) to build EU-wide response capabilities, the EU Cyber Blueprint
7
to support EU-level crisis management cooperation, the 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox
8
(5G Toolbox) and the Cybersecurity Skills Academy
9
to address the growing challenge of the cybersecurity talent gap. This cybersecurity framework was complemented by sector-specific legislation, i.e. the DORA Regulation for the financial sector, NCCS for the electricity sub-sector, PART-IS for the air transport sector, a nd policy such as the EU action plan on the cybersecurity of hospitals and healthcare providers
10
(see Annex 9 ) .
With such an extensive regulatory and policy framework in place, the CSA revision comes to provide the necessary tools to make such framework more effective and efficient in delivering the expected results, provide for a stronger European dimension and leverage and fill in the remaining regulatory gaps . Given the coverage of horizontal and sector-specific legislation, and the fact that numerous businesses provide multiple services across the internal market, it is necessary to explore further ways to facilitate compliance with cybersecurity risk-management requirements arising from different regulatory instruments. Simplification measures should unlock resources to strengthen the operational cybersecurity preparedness of entities in Europe’s critical sectors. These needs were also confirmed by the responses to the public consultation (see Annex 2).
This impact assessment therefore analyses the needs for an updated and stronger legislative framework, which would entail: (1) the revision of the mandate of ENISA to adapt it to the evolving cybersecurity threat landscape and the main stakeholders’ needs; (2) the revision of the ECCF , to expand and clarify its scope and improve its governance and procedures and (3) targeted amendments to the NIS2 Directive to facilitate and align compliance across the internal market and (4) filling in regulatory gaps by setting up a framework at EU level to enhance ICT supply chain security against the non-technical risks.
For what concerns ENISA, t he European Parliament underlined that with increasing cyber threats, ENISA’s budget should be accordingly increased
11
and the motion for a resolution on European technological sovereignty and digital infrastructure
12
highlights the need to close the digital skills gap . The Council   has stressed the need for focused and clearly defined mandate, “with concrete strategic objectives” and invited the Commission to examine and strengthen ENISA’s role in supporting operational cooperation. The Council acknowledged ENISA’s role in the ECCF, underpinning trust in ICT products, services and processes”
13
.
In the ProtectEU Strategy , the Commission further stated that a harmonised approach to the security of the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) supply chain can address the current fragmentation of the internal market caused by different approaches at national level, avoid critical dependencies and de-risk ICT supply chains from high-risk suppliers, in this way securing critical infrastructure. The Economic Security Strategy also highlighted the need to make the EU’s economy and supply chain more resilient in order to promote its own competitiveness.
14
The need to address disruptions of supply chains and cyberattacks was also highlighted in the Preparedness Union Strategy and the White Paper for European Defence
15
. The co-legislators further share the sense of urgency to take enhanced actions to ensure the security of ICT supply chains. T he European Parliament called on the Commission to develop binding ICT supply chain security legislation that addresses non-technical risk and to “exclude the use of equipment and software from manufacturers based in high-risk countries, particularly China and Russia”
16
. Members of the European Parliament also called for urgent action to secure telecommunications infrastructure against undue foreign influence and security risks
17
. Digital supply chain risks are further raised in the resolution on European technological sovereignty and digital infrastructure
18
. The Council in its conclusions on the Future of Cybersecurity
19
, reiterated its commitment towards ensuring the security of the ICT supply chains and noting the relevance of non-technical risk factors
20
.
In his 2024 report on ‘ The Future of European Competitiveness’ , Mario Draghi highlighted the need to   increase   security and reduc e dependencies   as one main areas of action needed in Europe
21
.   EU companies should maintain a foothold in areas where technological sovereignty is required, such as secur ity , referring to e.g. supply chain security needs .   In particular, the report stresses the need to e nforce compliance with the EU Toolbox for 5G security within a set timeframe to ensure that sensitive elements are from trusted supplie rs , and preferably from EU providers.   The report further underscores the need to fill in the skills gap in Europe.
Finally, t he CSA revision would come to complement the Critical Entities Resilience (CER Directive) Directive which provides supply chain aspects as part of resilience measures of critical entities. Moreover, it would complement upcoming initiatives under preparation, such as the Cloud and AI Development Act (CA I DA) which aims, among others, to tackle the lack of a competitive EU-based offer of cloud computing services at sufficient scale to serve highly critical use cases or sectors; the upcoming Digital Networks Act (DNA); and the public procurement framework
22
which is currently under evaluation.
23
2. Problem definition
2.1. What is/are the problems?
There are four main problems identified in relation to the current CSA, as well as more widely in relation to the effectiveness of the current EU cybersecurity regulatory framework. The problems identified were broadly confirmed by the public consultation, the main stakeholders concerned by the respective frameworks, as well as by calls of European Parliament and Council.
2.1.1. Problem 1: Misalignment between the Union’s   cybersecurity policy   framework and stakeholders' needs in an increasingly hostile threat landscape
The CSA gives since 2019 a permanent mandate to ENISA. However, the fast-evolving cybersecurity landscape and its consequences on real-world economy (see   Annex 7 )   and growing geopolitical instability
24
led over the past 5 years to a gradual extension of ENISA’s tasks through various legislative instruments   (see Annex   9) .   Furthermore, other new needs emerged, such as an increasing demand for more effective standardisation and certification process es to facilitate cybersecurity measures and l evel the playing field or an increasing need to address the cybersecurity skills gap and take more effective actions in this regard. With the recent legislative instruments , only some of the emerging needs where ENISA can play an important role ,   were tackled , but these were rather address ed disparately, and could not achieve a reboot of the overall focus of ENISA on most pressing needs where such a European agency can play a decisive role .
O verall, whilst   Member States and industry, value ENISA and its advisory role in policy implementation, they also indicate that the agency is not able to implement its mandate efficiently and effectively
25
.
First , ENISA does not meet stakeholders’ needs in supporting efficiently cooperation among Member States and bringing a consolidated European perspective to Member States and industry on situational awareness at the EU level
26
or in reaching its full potential to support implementation of cybersecurity measures and raise the bar for cybersecurity standards . The NIS2 Directive and the CRA brought ENISA more responsibilities for holding an overview of vulnerabilities exploited across the internal market. With the ex panded regulatory framework, ENISA is expected to support more effectively Member States in their overseeing of compliance with cybersecurity requirements . The recently adopted Cyber Blueprint intends to improve coordination in cyber crisis management and to provide for clear roles and responsibilities. The CSoA further introduces measures such as the EU Cybersecurity Reserve
27
, explicitly recognising the need for additional support to address significant or large-scale cybersecurity incidents
28
. ENISA’s role as a secretariat to the CSIRTs network   and EU-CyCLONe   is limited to providing coordination , requiring reflection on additional tasks and responsibilities for contributing to developing a cooperative response to large scale cross-border cyber incidents and
29
. In 2024, the Agency further did not meet its targets to “ provide regular risk monitoring (…) and provide specific risk assessments and threat landscapes as requested by Member States” (target set on 50%, result for 2024 was 30%)
30
.   The capabilities for developing standards and technical specifications to support implementation of CRA or ECCF are insufficient and the existing processes lack agility and adaptability to the pace and extent of market needs.
Second , the   de - prioritisation of the Agency towards cybersecurity skills-related activities
31
marks a discrepancy with stakeholders’ expectation to see ENISA leading skills -related activities , such as the development of an attestation scheme for cybersecurity skills   supported by   69.43% of respondents to the public consultation ( see Annex 2 ) . This disengagement is further in contradiction with   the ever-growing   gap in the cybersecurity workforce , which continued to increase from an estimated 274,000 missing professionals in 2023 to 299,000 in 2024
32
( + 9% ) , leaving   public administrations and companies, in particular SMEs vulnerable due to lack of in-house cybersecurity expertise
33
.
Th e cybersecurity training offer is well developed by market actors such as higher education institutions, vocational education and training providers and companies
34
, and regulators and other non-market actors   are adopting strategies and recommendations to address the skills and talent shortages
35
. However , the absorption of cybersecurity-specific roles into existing non-cybersecurity related roles
36
shows the need   for lifelong learning and established ways to prove competences to ensure career evolution
37
. In this regard, the cybersecurity labour market increasingly relies on individual cybersecurity certifications : non-formal cybersecurity education through certification   allows for recognition of skills associated to cybersecurity professionals
38
, which is outpacing formal education in cybersecurity
39
.
However, European individual certifications market suffers from market failures . In particular, reputation-based individual certifications are leading to market control , where job advertisements for cybersecurity positions display an oligopoly of private actors. This market also suffers from negative externalities : whereas the labour market can, to the extent that they ease hiring processes and career evolutions, benefit from market-recognised individual certifications, they impede the growth for other, less known certifications, harming the emergence of new providers.
To address this, ENISA has been entrusted in the communication on the Cybersecurity Skills Academy with the development of a pilot project exploring the set-up of a European attestation scheme for cybersecurity skills . Despite having launched the pilots in 2024 and Member States support, materialised by ENISA’s Management Board’s call to further enhance the concept of attestation of skills
40
, the Council call to build on the Cybersecurity Skills Academy
41
, and eight Member States are taking part in the ENISA-run pilots
42
, the project is moving forward at slow pace.
Third , ENISA operates alongside a range of complementary cybersecurity EU-level actors, including CERT-EU , Europol (for cybercrime) and the European Cybersecurity Competence Centre (ECCC). While their mandates are clearly delineated, synergies to avoid fragmentation and enhance collective resilience, especially in operational response, strategic coordination and innovation programming, have not sufficiently materialised. This problem has the potential of impacting the EU’s security at a time where EU agencies and bodies in justice, home affairs, and cybersecurity play a key role, in line with the ProtectEU Strategy
43
.   Additionally, s tructured cooperation between ENISA and the ECCC is not delineated in a way as to ensure synergies between their activities and plans. Further, while a representative of ENISA is a permanent observer in meetings of the ECCC’s Governing Board under the ECCC Regulation
44
, there is no equivalent provision in the Management Board of ENISA. This renders the collaboration fragmented and inefficient.
2.1.2. Problem 2: Stalled implementation of the ECCF
The CSA (2019) set up the ECCF for the development of voluntary EU cybersecurity certification schemes   for specific ICT products, services, processes, and, through a later amendment, for managed security services, to ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity and avoid fragmentation. However, despite broad support and acknowledged value of the ECCF and the efforts harmonise cybersecurity certification across the EU, significant challenges remain.
Member States and industry have voiced their concerns over the   lengthy process of selection , elaboration and adoption of cybersecurity certification schemes, with Member States recurringly noting their “slow and challenging development” 45 . The reply to public consultation further shows dissatisfaction of over 70% of the respondents with the time required to develop and adopt the schemes. Companies are particularly critical in this regard, showing alignment between large companies (80%) and small companies (78%).
Indeed, nearly five years after the CSA’s entry into force, only one of five requested certification schemes (the European Common Criteria-based cybersecurity certification scheme (EUCC)), was adopted, while the EU Cloud Certification Scheme (EUCS) and the EU 5G Cybersecurity Certification (EU5G) have faced repeated delays of four to five years or even blockage . Meanwhile the expectation and market standard for scheme development is estimated to be 2-2,5 years
45
. This stalled implementation of ECCF triggers real-world strategic, security and business problems:
First ,   it has   hindered its capacity to support the implementation of a robust cybersecurity framework across the EU . In the current setting, it cannot effectively deliver the needed support for the compliance with the security requirements laid down by multiple Union legislative acts (eIDAS2, CRA, NIS2, CSoA).
Second , the businesses could not consider certification a viable business opportuni ty. The first Union Rolling Work Programme for Cybersecurity Certification (URWP) 49 , intended to define priorities and identify suitable ICT products, services and processes for certification, was only adopted in 2024, nearly 4 years after the date set out in the CSA 50 .   Unclarity of coverage of risks and mixing of aspects that go beyond technical risks also affected the predictability of upcoming certification schemes.
Third , while there is an expectation from both businesses and authorities for certification schemes to support compliance processes, the absence of EU-wide certification schemes forces Member States and industry to rely on national-level schemes (e.g. for cloud services; the German C5 attestation 51 or the French SecNumCloud 52 ), placing additional burden on companies, in particular SMEs, and hindering competitiveness . This lack of harmonisation, where providers of cloud services need to comply with four different sets of security requirements to provide their services in Germany, France, Spain and Netherlands, complicates cross-border procurement, limits the scalability of cybersecurity solutions, forcing providers to develop software solution per national market. It also burdens SMEs with navigating multiple non-aligned or non-standardized schemes lacking mutual recognition and limit their possibility to scale-up.
Annex 10 provides a general overview of ENISA’s key stakeholders, their expectations and unmet needs, including with regards to certification .
2.1.3. Problem 3: Complexity and diversity of the cybersecurity - rel ated policies impacting the Union’s cyber posture
The EU has horizontal and sectorial cybersecurity-relevant acts or policies, as mentioned in Section 1 . These require entities to take cybersecurity risk-management measures and demonstrate compliance with requirements as set out in Union or national transposition law.
First , w hile these requirements are designed to achieve the specific objectives of the respective acts , the public consultation evidenced that the   similar cybersecurity risk-management measures required under different legal acts, and various required ways to demonstrate compliance , therewith creates high administrative burden on businesses
46
. Many respondents indicated that multiple frameworks apply to their entities, including NIS2, GDPR, DORA, CER and the AI Act. For instance, diverging compliance requirements for security measures from various legal acts are evidenced in their deviating rules and terminology as can be seen in Guidance Materials developed by an Aviation Cybersecurity Subgroup under the NIS Cooperation Group.
47
In the Implementation Dialogue on Cybersecurity Policy held by EVP Virkkunen on 15 September 2025, stakeholders raised concerns about the cumulative burden of demonstrating compliance with multiple cybersecurity obligations set out by various Union acts. For instance, in the aviation sector reportedly it took two to three months to map the NIS2 Directive and PART-IS for an entity’s systems, raising doubts whether this is manageable for smaller companies. The stakeholders also raised that SMEs are struggling to interpret which regulations apply to them and in what manner and to ensure compliance without exhausting their resources. This fragmentation increases administrative overhead , undermining a unified EU market approach .
Second , u ndertakings and groups of undertakings which have entities falling under the jurisdiction of several Member States , are often subject to different approaches to supervision of cybersecurity requirements across Member States , which can result in   an administrative burden when   demonstrating compliance , as the entities have to invest time and resources required to map in particular national frameworks internally for compliance purposes .
48
Entities which are subject to different national cybersecurity frameworks may have to obtain several certifications, increasing costs for compliance.
Third, r egarding the scope of application of the NIS   2 Directive , certain challenges to the interpretation of provisions for both the entities and the Member States were systematically brought to the attention of the Commission services ,   notably during meetings of the NIS Cooperation Group, demonstrating the need for clarification .   For example, the definitions of healthcare providers, electricity producers and entities from the chemical sector   have been criticised as providing for a wider scope than envisaged during the preparation of the NIS2 Directive
49
.   Likewise, stakeholder feedback has highlighted disproportionate requirements arising from the application with regard to certain entities that would be subject to the Directive irrespective of their size , such as domain name system (DNS) service providers
50
.
2.1.4. Problem 4: Increasing ICT supply chains security risks
2.1.4.1.   Key concepts around ICT supply chain and interplay between technical and non-technical risks
First, understanding information and communication technology (ICT) supply chains security risks requires defining supply chains and ICT supply chains, and clarifying the notions and distinction between technical risks and non-technical risks.
Supply chains can be defined as the entire sequence of activities, organisations, resources, and technologies involved in the production and distribution of goods or services   from raw material extraction to final delivery to consumers, including disposal or reuse. Within supply chains, ICT supply chains can be identified as a network of entities, processes, and technologies involved in the development, delivery, and maintenance of ICT products and services, including provision of support during ICT products and services’ life cycle
51
. This includes hardware, software, and digital services that are critical to the functioning of modern digital infrastructure. They underpin critical infrastructures and ensure the flow and provision of essential goods and services – from transport, digital infrastructure and semiconductors to energy, food, medical supplies, banking. In a time of heightened geopolitical tension, control over ICT supply chains can be used as a tool of influence and coercion.
ICT supply chains are vulnerable to two types of risks:
· technical risks can be defined as dangers arising from failures in the components, configurations or human error within the supply chain or from disruption of the supply chain as such. Technical risks may occur accidentally or result from malicious cyber activity
52
, such as a cyber threat actor exploiting a vulnerability to compromise a network/system. Technical cybersecurity risks such as phishing or a malicious software update, can affect both software or hardware, or arise from potential deficiencies in the security processes of any stakeholder along the supply chain. Existing regulatory framework such as the current CSA, the NIS2 Directive and the CRA address such technical cybersecurity risks.
· non-technical risks could be defined as the likelihood of the supplier being subject to undue influence by a third country with the potential to cause loss or disruption of the service provided or to compromise the product manufactured by an entity or to lead to exfiltration of data, including for the purposes of espionage or revenue generation . This could be the case when the suppliers of services or products are established or controlled by entities from certain third countries, subject to laws which require entities under their jurisdiction to report information on software or hardware vulnerabilities to authorities of that third country prior to those vulnerabilities being known to have been exploited .
Second , regarding the interplay between technical and non-technical risks , these should not be regarded as being mutually exclusive. For instance, a software vulnerability (technical risk) can be weaponised where the law and governance in place in a given country leads to mandatory reporting to a public authority before a patch is available (non-technical risk).
Additionally, in practice, non-technical risks alone – i.e. with no interplay with technical risks – can result in arbitrary and possibly extraterritorial governmental access to any kind of company operations or data, including sensitive data. Non-technical risks can enable a third country to engage into economic espionage, carry out malicious cyber activities or campaigns against the Union and its Member States, or engage in irresponsible state behaviour in cyberspace, leading to potential systemic supply disruptions, in particular in the case of technological lock-in or supplier dependency. Non-technical risks can also be linked to concealed vulnerabilities or backdoors.
2.1.4.2. Destabilisation and disruption using ICT supply chains security risks
Concerns over the security of ICT supply chain are apparent from the public consultation, as well as calls from European Parliament and Council against a background where the current EU regulatory framework does not contain dedicated instruments to address non-technical risks.
Respondents elaborated on the types of threats contributing to ICT supply chain-related cybersecurity incidents, commonly citing compromise of third-party software components, insertion of malicious code during software development or updates, and poor security practices among suppliers (see Annex 2) . These replies echo the findings of ENISA. According to the Agency’s Threat Landscape 2024, supply chain attacks remain one of the seven prime threats to cybersecurity
53
. It was already in 2021 identified as the second most prevalent initial vector for infection
54
and was estimated that between 39% and 62% of organisations were affected by a third-party cyber incident
55
.
First , ICT supply chain attacks entail strong financial, economic and societal impacts. A supply chain breach, even if seemingly small, can expand through the supply chain through lateral movement, affecting interconnected suppliers, partners, and customers, triggering a chain reaction often referred to as the domino effect
56
. Supply chain compromises take the longest time to detect and contain (267 days)
57
(see Annex 7, part 1) . Their aftermath includes direct and indirect costs ranging from costs of IT support to reputational and financial damage, severely impacting end users and, in some cases, leading to business closures due to customers losing confidence in the company’s ability to protect their data
58
. In this regard, the average global direct cost of supply chain compromise as initial attack vector is estimated at USD 4.91 million
59
(see Annex 7, part 1) . The breach may further lead to rise of cybercrime against end users through ransomware attacks or data theft.
60
Figure 1: Illustration of supply chain dependency
Example of an impactful supply chain attack: The SolarWinds case
In December 2020, malicious activity that led to the compromise of the software of a major provider was exploited to access data of more than 18,000 of the providers’ customers. According to CERT-EU, t he attack was a very sophisticated supply chain attack
61
. According to a survey
62
, 85% of SolarWinds cyberattack victims said the attack had an impact ranging from ‘small’ to ‘significant’. One of the most notable impacts was   its financial fallout. On average globally, the attack cost companies 11% of their annual revenue. These financial costs include incident response and remediation, system upgrades, legal and regulatory fines, customer notification and support, operational disruption and downtime, in addition to a wide range of indirect and long-term costs such as reputational damage and loss of trust, loss of intellectual property and sensitive data, insurance premium increases, litigation and legal fees, or loss of competitive advantage.
Beyond impacts for supply chain actors and possible direct impacts on public entities, ICT supply chains attacks can lead to indirect impact for governments, with a need to step in to protect national supply chains (see further in Annex 7, parts 2 and 3) .
An example of state-level impact of ICT supply chain attacks: the Jaguar Land Rover case
In September 2025, a major cyberattack forced Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) to halt production across its factories in the UK, China, Slovakia, and India, after its IT systems were effectively disabled by the attack. As a consequence, the manufacturer is forced to suspend production for weeks , crippling the automotive manufacturing sector, disrupting global supply chains, and threatening SMEs and thousands of jobs
63
, 30,000 people being directly employed at the company's UK plants and 100,000 working for firms in the supply chain
64
. The incident triggered a 1.5 billion pounds loan guarantee from the British government to protect affected jobs.
Second , weakening of the ICT supply chain entails risks to European economic security
65
. The exposure to non-technical risks of the supply chain for ICT products has been internationally recognised in the context of efforts to ensure economic resilience and security, with a commitment to ensuring that “sensitive technologies that are crucial for national security or could threaten international peace and security are appropriately controlled (…)”
66
. Further, the Cybersecurity Working Group of the G7 agreed that in order to address Internet of things (IoT) cybersecurity in its entirety, both technical and non-technical risks , including the overall risk of influence of an IoT product vendor by a third country, should be taken into account.
67
At the global level , several international partners have taken or are planning action in this field to strengthen supply chain security, with the UK and Canada providing for legal safeguards to security of the telecommunication infrastructure, including from high-risk suppliers, the US and Australia having even broader approach.
The EU’s 2023 Economic Security Strategy also recognised as a priority the promotion of our own competitiveness by making our economy and supply chains more resilient bolstering innovation and industrial capacity .
68
Third , ICT supply chain is a vector for disruption in a geopolitically instable world.   Among non-technical risks, state-backed cyber campaigns targeting critical infrastructure have reached unprecedented levels of scale and sophistication. Hostile foreign states and state-sponsored actors seek to infiltrate and disrupt the EU’s critical infrastructure and supply chains, not merely for intelligence gathering, but to establish latent control and disruption capabilities . At the same time, state-nexus threat actors have always been increasingly adept at understanding the environments they infiltrate
69
. They strategically deploy tools to conduct thorough reconnaissance and prevent the detection and analysis of their implants by employing robust anti-forensic measures
70
. Predominantly, actors associated with Russia, Iran and North Korea continue to deploy disruptive malware
71
. These activities oftentimes have the aim of espionage, i.e. to gather political, military and economic intelligence; or strategic disruption, i.e. to position oneself in critical infrastructure for a possible disruption of essential service in the future, for instance in the case of a conflict.
Example of a state using ICT supply chains as a means of disruption
The Chinese state-sponsored ‘ Salt Typhoon’ campaign
72
, whereby the threat actor gained access to targets through a partner or a vendor or, targeted telecommunications entities around the world with the potential for major cascading effects including on public safety and Union security. Chinese state-sponsored actor ‘ UNC5221 ’ compromised dozens of organisations worldwide by targeting vulnerabilities in Ivanti IT security products. These activities should be placed in the context of Chinese companies owning or having stakes in a wide range of European critical infrastructure, including ports, airports, customs, electricity companies, wind and solar farms and telecommunication, as well as the strategic aim of China to secure its access to EU markets and technologies.
73

2.2.1. Driver 1 – Increasingly hostile and unpredictable threat landscape in a rapidly evolving technological environment (horizontal driver) .
The threat landscape, as well as the security and defence prerequisites for Europe, have changed significantly since 2019
74
. These realities triggered a renewed need for a stronger and more strategic role of ENISA   as well as for a stronger leveraging position of the EU globally, while building own capabilities in a more sustainable manner in a number of areas, such as vulnerability disclosure , where there are current dependencies of common vulnerabilities and exposure services on one third country government steer and funding, as well as   management or standardisation.   Russia is waging a hybrid campaign against the EU and its Member States , using cyberattacks as one tool; China is seeking to advance its geopolitical agenda through control of supply chains , exploitation of software vulnerabilities and economic dependencies: these trends demand increased operational cooperation , a t the forefront of which enhanced   shared situational awareness   among Member States , EU entities (see Annex 10 ) . In addition, after Brexit, the EU is not part of the main intelligence network (the Five Eyes alliance between the US, CAN, UK, NZ and AU).
Furthermore, technical evolutions such as AI are giving both cyber criminals and non-state and state actors a whole new set of capabilities, reducing the time for mass exploitation of vulnerabilities from weeks or months to a matter of days.   Emerging technologies   are further considered by cybersecurity professionals to be the biggest challenge to come in the EU in the next two years
75
. The World Economic Forum (WEF) acknowledges that skills in operating AI and defending against it are becoming increasingly important , and c ompanies must commit to equipping their workforce and   educational curricula should   “ mirror the dynamic of   cyberthreat landscape and emerging technologies ”
76
.   While ENISA is uniquely placed to facilitate this shared awareness , the Agency is currently not appropriately equipped to enhance its support in this area.
The evolution of geopolitical landscape considerably affected the ECCF . According to the 2024 Evaluation Report, 49% of stakeholders considered that geopolitical factors impacted the ECCF negatively or highly negatively. In particular, the politicisation of the discussion related to the structure of the cloud computing market in Europe (heavily dominated by non-EU players) impacted the development of EUCS. Triggering factors included international developments such as the adoption of the US Cloud Act and the related privacy concerns. Several other EU initiatives, such as the European strategy for data
77
, and the subsequently adopted the Data Act and the Data Governance Act, reflected the increasing concern about the protection against unlawful access to data stemming from third-country legislations that have extra-territorial effects in conflict with EU laws.
In this context, the uncertainty related to the scope of the ECCF as to the types of risks covered ( see Driver 8) became prominent. It created political bottlenecks in the preparation of candidate schemes due to disagreements between Member States. It has also triggered criticism regarding the lack of transparency of the framework and insufficient stakeholder involvement
78
and that the certification would go against the security interests of the EU by certifying hyperscalers, and creating overdependency on non-EU provider.
2.2.2. Driver 2 – Regulatory gaps (horizontal driver)
Since the adoption of the CSA in 2019, the EU cybersecurity regulatory landscape evolved considerably (see Section 1) .
Each of the instruments is either filling regulatory gaps or resetting focus of policy objectives and compliance facilitation. Main regulatory gaps were identified and are further detailed in Annex 9 .
